guides.title: Acrylic, enamel and oil products compared
guides.summary: Acrylics thin with water and dry fast; enamels and oils need a spirit thinner, stay workable longer and lift each other.
body: Acrylics are water based. They thin and clean up with water and dry in seconds to minutes. Most hobby paint, washes and one-coat paints are acrylic.

Enamels thin with a spirit thinner, such as odourless white spirit. Never mix water into them. They stay workable for hours, so you can blend, move or wipe them off completely, which suits washes, streaks and mud.
Oil paints also thin with white spirit and take the longest to dry, often a day or more. That long working time is what makes them good for smooth blends, filters and washes.
Spirit thinner softens and lifts enamels and oils already on the model, but it does not touch dry acrylic. So acrylic effects can go on last, over dry enamel or oil work, without disturbing it.
Acrylic over enamel dries almost at once, so thin it a little and build it up gradually rather than trying to blend it.
Before enamel or oil goes over acrylic, let the acrylic dry fully and give it a coat of gloss varnish. The solvent then moves over the surface instead of soaking in or staining.
Glossy enamel effects read as wet, matt ones as dry. Use the same type of product on the model and its base so the colours and finish match.

guides.title: Cleaning an airbrush between colours
guides.summary: Flush water and cleaner through after each colour and back bubble the cup so paint never dries inside.
body: Tip out leftover paint into a waste pot or remove it with a pipette, then wipe the cup with an old brush or paper towel. Avoid blowing leftovers out through the nozzle, which pushes flakes into the tip.
Add water to the cup. A small spray bottle of water knocks most paint loose quickly and saves cleaner. Spray or tip it out into a cleaning pot.

Back bubble: cover the nozzle with a finger, cloth or soft sponge and pull the trigger so air pushes back through the cup. Tip it out. Repeat two or three times until it comes out clean. If you mix paint by back bubbling, always clean that way too.

If it is still dirty, add airbrush cleaner, scrub the bottom of the cup with an old brush, bubble it, then spray clean water through. Wherever paint went, cleaner goes; wherever cleaner went, water goes.
After primer or varnish, also work a few drops of strong isopropyl alcohol through so nothing dries into a hard film. A mild cleaner is gentler on seals than strong solvents for routine use.

Pale pigments like white can settle in the cup. Swab the needle in the cup with a cotton bud soaked in cleaner before pulling it out, then swab the cup. Paint drying on the needle tip while you work wipes off with a fingertip or soft brush; a light film of needle lubricant slows it down.

Before the next colour, spray plain water onto card. It should mist evenly with no spitting. If it still sputters, check paint thickness, pressure, needle seating and that the nozzle cap is fully tight: a loose cap sends bubbles into the cup.
Doing this between every colour and at the end of each session avoids most clogs and saves full strip downs. A quick rinse is enough between similar colours; dark to white needs a full clean.

guides.title: Deep cleaning an airbrush
guides.summary: Strip the airbrush down, soak and scrub the parts, clear the nozzle, then oil and rebuild it.
body: Strip it down when the spray pulses, spits or stops while air still comes out, or bubbles push back into the cup, and a normal flush has not fixed it. Do not strip it every session; that wastes time and wears the parts.

Unplug the hose. Work over a white paper towel, never over an open sink, and lay parts down in the order they came off. You need cleaner, water, an old toothbrush, pipe cleaners or interdental brushes, a needle tool and a silicone free airbrush lubricant.

Take the needle out first so it cannot be bent while you work. Loosen the chuck and draw it straight out by its blunt end. Wipe it with cleaner, always pulling towards the tip. Then unscrew the caps and nozzle; some nozzles have a tiny tip that unscrews from a housing and is very easy to lose.

Soak only the bare metal nozzle and cap parts in cleaner for a few minutes, keeping seals and plastic out. Scrub the cup, push pipe cleaners through the body, and clear the small air hole beside the paint hole. Move a cleaning tool from cleaner areas into dirtier ones, never back.

The nozzle causes most clogs. Clear it with a reamer or needle tool, twisting gently; forcing it can split the soft metal. Hold it to the light to check the hole is a perfect circle. A split or uneven opening needs replacing, because no cleaning will fix it.
Check the needle by dragging it backwards across paper while twisting. If it catches, the tip is bent or hooked; replace it or gently straighten it.

Let every part dry fully. Put a tiny dot of lubricant on each thread and a thin smear on the needle. Rebuild in reverse order, finger tight only. Hold the trigger down while sliding the needle in until it stops on its own, no further, then test with water on card.

Strong solvents perish seals, so stick to airbrush cleaner, water and a little isopropyl alcohol. Practise taking it apart so you know every piece. Between sessions, leave a little cleaner in the capped cup and empty it before use.

guides.title: Thinning paint for the airbrush
guides.summary: Thin paint with airbrush thinner to about the consistency of milk, and test on paper before the model.
body: Ordinary brush paint is far too thick to spray and will clog the nozzle. Paints sold ready to spray are usually fine for base coats but spray better a little thinner for blending. Never put texture paste through an airbrush.

Mix in a small dish and move it to the cup with a dropper, which keeps lumps out of the nozzle. For quick jobs, put thinner in the cup first, then paint, and back bubble gently at low pressure. Avoid stirring with a brush, as one loose bristle can block the nozzle. Do not overfill the cup.

Aim for whole to semi skimmed milk with no lumps: pull a little up the side of the dish and it should run straight back down. Equal parts is a fair start for dropper paints; thick pot paints may need two or three parts thinner. Go thinner, like ink, for detail and small nozzles. Test, as there is no fixed ratio.

Use airbrush thinner, or distilled water rather than hard tap water, which leaves deposits. Add a little flow improver or retarder if paint keeps drying on the needle tip. Never use household glass cleaner. Solvent-based paints need their own matching thinner. Mix fresh each session; old, half dried paint sprays badly.

Speckled, grainy or spattering spray means the paint is too thick or the pressure too low: add thinner a few drops at a time. Spidery, web-like runs mean it is too thin, too close or the pressure too high: add paint. Blocky, one-pass coverage means it is too thick for a smooth fade.

Match thickness to the job. Thicker paint for base coats on big models sprays around 25 to 30 psi from further away. Thinner paint for fine work sprays around 15 psi, close in. About 20 psi is a good everyday setting to learn at. If paint will not flow, thin it more rather than turning the pressure up.
Most spraying problems come down to three things: pressure, distance from the model and the paint to thinner ratio. Change one at a time and test on paper or your hand.

Light colours over dark often speckle. Inks spray very smoothly, so a white ink or a little ink mixed into the colour helps for highlights over black. Metallics are the opposite: shake them well and thin only slightly, about ten parts paint to one of thinner.

guides.title: Priming with an airbrush
guides.summary: Spray thinned primer in short, light passes at around 18 to 20 psi, building two thin satin coats.
body: Use a primer made for the airbrush and a nozzle of 0.3 mm or larger; smaller ones clog with primer. Wash the models first to remove release agent, and fix them in a holder so both hands are free. Humidity changes how each primer behaves, so it is worth trying a few.

Always put a few drops of thinner in the cup before the primer, so it wets the nozzle and primer cannot dry there first. Mix about three or four drops of primer to one of thinner. To check, drag a little up the cup wall: a droplet that forms and slowly slides down is right; one that runs is too thin.

Spray in short, controlled bursts at around 18 to 20 psi, test on paper towel first, and sweep across the model without pausing on one spot. Turn it as you go so every side and the underside get covered. Do not pull the trigger fully back and hose it. Large models can take thicker primer and more pressure.
The surface should look satin as it goes on. If it looks wet and glossy you are flooding the detail: stop, let it dry, and go lighter.

Apply two thin coats, letting the first dry for a few minutes, and let it dry fully, ideally for an hour, before painting. Over black, white primer looks grey at first and dries duller than it looks wet. White primer is chalky and clogs more, so a slightly higher pressure, around 35 to 40 psi, helps.
When priming a batch, rinse the cup every few minutes. Primer drying round the rim makes flakes that clog the nozzle. Clean with a few extra drops of isopropyl alcohol.

Solvent-based surface primers spray thin, smooth and hard, sand within about half an hour and rarely clog. Thin them only with their own thinner, clean with lacquer thinner, and wear a respirator with good extraction.

guides.title: Airbrush safety and ventilation
guides.summary: Wear a respirator mask rated for paint particles, ventilate the room, and take most care with cleaners and solvents.
body: Airbrushing puts a fine mist of paint in the air, even with water-based paints. A non-toxic label means it will not poison you if swallowed, not that it is safe to breathe as a spray.

Wear a respirator with filters rated for paint particles every time you spray. Solvent paints, primers and varnishes also need activated carbon filters; a simple dust mask does nothing against fumes. Check the seal each time you put it on, as a loose fit lets air go round the filters.
Filters wear out. With light use a set can last a few years; heavy use wears them much faster. Follow the maker's guidance on when to replace them.

Spray into a booth if you can. One with a hose venting outside pulls hardest; a filter booth can sit anywhere. Otherwise ventilate well, but an open window alone is not enough, and a fan only helps if it pushes air outside.

Airbrush cleaners, strippers, varnishes, enamels and solvent-based primers are harsher than acrylic paint. Keep the mask on while cleaning; many people take it off to clean, which is the wrong way round. Flush into a cleaning pot, wear gloves with strong cleaners if you like, and keep lids on.

Spray aerosol cans outdoors or with strong extraction, not indoors, as many hobby booths are not built to catch their solvent. Keep heat, including a hair dryer, away from fresh aerosol primer until the fumes have cleared.
Lower pressure, under about 30 psi for most work, puts less mist in the air. Even water based paint can irritate your airways, so do not skip the mask for short jobs.
Read the label or safety sheet for everything you spray, decide on a safety level you are comfortable with, and set the room up before you start.

guides.title: Airbrush and compressor setup
guides.summary: A gravity fed, dual action airbrush and a compressor with a tank and regulator cover most miniature work.
body: Choose a dual action airbrush: pressing the trigger down releases air, pulling it back adds paint, and the further back, the more paint. A rear stop screw that limits the pull helps while learning. A light body tires your hand less over long sessions.

Gravity fed, with the cup on top, suits the small amounts of paint used on miniatures and needs less pressure. A nozzle of about 0.3 to 0.4 mm handles both priming and detail; smaller gives finer lines but clogs more and needs perfect thinning.

Learn on a low cost airbrush if you like: you will make cleaning mistakes, and an entry level one sprays well. Others prefer a better one from the start, as a poor one causes constant trouble. Either way, pick one whose spare needles, nozzles and seals are easy to get. Spend the extra on the compressor.

The compressor must have a pressure regulator and a moisture trap. A tank lets the motor fill it and rest, so it runs quieter, steadier and lasts longer. Tiny battery or USB units and cans of compressed air cannot hold steady pressure and spatter. Check the hose thread fits your airbrush; adapters are cheap.

Set pressure on the regulator. About 1.5 to 2 bar, roughly 20 to 30 psi, suits most work. Go to 15 to 20 for close detail and glazes, and up to about 40 for priming and big areas. Quick check: spray air at a fingertip; a small dimple is fine, a flattened fingertip is too much. Empty the water trap now and then.
For less noise, stand the compressor on a folded towel or foam, away from walls and desk legs. Never wrap it up, as it will overheat. Switch tank compressors off at the wall when done.

Keep nearby: airbrush thinner, airbrush cleaner, a spray bottle of water, a large cup for waste and a cleaning pot to rest the airbrush in. A quick release connector and thread seal tape for leaky joints help. Keep the needle cap on, as a bent tip ruins the spray.
Before a session, clear dust from the area, put down something absorbent to spray over, and wear a respirator rated for paint particles.

guides.title: Converting a whole force to a theme
guides.summary: Set a few shared build rules and themed parts so a converted, mixed collection still reads as one force.
body: Before building, decide a short list of features every model will share, such as one helmet or hood style for the rank and file. Write the rules down, especially if more than one person is building.
Mark rank with extras that build up: plain troops first, then tabards, then pelts, banners and fancier helmets for leaders.
Heads do the most work, so use only heads you really like. Hoods suit fisher folk, wild beards suit tribal warriors, full-face helmets make a grim, faceless force.

To make distinct groups cheaply, use a few kits from the same range that share joints. Vary armour, weapons and shields to fit how each group lives: rough tunics and tools, padded jackets, or mail and surcoats.
Add small repeated touches across the whole force, such as extra rivets, spikes, bells, trophies or long paper seals.
For a model from another range, add bits from your own kits and clean any mould lines on added plastic parts. Paint it in the same palette, down to small details like flame colour.
Finish every base with the same signature features, such as mossy rocks, glowing fungi or carved stones, so the collection ties together.

guides.title: Glue and tools for basing
guides.summary: Use white PVA glue for sand and ground cover, super glue or epoxy for firmer bonds, and a spatula for texture paste.
body: White PVA glue is the main basing glue. It suits sand, grit, cork, moss and loose cover, dries clear and stays slightly flexible. Thin it a drop of water at a time until it flows off the brush without running, about like melted ice cream.

Three ways to add grit: brush on glue and dip the base in sand; pile loose grit on and drip very thin glue beside it so it soaks in; or mix glue and grit into a paste and spread it. Build deep texture in layers, each one dry first, and mix grit sizes.

Thin super glue is quick for fixing rocks on single bases: put a drop on scrap and apply small dabs with a pin. Gel super glue holds tufts firmly on models that get handled, but super glue can leave a white bloom round tufts and moss; PVA avoids it.

Use two-part epoxy for heavy rocks, large resin pieces and anything that must never come off. Plastic cement only works on styrene, such as plastic card and sprue. Hot glue and UV glue are fine for holding a part in place, but back them up with a stronger glue.
Spread texture paste with a small spatula instead of a brush. It loads more easily and spares your brushes. Two different pastes give more believable ground than one.

Lock texture in before heavy drybrushing: mist with watered PVA, or brush gloss varnish over dry sand and paste, then prime. If sand still rubs off, drip a stronger glue onto it from the brush without touching the surface. Finish with matt varnish to hide the glue's sheen.
Base and paint the model separately where you can. If you must prime a base with a painted model already on it, wrap the model in kitchen foil and brush the primer on carefully.

Do not dry PVA and sand with a hair dryer; the heat can crack the sand or warp the model. Air drying clay shrinks as it cures and can curl off a thin base: use a thick base, give it a week, and fill any gaps with putty.

guides.title: Batch building models
guides.summary: Build the same model several times in a row, one step at a time across all of them, to finish a unit faster.
body: Repeating one build several times is much faster than switching between different models. Start a new army with the simple, common models; they teach you the kit before the big centrepieces.

Open every frame at once. Clip the same part from all of them, clean them all, then glue them all, step by step. Clip with the flat side of the cutters towards the part, and hold it on the last cut so it does not fly off.
Keep the parts for each model in a separate tray, cup or pile on the instructions so options do not get mixed up. This works best in one sitting.
For large, complicated models, work piece by piece instead: clip, clean and glue one part, then the next. It is slower, but you can stop any time because unused parts stay on the frame.
For variety in a squad of doubled poses, build the first set as shown, then move each pair of arms to a different body for the second set. Glue the weapon arm first, then slide the other into place.
Plan which models will be painted in sub-assemblies before you start, so you leave the same parts off every one. Crews can go on temporary bases with a dot of super glue.

Good cutters, a sanding stick and the right glue save seconds per part, which adds up across a large batch. Even so, cleaning and building a box can take days of hobby time, so plan it as its own stage.

guides.title: Perfectionism and fear of ruining a model
guides.summary: Accept imperfect results and finish models, because finishing and moving on improves you faster than polishing.
body: Being a little unhappy with a finished model is normal. You learn while painting it, so by the end it already looks slightly behind your skill.
Close up, every model shows faults. At arm's length, where it is usually seen, most of them disappear. Judge it from there.
If more tidying risks spoiling the work, stop and call it done. A long break from a model you are stuck on is fine too; come back when you want to.

Extra hours on one model teach less than finishing it, looking at what went wrong, asking for feedback and starting the next one. Set one realistic goal per model rather than trying to master everything on it.
Avoid stripping and redoing old models again and again. You never finish anything, and waiting for stripper can become a reason not to paint at all. Keep older work as a record of progress.
Afraid to ruin a special model? Paint can be stripped, and the model you are saving will feel less special once something new arrives. Saving it forever just means never starting.

Compare yourself with your own earlier work, not with expert painters, and take a break from social media if constant comparison wears you down. Writing your name and the date under each base makes progress easy to see. If a model seems to go backwards, find which technique slipped and practise just that.

Watch for all-or-nothing thinking, putting off starting and harsh self-talk, and name the fear behind them. If perfectionism stops you enjoying the hobby, or life more widely, talking to painters who understand or to a therapist can help.

guides.title: Brush care and cleaning
guides.summary: Keep paint off the metal collar, rinse often, never leave brushes standing in water, and clean them with brush soap.
body: Paint that dries in the metal collar forces the bristles apart and ruins the point. Acrylic does not soften again once dry. A tip can be fixed; roots cannot. Thin washes and one-coat paints wick up fastest, so keep your best brush away from them.

Load only the front half of the bristles, drawing the brush at a low angle through the paint. Drag the brush rather than pushing it, and do not jab it into tight gaps, as both splay the bristles and force paint up.

Rinse every few minutes and each time you put the brush down, and keep a separate water pot for metallics so flakes do not end up in other colours. Clean by pulling the bristles upward against the side of the pot. Never leave a brush standing bristles down in the water.

After a session, lather with brush soap in cool or lukewarm water, never hot, which softens the glue holding the hairs. Work it in gently toward the collar, rinse until the lather shows no colour, and reshape the tip. Dry brushes flat, then keep them flat or bristles up, with caps on for travel.

When grime builds up near the collar, deep clean: dip in isopropyl alcohol, drag across a paper towel, then soap and rinse. For a regular painter that is about monthly. Brush restorer works by soaking just the bristles for 10 to 30 minutes, handle out, but check it suits synthetic hair first.
Now and then leave soap in the brush overnight with the tip shaped, and wash it out the next day. This can bring back a brush that looks ruined. Dried PVA softens with a soak in water and soap.

A hooked synthetic tip often springs back if you dip just the bristles in water off the boil for a moment, shape the point, then rinse cool. Trim stray hairs with a sharp blade rather than pulling them. If a split tip will not recover, retire it to drybrushing, glue and rough jobs.

Point the brush by rolling it on the palette or a damp tissue, not in your mouth, as some pigments are harmful to swallow. Before using masking fluid, dip the brush in liquid soap and wash it straight after.

guides.title: Brushing a coat over spray primer
guides.summary: Give sprayed colour one brushed coat of the matching paint so later touch-ups do not show.
body: A sprayed colour and the same colour from a pot dry with a different sheen and texture. If you tidy mistakes later with the pot colour, the patches show against the sprayed areas.
After a coloured primer or spray, brush one or two thin coats of the matching paint over the main areas. Every later touch-up then blends in.
Keep that same pot as the clean-up colour for the rest of the model. With a brushed base under everything, any slip can be painted back over invisibly.
For black, dust the primer on lightly so detail stays crisp, then brush thin coats of black paint over the whole model. Over a grey primer, plan on two thin coats.

On big models, black spray often misses spots or dries with uneven sheen, and drybrushing shows every difference. Thin a matt black until inky and brush one coat over everything with a large brush first.

A brushed coat also helps washes. Fill any recesses the spray missed, then brush a thin coat of the main colour over the area and let it dry fully. The wash flows evenly instead of catching on a dusty spray finish. For a red that covers poorly, fill gaps with a bright orange first.
If you expect to touch up, pick a spray that has a matching brush paint. General purpose sprays rarely match any pot, so fixes over them stand out.

guides.title: Priming by brush
guides.summary: With nowhere to spray, brush on thin coats of primer with a soft brush, dabbing it into recesses and leaving it once it skins.
body: An undercoat gives later paint something to grip, and it does not have to come from a spray. Always prime, even if the plastic is already the right colour. Wash parts in lukewarm soapy water first; leftover release agent makes primer bead and pool.

Bottled primer separates, so shake it well, then let it settle a moment so the bubbles rise. Pour a little into a dish or cap. Use it neat, or add only a tiny drop of water so it flows off the brush: too thick blobs and traps bubbles, too runny may not grip.

Use a large, soft brush: a round, a mop or even a soft make-up brush. Stiff bristles whip up bubbles, and a small pointed brush is slow and hard to load. Load it so the bristles stay in shape without the belly bulging.

Dab and poke primer into every recess so no air gets trapped, then roll the brush to spread any pools, using light pressure. Work in sections on large models. Once a film starts to form, leave it alone; brushing on makes it bumpy and streaky.

Let it dry 10 to 30 minutes, until fully matt. Add a second coat only where it is patchy, and stop before detail softens. If it pools or bubbles before skinning, wipe it off with a damp brush and redo it; once skinned, let it dry before fixing anything.

Without primer, a thinned high-coverage base paint in the model's main colour can stand in: a couple of drops of paint with about a brushful of water, brushed on with an old brush in two or three coats. The whole model is then that colour, so any slip can be tidied with the same paint.

Artist's gesso is a cheap, tough brush-on primer, but it is thick: thin it with water and keep it out of fine detail. Brushed matt varnish can work as a clear primer in a pinch, though it does not even out the colour.
For touch-ups, spray primer close against the inside wall of a tall cup until it pools at the bottom, then brush it on. Wear a mask, as this throws up a lot of mist.

guides.title: Which brush size to use
guides.summary: Use the biggest brush that still keeps a sharp point, as it holds more paint, stays wet longer and works faster.
body: The point matters more than the size. A large brush with a good tip can still paint fine detail, so judge a brush by its tip, not its number.
A bigger brush has a larger belly, so it holds more paint, dries on the tip less and sends you back to the palette less often. This helps most with washes and glazes.

One smooth stroke from a larger brush covers a cloak panel that would take a dozen dabs with a small one. Fewer strokes mean less chance of dragging half dry paint. On big flat panels, such as vehicle hulls, a wide flat brush is faster still.

As a guide: size 2 or 3 for a normal infantry figure, 3 or 4 for larger figures, and 4 to 6 for big monsters. Sizes vary between makers, so treat the numbers loosely. Only drop to a small brush to reach into tight corners.
Small brushes run dry quickly. On large areas the paint dries before you finish, and blending turns into patchy layering.

If control feels poor, the brush is usually overloaded rather than too big. Wipe the excess on the palette edge or a tissue before touching the model. Use the side of the bristles for broad strokes and blending, and the very tip for lines and detail.
For eyes, a size 0 is a good middle ground: big enough not to dry out, small enough not to flood the socket. With anything tinier, go straight from palette to model without pausing.
A worn brush with a firm tip can still do the tiniest dots and edges for a while before you retire it. A floppy, unpredictable tip is the one to replace.

guides.title: Old brushes for rough jobs
guides.summary: Keep worn brushes for drybrushing, stippling, glue and texture paste so your good brushes keep their point.
body: Do not throw a brush away the moment its tip goes. When it will not hold a point, the hairs fork, or dried paint will not come out, move it down to jobs that would wreck a good one, and keep each brush to its job.

Drybrushing wears bristles fast. A slightly worn small brush suits controlled overbrushing on edges; a worn medium one gives a bolder drybrush than a soft one. Soft make-up brushes are a cheap alternative. Make sure the brush is fully dry before loading it.

Stippling splays tips fast. Use synthetic, old or soft make-up style brushes for it, and if you must stipple with a good brush, do it gently. Trimming an old brush flat across the tip makes a useful stippling brush.

Use old brushes to spread PVA, spoon texture paste or snow, push pigment around and jab primer into crevices. A cheap flat covers terrain fast; a small round reaches round feet. Never put super glue on bristles: apply it with the handle end instead.

Solvents for enamels and oils are hard on hair, especially natural hair, so keep old synthetics for that work and for mixing harsh liquids. An old brush is also handy for moving paint or varnish from a pot to the palette. Do not stir clean pots with dirty bristles.
The handle is a tool too. Shape epoxy putty with the rounded end, sharpen it in a pencil sharpener to clear a clogged nozzle, or put a blob of sticky tack on it to hold tiny parts.
Label or mark rough brushes, especially the glue brush, so they do not creep back into detail work.
Two cheap extras save good brushes too: a silicone colour shaper smooths damp putty and scoops and mixes paint, and a large soft make-up brush dusts finished models.

guides.title: Building a gaming board
guides.summary: Build a light, tough board from foam tiles on wood, toughened with filler and textured with sand and grit.
body: Start with a solid flat board such as an old table top or a sheet of wood, and glue polystyrene foam tiles on top. The foam keeps it light and lets you cut different levels.

Lay out buildings and features on the foam and mark their outlines with a pen. Then cut the foam into levels, such as a sunken road or a raised bank, test fitting as you go. Textured plastic sheet, such as cobbles, can cover roads and yards.
Glue the buildings down, then spread household filler over the open ground. It adds texture and makes the soft foam much tougher.

Once dry, brush on watered down PVA glue and scatter different grades of sand, grit and small stones so the ground is not one even texture. For rounded banks, repeat glue and sand in two or three layers, letting each dry.
When everything is dry, spray prime the whole board, then drybrush, wash, and finish with tufts and powders.

For a board that packs away, cut rigid insulation foam about 5 cm thick into panels and hinge them with tape on both faces so they fold up zig-zag. Never lean on foam; use clamped plywood or MDF if you need to.
Square tiles about 30 cm across can be swapped and turned for many layouts; around 18 cover a 90 by 180 cm table. Leave open ground on each so several figures can stand there.
For the quickest board, lay a fleece cloth over foam offcuts or books to make rolling hills. A fake fur fabric trimmed to grass height and airbrushed dark to light makes a convincing grass mat.
keywords: how to make a gaming table

guides.title: Building ruined walls and floors
guides.summary: Plan where walls broke, show what they were made of, and pile rubble where it would fall, using offcuts for debris.
body: Plan the damage. Walls break from the top down and around doors and windows, and corners stand tallest. Draw the break line on the wall before you cut.
Cut walls from foam board, thick card or plastic card. On plastic kit walls, cut roughly with clippers and a blade, then snap off small bits with pliers so the edge looks shattered, not sliced.
Show what the wall is made of. Expose bricks or stones along the break, add a few loose bricks cut from foam or card, and poke wire rebar out of concrete edges.
Floors: use card or plastic sheet with planks or tiles scored in. Break holes with ragged edges and let joists stick out underneath. A floor that sags or hangs at an angle reads well.
Rubble: pile it where things fell, against the foot of walls and under holes. Mix large chunks, mid pieces and fine sand and grit, and fix it with thinned white glue.
Kit offcuts make good debris: spare sprue, broken parts, leftover pillars and doors. Cut them up so their original shape is not obvious.
Mount the ruin on a thin, sturdy base such as hardboard or plastic sheet with bevelled edges. For gaming, keep floors flat and wide enough for models to stand on.
Paint it dark first and drybrush lighter, then add soot around holes and dust over everything at the end.

guides.title: Building your first plastic kit
guides.summary: Read the instructions, clip parts with care, scrape mould lines and glue with a light touch of plastic glue.
body: Read the instructions before cutting anything. Many kits have head or weapon options, so decide what you want first. Follow the steps in order and tick each one off in pencil, so you can stop and pick up again later.

Before each stage, set aside only the frames that stage uses, and sort parts into small piles by sub-assembly. Work on a cloth over a hard, light surface so dropped parts do not bounce away; avoid working over carpet. If a step seems wrong, re-read it; it is usually a missed detail.
Clip each part a short way from the model, with the flat face of the cutters towards the part, and a hand under it so it does not fly off.

Trim the leftover nub with a sharp hobby knife. Let the blade do the work and keep your fingers out of its path. Scrape mould lines off with the back edge of the blade; they are hard to see now but obvious once painted.

Dry fit parts before gluing. Push fit pegs and lugs often hold parts apart. Trim about a third off a peg or nick the rim of its hole, or cut the lugs off if you are gluing anyway, so the halves meet flush.

Use plastic glue sparingly on one side, press together and hold for ten seconds or so. Too much squeezes out and blurs detail. Give each joint a minute before adding the next part. Once set, scrape any squeezed-out glue off a seam with the knife and fill a gap with a little putty.
Check which base the model needs, then glue the feet down with a small dab. Give the finished model a last look for mould lines and gaps.
On very small kits a few gaps and tabs are hard to avoid, and they are rarely noticed once painted. Hold tiny models on a stick or holder rather than in your fingers.

guides.title: Building models and terrain from card
guides.summary: Print templates on heavy card, back them with cereal-box card, score every fold, and glue the tabs to build cheap vehicles and scatter.
body: Print templates on heavy card, around 300 gsm. For vehicles, rough cut the pieces with a margin and glue them to the plain side of cereal-box card with a glue stick. The backing adds weight and stiffness.
Cut the parts out, leaving glue tabs a little longer than drawn so there is more to stick to. Add an extra tab if you want to close an open bottom.

Score every fold line with a craft knife, through the printed layer and partly into the backing but never right through. Scoring is what gives crisp folds. Fold along the scores and dry fit to see which tabs tuck under which panels.
Super glue the tabs on every structural join and press them in place. Leave the printed lines showing, as they help you place later parts.

For depth, cut armour plates or panels from card, glue them onto backing card, cut them out again and fix them on. The extra layer adds detail and stiffens the shape. Cut large flat tops from thicker card so they do not sag.
Use a hole punch for small round parts such as hatches and lenses rather than cutting tiny circles. For a turning turret, glue a washer under it and a magnet in a washer on the hull.
Card soaks up paint and can warp, so brush on a thin coat of varnish or watered PVA to seal it before painting.

guides.title: Carving stonework and cracks
guides.summary: Score stone blocks and cracks into plaster or hard putty, keep them irregular, and soften the edges.
body: Work in plaster or a putty that sets hard and can be sanded, not a soft flexible one. Plaster is cheap: carve single stones, or cast a slab in a frame and cut whole bases from it. A soft wood block also carves well for steps.
Sand hardened putty flat before carving. For a base, a medium-fine grit is enough.

Score the joints between blocks with a needle so each stone reads as its own piece, close to its neighbours but clearly separate. If you tilt a stone, keep its sides square so it still looks cut. For brick, cover a core in epoxy putty and score the lines with a blade.

Cut cracks with the tip of a sharp knife as a few lines that follow sensible lines of stress, such as out from a corner or an impact, rather than random zigzags. Follow any cracks on nearby parts. Short Y shaped cracks make stone look old and broken quickly.

Run the side of the blade along each line from both sides to widen it slightly and soften the edges. Decide how old the stone is: ancient stone wears rounded, so soften over-sharp edges with a file or sanding stick. Only fresh breaks stay crisp.
Lift a small piece out with a needle and glue it back slightly apart. Bits that break off by accident can be reused the same way as damage.
For worn loose stones, cut a pile of small blocks and roll them between your palms to round the corners. Bed them in putty so you can arrange them unevenly before it sets.
Keep it restrained. A few cracks look more natural than many.

guides.title: Cheap and free basing materials
guides.summary: Garden grit, found sand, tea leaves, twigs, tile grout, cork, old sprue and small coins make good basing for very little.
body: Miniature garden sections at garden centres sell sand, grit, pebbles, moss and twigs in big bags. A base uses a pinch, so one bag lasts years, and much of it is close to tabletop scale.

Collect several grades, from very fine sand to small pebbles, and sieve them apart. Larger flat stones give a figure something to stand on and add height. Mixed colours do not matter, as it all gets primed.
Tumbled crushed glass chips have no sharp edges and a striated face that looks like rock once primed. Never break glass yourself; use only the ready tumbled kind.

Sand, dirt and small stones from outside are free. Bake them on a tray at about 175 C for half an hour to kill anything living and burn off plant matter. If your models use magnets, run a magnet through the sand to pull out iron grains.

From the kitchen and the toolbox: dried tea leaves pass for leaf litter, coffee grounds make soil but need sealing with varnish so they do not go mouldy, sanded tile grout is glue and grit in one, and torn cork makes rock faces.
Small twigs make fallen logs. Bake them on a low heat for a long time to dry them out, then place them at varied angles. Coffee stirrers make planks, and lichen-covered twigs can be left unpainted.
Old sprue chopped into chunks makes rubble. Bristles cut from an old brush and glued into cracks make weeds, and plastic broom bristles painted gold and cut very short make spent shell casings.

Low value copper coins make heavy, cheap bases that stop light figures falling over; cover them with texture paste like any base. Glue everything down, then prime the whole base; black left in the gaps reads as shadow. Seal foam with PVA first, as spray can melt it.

guides.title: Choosing brushes
guides.summary: A round brush with a sharp tip and a fat belly, around size 0 to 2, does most jobs better than a tiny one.
body: Match the brush to the job, so rough work never wrecks your detail brush. A few cheap brushes plus one or two good ones cover everything.

For detail, get a plain round pointed watercolour style brush. It should spring back to a sharp tip after each stroke and have a fat belly that holds paint. A size 0 to 2 does most work, including edge highlights and eyes.

Sizes are not consistent between makers, so compare the actual brush rather than the number. Swirl a new brush in water to wash out its stiffening binder: the tip should spring back to a sharp, even point. A tip that forks in two when wet is faulty; natural hair splaying as it dries is normal.

Synthetic brushes are cheap but respond less to pressure and their tips curl and wear quickly, so fine work takes more corrections. Natural hair holds more paint, keeps a firm point and lasts longer. Blends are a cheap middle step. Many painters start on synthetics and move to natural hair once their cleaning habits are solid.

For base coats, washes, inks, one-coat paints and wet blending, use a larger synthetic, around size 4 to 8. Paint gets into the collar, so keep these cheap and replace them when worn. Use old or cheap synthetics for metallics, glue and texture paste too.

Other shapes have their uses. Short-haired brushes snap back well for eyes and freehand but hold less paint. Long thin liners run washes into panel lines. Flats and filberts cover big surfaces, and stiff hog brushes suit drybrushing terrain.
Soft makeup brushes from a multipack make smoother, less chalky drybrushes than stiff flat ones. Old natural brushes that have lost their point still suit mid-stage layering.

On a budget, a cheap brush with a good tip is fine for tabletop painting. For fine detail a mid-priced natural hair brush is a big step up; the dearest is not always the best. Brush feel is personal, so try more than one before settling.

guides.title: Choosing glue
guides.summary: Plastic glue welds plastic to plastic, while super glue suits resin, metal, mixed materials and quick fixes.
body: Plastic glue, or plastic cement, melts plastic parts together, and a good weld is often stronger than the plastic around it. It only works on bare plastic, so scrape off any primer or paint first. Bigger contact areas make stronger joins.

Thin, watery cement wicks into a closed join: hold the parts together and touch the brush to the seam. For a peg, put the glue in the hole. Hold for about 15 seconds. On its own it is weaker, so use it where parts already hold by friction.

Thicker cement in a needle tip bottle suits beginners and gives time to line parts up. Keep the cap on. If a warm room pushes out a bubble, squeeze it back first, and clear a blocked needle with a fine pin.

Plastic glue softens the surface, so keep fingers and extra glue off the join or you leave prints and melted detail. Avoid very strong types on fine parts. Angled parts on a tiny contact point slowly droop as it sets; use super glue or a pin there.

Super glue works on resin, metal, plastic and mixed materials; wash resin in warm soapy water first. Plastic glue will not bond resin or metal. Thin super glue wicks into tight seams, medium suits most jobs, and gel gives time to adjust and stays put on upright joins. A toughened type survives knocks better.

Super glue grabs fast and usually snaps cleanly at the joint, so you can test a pose and redo it. Use plastic glue where you want a permanent bond and super glue where you may change your mind, or on painted parts. Acetone softens super glue to undo a join, but can harm paint. Scrape off old glue before refitting.

An activator sets super glue almost instantly, handy for fiddly bits and heavy limbs; too much makes the joint brittle. The spray coats everything, so touch the end of the dip tube to one part, put glue on the other and press. Open a window. Get small tubes of glue and cap them at once, as opened glue thickens.

Use two-part epoxy for heavy or stressed parts; it fills gaps and gives time to line them up. Use white PVA for basing materials and for foam, which solvent glues melt. Clear parts need a clear-parts glue, as super glue fumes fog them.

guides.title: Choosing hobby paints
guides.summary: Most paint ranges are fine, so start with the colours you need and look for strong pigment and a white that covers well.
body: Almost no hobby paint range is truly bad, and the differences are small. Pick what is easy to get hold of and learn how it behaves. Try a few colours first: check they flow off the brush and that reds, whites and blues cover about as well as each other. Water-based ranges mix together fine.

Start with the colours your current models need and add a paint only when a project calls for it. A premixed pot is worth having for a colour you would otherwise mix every time. Two sets that do the same job rarely solve a painting problem.

Pigment strength matters most. Strongly pigmented paint covers in fewer coats, so the finish stays smooth instead of muddy. Cheap craft paint is made for paper: on models it covers and grips poorly, dries slowly and smears when handled.
Dropper bottles are easy to dose and often come slightly thinned. Pots are fine but dry out faster and need thinning. Plain tap water is all you need to thin either at first; mediums can wait.

Very matt paints let you decide where light falls but look less rich and turn chalky if highlights step up too fast. Satin paints look deeper and are more forgiving. A good habit is satin for the early layers and matt for the final highlights.

Whites, blacks and metallics vary most between ranges. A white that covers black in one thin coat is worth seeking out. Metallics made with real metal powder look more like metal than mica ones. A light and a dark neutral steel, a warm gold and a copper cover most metals.
Thick, tube style artist acrylics are much denser than hobby paint. Use them either spread thick like butter or thinned right down to glazes. At layer thickness they go streaky.

Transparent one-coat paints, inks, glaze medium and fluorescents are useful additions later; test anything new on a spare part first. Even so, a good brush with a sharp point makes more difference to your results than which paint range you use.

guides.title: Choosing a primer colour
guides.summary: Always prime, and pick white, grey, black or a colour by what covers most of the model and how you will paint it.
body: Paint on bare plastic or metal rubs and scratches off. Primer is what makes paint grip, so always prime first. A matt primer gives more grip than a glossy one.

Acrylic paint is slightly see-through, so the primer tints the first coats, most of all with thin or light paints. The same colour looks darker and duller over black and brighter over white. The effect fades with each coat.

White or a very light grey suits bright, saturated schemes and translucent one-coat paints and inks, and shows clearly what each wash does while you learn. Yellow, orange, pink and pale blue cover far more easily over it. Dark colours need extra coats over white, but that is still easier than light over black.

Black gives instant shadow, and any spot you miss deep in a recess just looks like shadow. It is the safer choice on models with areas a brush cannot reach, and it suits silver, all-metal models and scenes lit from below. Avoid it under yellow and orange, which can turn greenish over black.

Grey sits between and is the safe choice if unsure, or if you can only have one can. It does not shift the colours on top and shows at a glance where a thin coat has not covered. A warm ivory or mid brown also lets most colours show their true colour in fewer coats.

Prime in the colour that covers most of the model: a knight in full plate in silver, a soldier in cloth and leather in sandy beige. It cuts out a base coat, most of all on batches of similar models; on a small, varied group it saves little. Coloured sprays separate more, so shake them longer.

Otherwise let the hardest or fiddliest colour decide. If dark areas fill the recesses, black primer does them for you. Skin covers far better over pale, so prime heads separately in white or sandy khaki. A mist of white over black gives bright colours an easier start while keeping dark recesses.

A small set of black, white, grey, brown, green and sand sprays covers most scenery and many armies. Bottled primers can also be mixed, such as white with a little brown for a warm base under skin. Paint one test model first; you may find a different primer saves more time.

guides.title: Tidying shading and lining mistakes
guides.summary: Cut back spilled lining with the lighter colour, and paint a dark mix back into recesses that caught highlight paint.
body: Dark lining spilling onto a pale panel shows badly. Let it dry, then paint the base or soft shade colour back over the overspill, cutting the line back to where it belongs.

If a wash or shade spread onto raised areas, paint the base colour back over the flats once dry, stopping just short of the recess and leaving a thin band of shade. Do this before highlighting so every highlight sits on a clean base.
Highlight paint slipping into deep lines kills the shading. Mix the shade colour with a little black and paint it back into the recesses.

Messy edges where two colours meet, or after fast blending, can be hidden with a soft dark wash. Stroke from the tip of a horn or spike down to its base and lift off there, so the wash pools in the join.
Light paint over dark wash covers slowly, especially white and yellow. Shade neatly in the first place and only clean up where it shows.
Skip cleanup on spots an edge highlight will cover or that cannot be seen.
Small slips near edges can become chips and scratches later. Paint awkward parts such as heads before gluing them in.

guides.title: Gluing and painting clear parts
guides.summary: Fix clear canopies and visors with PVA so they do not fog, and give paint a grip film on clear frames.
body: Leave clear parts off the model until the painting is finished. Check which way round they go before gluing, as many small clear parts only sit snugly one way.
Glue them with a tiny amount of white PVA glue in the back corners. It takes longer to set but dries clear and matt. Wipe away any excess with a finger; it will not show once dry.
Avoid super glue here. Its fumes leave a white frost inside clear plastic that cannot be cleaned off. Plastic glue melts paint and clear plastic and barely holds canopies anyway.

Paint on clear plastic often beads, pulls away or looks streaky. For canopy frames, lightly scuff the frame lines with a fine abrasive, or brush on a thinned coat and wipe it off with paper towel or a sponge.
The faint film left behind gives the next coat something to grip. Then paint the frame normally, building up thin coats.
Do not varnish clear parts; varnish, spray most of all, turns them cloudy. If a canopy has to be on while you varnish, mask the clear areas with tape first.

For clear effect parts such as flames, crystals and energy, a light coat of satin varnish works as a primer without clouding them. Paint them with inks, washes and thin glazes so light still passes through, and fix them with a tiny dot of glue at the contact point.

guides.title: Clipping parts off the sprue
guides.summary: Use flat faced cutters a little away from the part, then trim and scrape the nub flush with a blade.
body: Choose cutters with one flat face and jaws that meet exactly. Curved or bevelled wire cutters leave a rough cut. Long, slim jaws reach tight spots. A cheap flat backed pair is fine to start with.

Very sharp, thin bladed cutters leave almost nothing to clean but are brittle. Keep them for small plastic parts and use a cheaper pair for thick frames and resin. A cleaner cut also stresses the plastic less, so thin parts are less likely to whiten or snap.

Use cutters, not a knife, to free parts; a knife can snap or slip into your hand. Cut in two stages: first through the frame a little away from the part with the cheap pair, then close in with the sharp pair, flat face towards the part, leaving a small nub so you do not bite into detail.
Cut the thinnest join first and the chunkiest last. Cutting a thick join first jolts the part and can snap a thin piece still attached.
Look before you clip. Some small pegs are locating plugs, not leftover sprue. If you snip one off, glue it back with a little super glue; it only needs to keep the part lined up.

Scrape the nub away with light, repeated strokes of a craft knife pulled towards you. Pushing the blade at the part makes it jump and gouge. Finish with a fine file or sanding stick and feel with a fingertip for bumps.
Parts are often numbered in build order on the frame. Clip and clean one at a time, in order, so small parts do not get mixed up or lost.
Change knife blades when they dull, and brush parts with a soft brush afterwards to clear shavings before priming. Younger painters can use a mould line scraper instead of a knife.

guides.title: Staying comfortable while painting
guides.summary: Sit upright with good support, rest your eyes, move often and loosen your grip to paint longer without aches.
body: You paint sitting straight or leaning slightly forward, so pick a chair that supports that. Reclining, lounge style or gaming chairs are built for leaning back. Height adjustment and firm lower back support matter more than looks.

Sit with your back straight and feet flat on the floor or a footrest; if they dangle, the chair is too high. Lift the model towards your face instead of bending over it, and let your shoulders drop. A raised work surface, around 95 cm, brings the work nearer eye level.
Change position, stretch and move every so often, and avoid sitting cross-legged for long. A desk you can raise or lower lets you switch between sitting and standing.

Eyes dry out from close focus. Take regular breaks looking across the room or out of a window, not at a phone. If you wear contact lenses, glasses can be more comfortable for long sessions. If vision problems carry on after you stop painting, see a doctor.

Use bright, diffuse, daylight-balanced light: glare makes you squint and dim light makes your eyes hunt for detail. Magnification, such as a head visor, saves you holding the model too close; make sure the headband is not tight.

Squeezing the brush hard while concentrating leads to finger cramps and shake. Notice your grip from time to time and loosen it. Do not press your wrist or forearms hard on a thick desk edge, which can cause numbness.
Talk heavy videos and podcasts pull focus from careful work and tire you over many hours. Quiet music is easier to paint to.
Shorter sessions spread over more days are easier to keep up than very long ones.

guides.title: Common beginner mistakes
guides.summary: Thick paint, unmixed pots, rushing and overworking cause most early problems, and a few habits fix them.
body: Thick paint clumps, streaks and hides detail, like crayon. Thin it on the palette to roughly the flow of milk and build colour in two or more thin coats.
Pigment settles in the pot. Shake or stir every paint before use, and mix on the palette with an old tool or the brush handle, not the bristles, which wears them out.
Close lids fully after use, or the paint skins and dries out. Moving paint into dropper bottles also cuts down on spills and waste.
Craft paint is made for paper and has weak pigment and coarse fillers. Paint made for models covers better and keeps fine detail.
Rushed strokes cause most mess. Slow down, and pick one or two areas per session instead of trying to finish the whole model in one go.
Very thin paint is not always better. Over-thinned paint for blending dries fast, runs into recesses and is hard to control.
Know when to stop. Reworking a nearly finished model rarely helps, so call it done and start the next. Most of your progress comes from painting more models.
Start with a small set of colours and learn to mix from them, and ask for honest feedback. Most people get pleasing results in a few hours and feel at ease with the basics within weeks.

guides.title: Using one-coat medium
guides.summary: Medium for one-coat paints thins the colour but keeps its flow and grip, giving softer, smoother shading.
body: Medium made for one-coat, contrast-style paints dilutes the colour while keeping the binder, so the paint still flows off raised areas and grips without pooling as badly.

Start at about half paint, half medium, or two parts paint to one for a stronger colour, and give two thin coats rather than one heavy one. Old pots that have thickened need more. Over a white or very pale base, thin as far as one part paint to six or eight of medium. Test on one section first.
The result is a softer, lighter colour that hides brush mistakes better than the neat paint.

Medium gives an even tint all over, even on smooth metal where paint thinned with water pools and goes patchy. Water suits pushing deeper colour into folds and feathering it out, and leaves more shine on metal edges.
Mixed with a one-coat paint or a normal wash, medium makes a clean shade that stains less. Cover the whole area, then push the pigment towards the recesses. Gaps in coverage leave hard lines.

Start thinner than you think. A second coat is easy; taking colour away is not. If an area dries too dark or patchy, paint over it with a matching opaque colour rather than adding more. Mixes with medium dry slowly, which helps in hot weather. A white spray base soaks paint fast, so work quickly over it.
You still need to mop up pools. Touch the belly of a clean, damp brush to a pool to lift it. Shake and mix the pot well first, as badly mixed paint can dry shiny.

One-coat paint also mixes with ordinary opaque paint, giving matching highlight colours that flow well over the one-coat base. Thinned to about one part paint to three of medium, a strong red makes a soft glaze for lips, nose tips and scars.

guides.title: Getting crackle paint to crack
guides.summary: Use crackle paste thick, with no water and little added colour, on a porous surface, for big convincing cracks.
body: Crackle paste splits as it shrinks. Thicker areas take longer to dry and give bigger cracks, which show up better once painted. It is dry when the colour is even; a hair dryer on low, held back and kept moving, speeds it up without harm.

New pots are often runny and give tiny cracks. Spread some on card for a few minutes to thicken it, or use the thicker paste gathered in the lid, and never add water. Blot the brush well after rinsing.

Layer thickness matters most: thin coats give fine sharp cracks, thick coats give big chunks. A second coat over the dry first one, or a coat over basing paste that is still wet, gives wider, deeper cracks.

Blob it on with an old springy brush and dab and pick at it rather than making parallel strokes. Stipple for an even crackle, or pile it up in one spot for a big split. Too much paint or fine soil mixed in stops it cracking; sand of a similar grain is fine.
Over a shiny surface such as varnish it cracks but flakes off. Use primer underneath, and seal flaking cracks with watered-down white glue.
Take the paste to the rim so the edge does not end up as a ring of tiny cracks, but do not pile it thick there; a heavy rim breaks off when the model is handled.

For cracked paint rather than cracked ground, use white glue under the colour. Spray or brush the top coat while the glue is still wet and white; once it dries, nothing cracks. Thick glue gives wide cracks, and clear two-step crackle varnish cracks only the layer over it.

Dried crackle is brittle. Give it two light coats of spray varnish before painting so it survives handling and washes, and glue down any skulls or rocks pressed into it. Over glue crackle, use a solvent-based varnish, as water-based can soften the glue.

guides.title: Cutting, texturing and sealing foam terrain
guides.summary: Cut dense foam board with a sharp blade or hot wire, press in brick and stone texture, and seal it before any spray paint touches it.
body: Use dense, fine-celled insulation foam board. It cuts cleanly and holds pressed detail. Coarse, beady packing foam crumbles and is poor for terrain.
Straight cuts: a long snap-off blade with a fresh section, and a steel ruler. Make two or three light passes rather than one hard push. A dull blade tears the surface.
A hot wire cutter melts through foam for smooth cuts and curves. Go slowly, keep the wire at the lowest heat that cuts, work in a well-aired room and keep your face out of the fumes.
Brick and stone: draw the lines into the surface with a ballpoint pen or blunt pencil. Press a ball of crumpled foil or a rough rock over it for texture, and push a few stone corners down for wear.
Shape hills and rock faces with coarse sandpaper or a rasp. Wear a dust mask; foam dust is fine and clings to everything.
Seal before spray paint. The solvent in many spray cans melts foam into a pitted mess. Brush on two coats of thinned white glue, a mix of glue and paint, or acrylic wall paint, and let it dry fully.
Then prime by brush, or spray lightly over the sealed foam. Always test on an offcut first.
Glue foam with white glue, a foam-safe glue or a low-temperature glue gun. Some superglues and solvent glues melt it.

guides.title: Cutting kit parts for conversions
guides.summary: Slice thin parts with a sharp blade, saw thick ones, nibble big pieces with cutters, and keep fingers clear.
body: Lay the part as flat on the table as you can, or hold it against a block or in a small vice. Keep your fingers out of the line the blade travels, as small parts slip easily. Hold the knife near the tip for delicate work and further up the handle for power.

For thin joints, slide a very sharp blade through in several small strokes, cutting away from your body. A dull blade needs more force, slips more and pushes the plastic outwards so the pieces will not rejoin cleanly. Change blades often, more so on soft metal.
For thicker parts such as a torso, use a fine saw with many small teeth. Short, light strokes; let the saw do the work. A coarse blade removes too much and wanders.
Leave about a millimetre spare when sawing, then shave it back with a knife until the fit is right.
To remove a sculpted flap or detail along a groove, score along the groove several times with a knife, then bend the part and it snaps free.
To cut down big armour pieces, nibble the waste away with sharp side cutters. Do not try to cut flush in one go; leave a little and file it smooth.
Clean the cut faces with files and a sanding sponge. A rounded file or a ball burr in a rotary tool can carve a curved seat so a new part fits snugly.
Dry fit after each change and trim pegs that stop new parts sitting flush. Keep offcuts like straps or mail; they may be useful elsewhere.

guides.title: Cutting plastic card and thick plastic
guides.summary: Score plastic card with a fresh blade and steel ruler in light passes; cut thick plastic with a fine razor saw.
body: Work on a cutting mat and mark lines with a sharp pencil first.
Fit a fresh blade. A blunt blade needs more force, and that is when it slips and cuts you.

Hold a steel ruler on the line and score lightly several times until the card goes through, or bend it and snap it along a deep score. Do not try one hard cut. Use a metal ruler, as a knife bites into plastic ones.
For round pieces, cut tubes and strips slightly long, glue them, then file everything flush in one go.

For stone slabs, score and snap thin card, about 0.75 mm, into irregular shapes, then trim some corners, bevel the edges and scratch the top so they look old and chipped. Work over a box lid to catch the shavings.

Clippers crush thick scenery plastic. A fine toothed razor saw cuts it cleanly: hold the part firmly, line the blade up on the angle you want, start gently, then saw with light, even strokes. Keep fingers well out of the blade's path.
File cut edges smooth, and file off bumps where parts meet so the glue has more surface. To fit a part into a gap, file a little and test often.
Blades, saws and cut metal mesh are very sharp. Young hobbyists should get an adult to do the cutting.

guides.title: Moving paint into dropper bottles
guides.summary: Pour pot paint into dropper bottles through a small funnel, add a mixing ball, and clean the funnel straight away.
body: Dropper bottles are easier to dose from and keep paint from drying out. Moving paint across from pots only needs a small funnel and a little care.
Use a small steel icing nozzle or tiny plastic funnels. Sit one in the neck of each empty bottle; the small gap around it lets air out. A dab of poster putty holds a loose funnel steady.

Add two or three drops of flow improver to a thick pot paint, not more, and shake it until fully mixed; washes can skip this. Tape the empty bottles down, then pour straight into the funnel. Scrape the lid and sides in with a damp flat brush so little is wasted.
Drop a non-rusting mixing ball into each bottle so the paint mixes easily when shaken.
Rest the funnel on tissue, press the dropper tip in lightly, then screw the cap on to push the tip fully home.
Peel the old label off with a hobby knife and tape it to the bottle, or write the colour on it, so you know which is which.
Clean funnels at once in warm soapy water, scrubbing with a small brush, then dab them dry for next time.

guides.title: Designing a good base
guides.summary: Keep the base the right size, vary its textures, build it big to small, and never let it hide the model.
body: Use the standard base or one or two sizes up. Too big looks empty unless it has something worth looking at; too small leaves no room. Stand big figures on the base before gluing, as one that overhangs often looks better a size up. Round plinths suit all-round viewing; square ones fix a front view.

Fit the ground to the model's story: a figure in furs suits snow more than desert. Use value contrast, with dark models on light ground and pale ones on darker. If unsure, a mid brown earth works with almost any colour.

Study the pose first. Place the figure a little off centre, leaving open space on one side, and let a slope run with a weapon or limb so the lines lead to the face. Raise the back so the whole figure shows, and keep large features away from the front.

Build from big to small: fix the largest rocks, cork or bark first, then fill around them down to fine sand. A big piece added last looks stuck on. Leave flat spots for the feet and dry fit often. For a heavy model, raise one foot on a putty mound and press the feet in slightly.

Mix several textures and small extras such as twigs, stones, tufts, leaves and spare kit parts, sealing real bark and twigs with PVA or varnish. Push bits partly into the ground so they look half buried, not laid on top. A tiny story of what happened there tells you which bits fit.

Let detail thin out towards the rim so nothing gets knocked off in the hand. Do not cover everything in grass: let soil show, cluster tufts unevenly with the odd single one, and use flowers sparingly. Drybrush an over-bright tuft with green to tone it down.

Keep base colours limited and complementary, such as greens under a warm red figure. Let a shared colour bleed between earth, rock and plants, and keep flowers soft and pale. Tie model and base together: dusty ground means dusty boots.

Treat the base as a frame; one or two well chosen items is often enough. On group bases, put kneeling figures at the front and turn repeated sculpts so no two look alike. Use the same basing across a group so it reads as a set. A good base lifts an average model.
keywords: what to put on a base

guides.title: Digital sculpting
guides.summary: Start digital sculpting with a tablet app and small practice projects, and cut detail deeper than seems needed for printing.
body: A tablet sculpting app that exports print files is an easy way in. Desktop programs work too but feel more complex at first. For parts that must fit an exact size, such as bases, a measuring CAD program suits better than a clay style app; measure the real thing with calipers.
Spend the first session trying every tool to see what it does. Then set small goals, such as a simple creature built from a few basic shapes. Start with a few brushes rather than the whole program.
Block out forms with spheres, cylinders and tubes, then clone, flip and resize them. Mask an area and push it in to make eye sockets or mouths, then smooth the edges.
Make one horn or tooth segment and repeat it with an array tool, tapering and curving the chain. Save parts like horns and teeth as their own files to reuse.
Copy a real object using a reference image overlay. Matching an existing design teaches precision quickly. Little and often, about an hour a night, builds the skill.

Detail that looks sharp at screen size can almost vanish at miniature scale. Make recesses and raised details deeper and bolder than looks necessary, and zoom out to near real size to check. Perfectly clean surfaces can look artificial; small irregularities give a piece life.

Digital work undoes mistakes instantly and copies or mirrors parts, but you only see a flat screen until it is printed, so proportions can surprise you in the hand. Some sculpt in putty, scan it, then refine it digitally.

Export an STL or OBJ file and open it in a slicer to scale and duplicate it across the build plate. With no printer of your own, a friend, a local gaming venue or an online print service can print your files.

guides.title: Disguising rough sculpts
guides.summary: Smooth blends, small freehand speckles and a strong expression draw the eye away from lumpy or soft detail.
body: Old hand-sculpted models often have lumpy, uneven skin and soft detail.
Build such areas with gradual thin blends rather than heavy drybrushing, which shows up every bump.
Add small freehand speckles, freckles or spots across rough skin. They break up the surface so the texture is less noticeable.
Not every sculpted detail needs painting. Matt black reads as shadow, so painting part of an awkward shape black hides it. Keep it truly matt or the shine gives the trick away.

Highlight placement reshapes things too. If fingers look too long, paint the tips black where they wrap round a hilt, leave ridges along the fingers in flat midtones, and paint the gaps between them thinner so they look wider.
A little extra saturation and a clear expression in the eyes make old, simple faces look far more modern.
Lean into odd features with bold, characterful painting rather than trying to hide them.

guides.title: Getting rid of rinse water, solvent and resin waste
guides.summary: Settle acrylic rinse water and bin the dried sludge, take solvents to a waste site, and cure resin waste solid before it goes anywhere.
body: Rinse water from normal brush painting holds only a little acrylic. Many painters pour it down the sink with plenty of running water, but some areas ask you not to, so check your local rules.
Kinder to drains: let it settle. Leave the dirty water in a jar for a day or two, pour off the clear water, and let the sludge at the bottom dry out. Scrape the dry skin into household waste.
For bigger amounts, such as airbrush cleaning water, use a wide tub and let it evaporate, or soak it up with cat litter or paper towel and let that dry before putting it in the bin.
Never pour white spirit, enamel or oil rinse, or paint stripper down any drain. Let the solids settle, reuse the clear part, and take the rest to a household hazardous waste site.

Resin is the strictest. Never pour liquid resin, or alcohol or water with resin in it, down a drain. Leave the dirty liquid in a clear tub in sunlight or under a curing lamp until the resin sets, then filter it and reuse or dispose of it.
Cure failed prints, supports and resin-soaked paper towels in sunlight or under the lamp until hard. Fully cured resin can usually go in household waste; check your local rules.
Wear gloves when handling resin waste. Keep all waste tubs labelled, closed and out of reach of pets and children.
keywords: is it safe to pour away

guides.title: Drilling gun barrels
guides.summary: Start a centred pilot hole with a knife tip, then drill straight and gently with a small hand drill.
body: Rest a sharp knife tip on the centre of the muzzle, hold it upright and twist to start a small pilot hole. A pin pressed into the centre also makes a starter dent. Check from straight on that it is central before pressing deeper.
If it is off centre, turn the cutting edge towards the side that needs enlarging and twist in small steps, or nudge the next turns of the drill towards the middle.

Drill with a small bit in a hand pin vice rather than a power drill, using very light pressure. Pick a bit that leaves a sensible wall; too big leaves paper thin sides. Turn it a couple of times, check the hole is still central, then go on. Stop shallow on thin barrels and back the bit out slowly.
Check it is straight from one side, then turn the model a quarter turn and check again.

Widen the mouth with a slightly larger bit, or twist a larger, older bit lightly to bevel the edge. Blow out the shavings and scrape off any burr. Where a barrel has side vents, drill past them, then open those through too.
Brush a little thin plastic glue round the muzzle to smooth it before priming.
Solid barrels pointing at the viewer look odd, so forward facing guns repay the effort most.

guides.title: Dry fitting parts
guides.summary: Test fit parts before gluing to find bad fits, and glue tight wraparound parts so they slot back after painting.
body: Fit parts together without glue first. It shows leftover nubs, gaps, which way round parts go and exactly where the glue needs to go. If something will not sit flush, look for a nub or mould line on the joining faces. Gaps you fix now need no filler later.
Dry fitting also shows which parts will block your brush, so you can decide what to leave off for painting.
If locating pegs or tabs force panels to bend, clip them off; plastic glue holds well without them. Shave a little off tight parts like hatches rather than squeezing them in and warping the kit.
Once the fit is right, scratch the joining faces lightly with a knife or file so the glue has more to grip. Washing parts in warm soapy water first removes release agent that weakens glue and paint.

For a part from another kit, paint a strong colour on one mating face, press the parts together while wet and pull apart. The rub marks show the high spots. Scrape them down and repeat until most of the surface touches, then stop before tinkering makes it worse.

For tight, wraparound parts like a cloak in two halves, dry fit the loose half in place. Put tiny dots of glue only on the contact points of the half you are fixing to the body, press it against the dry fitted piece and hold for a minute or two.
Once set, the dry fitted piece comes off cleanly and slots back exactly after painting.
Sticky tack holds parts together while you check angles and poses. Rubber bands hold large boxy assemblies while the glue sets.

guides.title: Using a dry palette
guides.summary: A dry palette gives exact control of paint thickness and suits inks, glazes and oils, but paint dries faster on it.
body: Any surface that does not soak up paint works: glazed ceramic, plastic, metal, glass, a tile or an old plate. Glazed ceramic with small wells is the easiest to live with, as it keeps colours apart and holds thin mixes.
A glass sheet is big and tough, but paint dries fast on it, thin mixes run about and it can break. Tiles and plates cost little but are small and dry paint quickly.

On a dry palette the only water in the paint is what you added, so mixes behave the same each session. You see how the paint acts from the pot and after each drop of water, which teaches you how much the brush picks up and lets go.

It suits inks, glaze mediums, oils and oil washes, which need a solid dry surface, and fine detail where you want exact thickness. Two-brush blending, wet blending and drybrushing all work from it too.
The catch is drying time. Plan your colours, put out small amounts and work briskly. A drop of drying retarder keeps a mix usable for longer.
A wet palette keeps paint open for hours and suits long glazing sessions, but it slowly thins the paint and needs fresh paper and mould control. Many painters keep one of each.
To clean glazed ceramic, soak it in water and dried acrylic slides off. Keep it covered against dust and start each session on a clean surface.

guides.title: Looking after a drybrush
guides.summary: Keep a drybrush domed and clean, wake it up before use, and wipe it on something that does not shed fibres.
body: A rounded, domed tip leaves soft, even drybrushing and fine stipple dots. A flat, splayed tip leaves streaks.

Load only the tip. Hold the brush upright and take paint from the edge of a thin line on the palette, so it stays in the top few millimetres. Paint that creeps to the metal collar is hard to remove and ruins the shape.
Clean it between steps, before paint dries in the bristles. Swirl or press it straight down when washing so it stays round. Scrubbing sideways flattens it. A little gentle soap lifts colour.

You can also clean it dry between colours: dampen it lightly and sweep it outwards over a rough textured surface, twisting as you go, never pressing back towards the collar. When a stroke on white paper leaves only a faint line, it is ready.
Before use, flick the bristles under a bright light to shake out dust and fluff, work in one drop of water, then brush back and forth on scrap paper.
Check the moisture on a painted scrap. The smear should dry almost as soon as you blow on it. Start on a hidden area of the model.
For wiping off, use proper kitchen roll, a microfibre cloth, bare wood or a cork tile. Toilet tissue sheds fibres onto the model, and card seals over once paint dries on it and turns the brush gummy.
Squeeze the bristles between your fingers to make the tip smaller for tight spots. Judge a drybrush by feel, not looks: soft bristles that do not clump are fine even when stained.

guides.title: Using drying retarder
guides.summary: A small amount of retarder slows drying for easier blending, but too much makes paint thin and blotchy.
body: Retarder slows acrylic drying so you have longer to blend colours on the model.
A liquid retarder is the usual choice and is easy to dose. Thick gel versions vary: some work poorly, while others add time without making the paint runny. Test a new one before relying on it.
You only need to roughly double the working time, which takes very little. Dip a damp brush in a drop of retarder, then pick up paint.
Too much thins the paint so far it goes blotchy instead of blending, and it takes ages to dry.
Vague all in one mediums mix several additives in unknown amounts. Separate retarder, flow improver and thinning medium let you control exactly what you add.
A wet palette and working in a cooler room also slow drying.

guides.title: Posing a model dynamically
guides.summary: Oppose arms and legs, lean the body into the move, and mock up the pose with sticky tack before gluing.
body: Decide the mood first: menacing, heroic, eager or calm. Pick the head, pose and any extras to support it, and choose colours after the pose is set.
When a leg is back, bring the arm on that side forward, and the other way round. A raised weapon arm with the other swung back reads as a forward stride.
Lean the whole model slightly into the movement and tilt the head to follow that line. A deliberately off-balance lean sells a charge or eagerness.
Look for strong lines through the model, such as a weapon following the line of a leg or a cloak that follows the stride.
Many kits have small locating nubs at joints that lock one pose. Cut them off and smooth the joint so the parts can turn freely.

Join the parts with small blobs of sticky tack and try poses on the base. Dry fit several heads, cloaks and weapons, check from the front and side, then glue the parts that keep falling off and build from there.

Arms with sculpted weapons only look right near their designed angle. If a raised arm looks awkward, find one made to point that way. Turn a hand holding a gun slightly outward so it does not sit flat against the body.
