Turn the head towards the action rather than dead straight: lowered looks threatening, tilted looks curious. Pose for the main viewing side, and keep the head loose for painting. A head level with the ground makes a strong body angle look deliberate.

guides.title: Editing model photos
guides.summary: Correct exposure and white balance, keep saturation gentle, and cut out or add backdrops by hand.
body: Shoot raw files if the camera allows it, as they keep far more room to correct light and colour. Turn on the editor's clipping warnings and keep blown highlights and crushed shadows off the model.

Make small overall changes: raise exposure until the model is clear but the highlights do not clip, open the shadows a touch, pull the highlights in, then add a little contrast or clarity so the photo does not look grey.
Use the white balance picker on the white or grey backdrop, then tweak until the colours match the real model beside the screen. Switch on the lens correction profile to remove distortion.

Go easy on saturation. Pushing it hard destroys detail and changes your colours, so nudge it only slightly. Aim for true colour, not hiding flaws. If your lights and camera never move, save the settings as a preset.
Close-ups show every speck of dust. Zoom in, scan the image in sections, and click each speck once with a healing brush just bigger than it. Undo and resize the brush if a fix smears.

For a pure white backdrop, select the highlight tones, add a curves layer and drag the white point in until the backdrop turns white. Paint the layer mask back over any pale parts of the model that blew out.

To cut the model out, trace round it by hand with a precise path tool, as one-click selections leave fringes. Put a new backdrop on its own layer, use an image you may use, and blur it slightly. For mist, set a smoke image on black to screen mode.

Save a full size copy, then crop to a set ratio, such as 4:5 or square for posts and 16:9 for wide shots. Resize to about 1600 pixels on the long side and keep the file to a few hundred kilobytes, so sites do not crush it.

guides.title: Filament 3D prints for terrain
guides.summary: Filament suits big terrain and resin fine detail; glue and fill the parts, then hide layer lines with filler primer or epoxy.
body: Filament printers suit large terrain. Resin gives finer detail but has a small build area and is messy in bulk. Standard filament is easiest and gives off little smell; a tougher filament suits pieces that get handled a lot.

Check the file is at your figures' scale, such as 28mm or 32mm, and read other people's comments on it first. In the slicer, finer layers look better but take longer. Add supports under overhangs so they do not sag or warp.
Clean off the supports and scrape rough spots with a hobby knife. Dry fit the parts, then join them with super glue.

Fill seams with a putty that grips plastic, as some liquid fillers do not stick to prints. Press it in with a wet fingertip or a rubber shaper, build it slightly proud, let it dry and sand flush. Filler closes seams but does not hide layer lines.
For layer lines on big pieces, use a thick filler primer: coat, let it dry, sand, and repeat until the lines are gone. Keep it off fine detail, which it buries.

Or brush a very thin coat of two-part epoxy resin into every recess; it levels itself over the lines. Mix only a little at the maker's ratio, thin with a drop of isopropyl alcohol if needed, and lift any pooling with a clean brush.

Epoxy thickens after about 10 minutes, so do large models in small sections with fresh batches. Leave it about 4 hours to harden. A wrong mixing ratio leaves the surface sticky. Clean tools with isopropyl alcohol.
Prime the smoothed print and paint it with the same acrylics as your figures so it matches them on the table.

guides.title: Finding time to paint
guides.summary: Short, regular sessions with a set stopping time fit around work and family better than marathon nights.
body: Pick a routine you can keep, such as an hour early in the morning or a short session once the house is quiet. Regular short sessions get more done than waiting for a free weekend.
Use small windows. Fifteen minutes is enough for a base coat, a wash or one detail.
Leave the desk ready, with models on handles and the paints for the next step set out. Being able to start at once is what makes short sessions work.
Set a stopping time before you start. Late sessions easily run hours over, and lost sleep costs more than the painting gains.
When energy is low, pick a simple task you enjoy rather than the hardest step on the model.
At night, a bright task lamp makes the desk usable. Use a lidded mug and keep the rinse water well apart from your drink, especially when tired.

guides.title: When you dislike your paint job
guides.summary: Most models look bad halfway, so name exactly what bothers you and fix one thing at a time instead of stripping.
body: Nearly every model goes through an ugly phase while layers are half built. It usually comes together at the end, with highlights and details, so keep going and finish. Let wet areas dry before you judge or touch them again.
If you feel impatient, put the brush down. Impatience shows as sloppy strokes and poor colour choices, and a model often looks quite different the next day.
Do not judge one area alone. It often looks better once the rest of the model has colour, and once it sits on its base.
Put the problem into words. Is it the colour, the contrast or the smoothness? Colours clash? Blends rough? Highlights too dull, or shadows too weak? Messy edges?

Each answer points to a fix: more contrast, a glaze to smooth a blend, a tidy-up pass with the base colour, or colours laid over the top that push it the way you want, such as reds to warm a cold, purple skin. If one fix does not work after a break, try another, even if it takes longer.

Watch for overcorrecting; fixing one fault can create the opposite one. Work in stages and reassess after each. Going back to earlier layers, such as pushing shadows out once the lights are in, is a normal part of painting.
If one large part clashes once the model is together, such as a cloak, repaint just that part in a hue that leans the same way as the rest of the scheme. Test it on a hidden spot first.
Look at finished examples of the same figure and ask what they have that yours does not. Focus on the next part, not everything left to do, and strip only as a last resort.
keywords: what is wrong with my model

guides.title: Airbrush bubbling back into the cup
guides.summary: Bubbles in the cup mean air is leaking backwards at the nozzle; seal and reseat it, then test with water.
body: Bubbles in the paint cup when you press the trigger mean air is escaping backwards, usually at the nozzle joint or because of a blockage. Foam at the front while spraying is the same leak, and often follows cleaning when the front cap or nozzle was not fully done up.
Tighten the nozzle cap and nozzle firmly but only until snug with the wrench. Overtightening damages it.
On airbrushes where the nozzle sits in a seat, brush a thin film of petroleum jelly around its base before refitting. Keep it away from the opening and air holes.

Put the trigger at rest before sliding the needle back in. It should slide with no resistance and seat fully forward. If paint sprays without pulling the trigger back, the needle is not seated: loosen the chuck and push it forward.

If it feels as if no air comes out, dried paint or varnish may have closed the small gap between nozzle and air cap. Clean the nozzle tip and the inside of the cap with cleaner on a fine, pointed cotton bud.
Paint leaking from the side means a loose part or a failed seal. Tighten it, or replace the worn rubber ring.

Test with plain water. If it still bubbles, check the needle chuck is tight, then look for a bent needle or cracked nozzle, which need replacing. If a loose trigger will not move the needle, it is stuck in dried paint.
If bubbling or a stuck needle continues after all that, strip the airbrush and give it a full deep clean, then reassemble with every part seated properly.

guides.title: Airbrush spider webbing and speckling
guides.summary: Spider webbing means paint too thin for the pressure; gritty speckling means paint too thick or dried on the tip.
body: Spider webbing is when sprayed paint runs out in thin streaky lines. The air is pushing too hard on paint that is too runny, or the brush is too close.

Fix it by adding a little more paint to the cup, lowering the pressure, moving slightly further away, or pulling the trigger back less. For close work, set the trigger stop to limit how far it pulls, and keep air flowing before and after the paint.
Speckling is a gritty, dotted spray, like a bad primer coat. The paint is too thick, the pressure too low, or paint has dried on the needle tip.

Fix speckling by adding thinner until the mix looks like milk; almost every time, thinning is the answer. Wipe dried paint off the needle tip with cleaner, and raise the pressure a little if it still spatters.
A chalky, grainy finish comes from thick paint or spraying from too far away, so the paint dries in the air. Thin a little more and move closer.

Pale colours and white speckle more easily because of their pigment. Thin them more than dark colours, around four drops of thinner to one of paint, and build several thin layers. If they then spider, mix a slightly thicker batch and mist light passes over the runs.
Some inks stay re-wettable for hours after spraying, so a flat white paint is more reliable for white base coats.
Test on card or your hand before spraying the model each time you change the mix or pressure.

guides.title: Airbrush spitting, pulsing or uneven flow
guides.summary: Spits, splatters and pulses come from water in the air line, an uneven air supply or a part clog; check air first.
body: Compressed air drops water as it cools in the hose, and the airbrush spits it out in drops. A moisture trap between compressor and hose catches it.
If it spits water, drain the trap with its bleed valve, lower the pressure a little, and work in a drier room if you can. Drain the trap often and replace worn filters.
If the spray pulses or comes out uneven, the air supply is not steady. A compressor with an air tank and a proper regulator smooths it out.
If the air is fine, check the needle tip and nozzle for dried paint, and make sure the nozzle, cap and needle chuck are all tight.
Thick or old paint also makes the airbrush sputter. Thin it more, or mix a fresh batch.
If paint will not atomise well, turn the regulator up or down in small steps and test on card each time.
Small compressors without a tank get hot in long sessions. Let them rest now and then, and switch off units that do not shut off on their own when you finish.
Most airbrush hoses use 1/8 inch fittings, but some compressors use 1/4 inch, so keep an adapter to hand.

guides.title: Fixing chalky highlights
guides.summary: Chalky highlights come from jumping to white too fast or overthinning; use smaller steps and glaze colour back over.
body: White is the strongest pigment, so going from a mid tone to white is a far bigger jump than it looks.

The chalky look comes from pale layers that never fully cover. Overthinned pale paint leaves specks with darker colour between them, and patchy layers stacked on patchy layers read as grainy. Give each step enough thin coats to go solid before the next.

Add white to the mix in small amounts so each step is only slightly brighter, or build the highlight from the base plus a little off-white. Stacking several thin coats of the same mix widens a highlight smoothly.
After each stage, thin the colour below and glaze it around the outside of the new highlight. Go back and forth until smooth.

If an area went chalky overall, glaze a saturated version of the colour over it, then reapply the pale highlight over a smaller area. First decide what is wrong: too bright, too grey, or too sharp a jump.

On skin, dot or stipple thin highlight paint, about half water, instead of stroking it. Very matt paints thinned heavily go chalky in glazes, and brushing into paint that is starting to dry always leaves texture.

After drybrushing, a one-coat paint or shade thinned with about three parts medium, brushed over the area, pulls chalky steps together. Soak up any pooling, then restore black in the deepest recesses.
If a glaze goes on too thick, repaint what was under it and glaze again.

guides.title: Chalky or grainy white paint
guides.summary: Keep white smooth with a high-flow white or flow improver instead of water, on a light primer, in thin coats.
body: Many whites are thick, grainy and cover badly. Straight from the pot they clump and fill detail, and the more white in a mix, the harder it is to pull into fine lines. Stir often as you work, because the pigment settles.

Water helps white flow but tends to leave streaks, even after several coats. Instead, mix an opaque white about one to one with a high-flow, ink-like white until even, or add a drop of flow improver or white ink. These smooth it without diluting the pigment.

A heavily pigmented artist white can be thinned a lot and still cover strongly; dab it on and feather the edge out. Mixing white about half and half with gloss varnish also helps it flow and cover evenly, and the sheen is not noticeable.

Start on a smooth, light primer such as white, ivory or light grey, or paint white over a pale tint rather than grey, and climb from tinted mixes to pure white. A rough or heavy primer coat shows through every white layer, so fix that first.
Test the mix on dark card: you want a thin film with no ridges. Put out only what you can use before it dries.

Lay on two or three thin coats with smooth passes, letting each dry. The first coat looking see-through is normal. Do not scrub at an area once it starts to set, and keep passes light where paint pools in panel lines and around trim.
Judge the finish only once dry; wet acrylic can look glossy and patchy when it is fine. Keep later washes off finished white areas.
For many white models, or large white parts, spray or airbrush the white base, with the parts kept off the model if needed. It is far faster and smoother than brushing white over black.

guides.title: Clearing a clogged airbrush
guides.summary: Most clogs are dried paint on the needle tip or nozzle; wipe it, flush cleaner through, and clean between colours.
body: If spray turns splattery or stops, check the needle tip and nozzle first. Wipe dried paint off the needle tip with a soft brush or cloth. In warm weather, or on a big batch, paint dries on the tip within minutes, so wipe it often, and spray a short burst away from the model before every pass.

Do not turn the pressure up to blast a clog through. It tends to spit a blob and then cause spidery runs. A few full trigger pulls can shift a tiny blockage, but cleaning the tip and paint path is the real fix.

Still blocked: spray airbrush cleaner, flow improver or isopropyl alcohol through. As a last resort, loosen the needle nut and gently slide the needle back and forth with air flowing, taking care not to bend the tip. Then strip and deep clean.

Never scrape the nozzle with your working needle or a metal reamer; it can bend the needle or split the nozzle. Use a soft brush, a lint-free swab, a wooden pick, or an old needle kept for the job. Disconnect the air before taking anything apart.
Do not drop the whole airbrush into cleaner, as seals and plastic parts can suffer. Replace a cracked nozzle or bent needle rather than soaking it again.

If the spray keeps stopping, the paint is most likely too thick. Thin and mix it in a separate pot rather than the cup, and strain old or lumpy paint. A little airbrush retarder stops normal paints drying at the nozzle.

Brush-on metallics have big flakes that thinning does not shrink, so use metallics made for airbrushing. Very matt paints also clog; for a dead flat finish, spray a normal paint and matt varnish it later.
Between colours, spray out, add cleaner, work the needle back and forth and repeat. At the end of the day, pull the needle, wipe it, clean the cup and give the needle a very light film of lubricant.

guides.title: Fixing mistakes after paint dries
guides.summary: Fix dried slips and colour on the wrong part with a matched colour, rebuild blends in thin layers, or hide marks as wear.
body: Let the mistake dry fully before you touch it. Working a wet slip builds thick, lumpy paint over the detail.
On a flat base coat, paint the original colour back over the slip in thin coats until it covers.

Repairs show mainly because of a hard, straight edge. Dab irregular patches that cross the edge of the mistake on both sides instead of tracing along it. Once the hard edge is gone, the rest is matching tone.

For a big, strong-coloured slip on a finished area, first stipple greys that roughly match the shading over it to kill the colour. Then rebuild with the original colours, thinned and stippled from the middle outwards, and repeat any drybrush or tint passes.

On a blend or glazed area, mix tones that match the surface right next to the mark and build them back in thin layers, dark to light; a wet palette keeps several mixes workable. On an airbrushed panel, dab primer on bare spots and wet blend the same colours back in the original direction.

A wash darkens the base, so the plain base colour leaves a bright patch, and rewashing leaves a tide mark. Mix a little black or the wash into the base to match, test it on a small spot, and keep that mix out while you highlight.

Where a strong colour slopped onto drybrushed details or metal, paint the darkest step back over it, such as the dark metal mixed with a touch of black, then repeat the final drybrush over just those parts.

If a trace still shows, add dots, scratches, freckles or a few dark chips across it so it reads as wear, but keep chips sparse. Keep each area's palette colours until the model is finished, for touch-ups.

guides.title: Fixing drybrushing problems
guides.summary: Blotches and streaks come from too much paint or a damp brush; glaze or wash back over to hide them.
body: Too much paint gives heavy blotches. Pick up paint from the edge of a line on the palette with the tip, never plunge the brush in, and wipe most of it off. Test on the back of your hand or paper, and build a heavy coat in several light passes.

Chalky, gritty drybrushing usually means the brush is too dry. Kitchen roll soaks binder out faster than pigment, so if it keeps going chalky, wipe off on a smooth non-absorbent surface and leave a trace of moisture in the brush.

If you have to press hard to get paint off, reload instead. Heavy pressure gives a solid coat, builds texture on smooth armour and can snap thin parts. A very soft brush, such as a make-up brush, with a light touch leaves the fewest streaks.

A brush that is still damp after rinsing makes the paint watery and streaky. Keep two or three drybrushes so one is always dry, and do not rinse between steps of the same colour; the leftover paint helps blend them. Thin tissue sheds fibres; use kitchen roll or a textured board.

Only drybrush over fully dry paint, or it smears. Over black, one pass looks muddy, so build two or three. A big jump from dark base to bright drybrush makes streaks stand out; add an in-between colour. Drybrushing leaves only a faint trace, so choose a lighter colour than you would for a layer.
Very matt paints drag and leave sandy peaks. A little medium makes them glide like satin paints. Use the largest brush that fits and brush across details, not along them.

To hide streaks or dustiness, brush a thin wash or a see-through glaze of the base colour over the area. On flat panels, glaze the middle of each panel once all drybrushing is done. If a wash knocks the highlights back, drybrush the highest points again.
Drybrushing shows mould lines strongly, so remove them before painting. A matt varnish at the end evens out the sheen.

guides.title: Frosted or cloudy spray varnish
guides.summary: Varnish dries white or cloudy from damp air, a poorly shaken can, heavy coats or spraying too far away.
body: A white, cloudy, fuzzy or frosted look after spray varnish usually means moisture was trapped under the varnish as it dried. Damp air is the main cause, but acrylic paint also holds water for a while after it feels dry, so let the model dry fully first.
Spray only on a dry, mild day, or somewhere dry and ventilated, ideally below about 50 percent humidity. A cheap gauge or the weather report tells you. Avoid cold, damp or very hot conditions.

Shake the can hard for at least a minute, until the ball rattles freely. Cans that sat unused for months separate, and the matting powder then lands unevenly and dries frosty. Matt varnish that dries shiny usually was not shaken enough.

Spray thin, even passes from about 15 to 30 cm. From too far away the varnish part-dries in the air and lands grainy; too close or too heavy and it pools and frosts. Let each coat dry before the next, or it stays sticky.

Warming the model gently with a hair dryer before spraying helps drive off moisture. Never run it while varnish mist is still in the air, as the solvent is flammable; wait until the air clears before warming the coat as it dries.

Through an airbrush you spray closer, control the air and depend less on the weather, so frosting is much rarer. Thin the varnish properly, as under-thinned varnish also goes grainy. Brush-on varnish is another way round bad weather.

To rescue a frosted model, leave it about 24 hours, then spray or brush another thin coat of a varnish you trust in good conditions. The fresh layer often soaks in and clears the haze. Touch up any spots that stay white with paint.

If that fails, brush a very thin coat of olive oil over it, leave one to two hours, wipe it off well, then lift the rest with a barely damp cloth and a drop of washing-up liquid. Dry it, warm it, and revarnish thinly. Test on a hidden spot first, and never use alcohol or acetone on the paint.

guides.title: Glow effects that do not glow
guides.summary: A glow reads only if it is lighter than its surroundings and fades slowly; overdone glows can be glazed back.
body: A glow is about light, not colour. Adding a strong hue to one side makes it more colourful but often darker. If the lit area is not visibly lighter than its surroundings, it will not read. Check a photo in greyscale; the source should be the lightest value.

Often the fix is to darken the rest of the model rather than brighten the glow; a candle barely shows in daylight. If the source blends into other bright surfaces, knock back a nearby highlight and deepen shadows on surfaces shielded from it. Glows are far easier on dark models and hardest next to near-white.

A glow that jumps from one band of colour straight to the base looks fake. Build a long fade with many thin glazes, each darker one reaching a little further out. If the glow colour will not blend over a very different base, such as blue on red, mix the two for the in-between steps.

Paint planes and edges facing the source in the glow colour, and finish with fine edge lines and small scratches on the parts that face it. Metal catches it strongly and from further away; cloth soaks it up and looks duller.

If it looks like a pale patch, shrink the bright centre and work on the fade. If it spreads too far, glaze the outer edge back with the base or a mid tone and keep the strongest light close to the source. Glaze the first glow colour back over chalky spots.

If a dark tint creeps into a bright glow, see-through colours will not cover it. Paint white back over the spot once dry and redo the glow colours in order, light to dark. Streaks usually mean paint too strong or a brush too small; thin more and use a larger brush.

Plan the glow from the start. Saturated yellows, oranges and greens glow most easily; reds and purples are harder. Try it small on a test piece, skip normal highlights where the glow will go, and with two light sources keep a dark gap between them so each one reads.

Do not overwork it. Once the main rings of light are down, most of the effect is there. Change one thing at a time, then step away and judge it at arm's length and under room light, not just the desk lamp. If a paint will not spray well for an airbrushed glow, build it by brush.

guides.title: Faces that look harsh or too old
guides.summary: Very dark creases and bright ridges age a face; keep wrinkles only slightly darker than the skin around them.
body: Skin reads as smooth, so a face with very dark recesses and bright ridges looks old, hard and severe.
That suits a battle-worn veteran but not a young or softer character.
Judge a face only once the rest of the skin and nearby areas have colour. Painted alone on a grey model, almost any face looks garish.
Do not shade facial creases as deeply as armour panel lines. Keep wrinkles only slightly darker than the skin around them.
Keep the darkest accents for a few places only, such as the sides of the nose, the eye sockets and under the lip.

If a face already looks harsh, glaze midtone skin over the deepest lines to pull them back. Block in the lips and other non-skin areas in a dark brown, then glaze shadow, mid tone and highlight back and forth until it softens.
Going a little too bright first is fine, since the glazes bring it back. Keep the brightest highlights small, on the nose, cheekbones and brow.

guides.title: Loose joints on posable kits
guides.summary: Fix floppy joints on a posable kit in place with a drop of superglue so it holds its pose.
body: Loose joints make a model topple over and chip while you paint or play.
Set the pose you want, then run a small drop of superglue into each wobbly joint.
Hold it still until it grabs. You lose the posing, but gain a stable model.
If you want to keep the joint movable, a thin coat of varnish or nail varnish inside the joint can tighten it a little.

Paint itself is a common culprit on snap-fit kits. It gums up the friction joints until poses sag or parts stop fitting, so pull the kit apart before painting and mask each socket and peg with small pieces of masking tape or poster putty.
Leave hidden inner frame parts unpainted, pull the tape out with tweezers afterwards, then plug the kit back together.
A heavier base also supports tall, top-heavy figures.

guides.title: Fixing messy edge highlights
guides.summary: Trim thick or wobbly edge highlights back by painting the colour underneath up to the line from the middle of the panel.
body: Mistakes are normal. Finish the whole highlight first rather than stopping to fix each slip. If a blob lands on a flat area while wet, rinse the brush and lift it off at once.

Once dry, load the colour underneath and start each stroke well inside the panel. Pull towards the highlight, creeping closer, so it trims the line thinner. A colour just brighter than the layer trims it too and leaves a soft extra step of light.
Pushing a softened dark wash or thinned shade up against the inside of a fat line also slims it, and is often easier than repainting. Dab out any that runs into an unwanted recess with a fingertip.
Each new edge line should be thinner than the one below, so the earlier colour still shows. Keep every colour of the sequence on the palette until you finish.
If highlight paint ran into a recess, dot a little wash or shade colour back in.

For a line that came out far too thick, glaze the colour underneath over it a few times, or repaint the base and wash again, then redo it in one stroke. The fat line still marks the right place, and every extra stroke is another chance to wobble.

Fat lines usually mean the paint is too thick or the brush overloaded. Thin it so it glides, wipe off the excess, and test long lines on the palette or your thumb. On long edges, run the side of the bristles along the edge rather than just the tip.

Edge lines suit hard edges only. Cloth, skin and hair need soft layers or glazes, and on heavily textured models a light drybrush can stand in. Later glazes can dull edges, so do one more edge pass at the very end.

guides.title: Fixing priming problems
guides.summary: Grainy, rough, tacky or thick primer that clogs detail comes from weather, distance, old cans or touching it wet.
body: Spray primer works best on a mild, dry day, roughly 20 to 28 C and under about 60 percent humidity. Damp air makes the droplets clump into a bumpy orange-peel surface. Cold makes the can splutter and the primer dry before it grips, so it clumps or flakes later. Very hot days cause trouble too.

Keep the can at room temperature. In cold weather, stand its lower half in lukewarm water, around 36 to 40 C, for five minutes, shake well, and rewarm it when it cools. Never heat an aerosol directly; it can burst. In summer, spray early or late in the day.

Fuzzy, sandpaper-like primer means you sprayed from too far away, so it dried in the air before landing. Too close, or too long in one spot, floods the detail and pools in recesses. Hold the can at a steady 20 to 30 cm and use short, light passes that keep moving.
One coat, or two thin ones at most, is enough. Give a thin patch another light pass rather than a heavy blast. A little plastic colour showing through is fine.

Primer skins over before the layer underneath is dry, and some stretch as they cure. Touching or rebrushing it then leaves streaks, bubbles and wrinkles. Leave it at least 30 to 60 minutes, and overnight in cool or damp weather; painting too soon can peel the primer off.

To rescue fuzzy primer, buff the rough areas with an old dry toothbrush. The buffed spots go a little shiny; dab brush-on primer over them if that bothers you. It works best on flat areas, and you rarely need to strip.

Primer that stays sticky and glossy has not cured, usually because the can was old or badly shaken. Bad orange peel is the same. Strip the model and prime again from a fresh, well-shaken can. Water-based primers do not go tacky this way.

Test on a spare bit of plastic when conditions are borderline. If the weather is wrong, wait, run a dehumidifier, or use brush-on primer or an airbrush indoors. Always spray somewhere ventilated; many spray booths do not clear aerosol fumes.

guides.title: Rough, ridged paint texture
guides.summary: Ridges, rings and rough patches come from thick paint or brushing over drying paint; thin it and leave it alone.
body: Ridges, ring marks and torn-looking patches come from two things: paint that is too thick, or brushing over paint that has started to dry. Thick paint and heavy coats also bury detail.

Acrylic starts drying as soon as it leaves the brush. Once an area goes tacky, often within about 15 seconds, leave it; going back drags it into ridges and rings. Move to another part and return only when it is fully dry.

Thin paint so it flows and covers in two or three passes, and spread it quickly rather than going over the same spot. Load the brush right: too much floods recesses, too little goes dry and streaky straight away. Wick extra water off on a tissue.
Thick coats dry slowly, while very watery paint and a hot, dry room dry fast. A hair dryer on a low setting speeds drying between coats.

Do not judge it wet. Acrylic looks worse wet, then settles, goes matt and lightens slightly as it dries. If it is still patchy once dry, cover it with another thin coat instead of scrubbing at it. Use fresh paint, not paint that has sat thickening on the palette.

Lumps usually come from dust, or dried flakes off a dirty brush, palette or water pot. Shave small bumps off with a new hobby blade, or sand dry ridges gently with very fine sandpaper, stopping before you cut into the model.
After smoothing a patch, repaint it thinly with a clean brush and fresh water, so new flakes do not undo the work.
Get base coats smooth before highlighting. Texture shows up badly under fine edge highlights.

guides.title: Paint or wash dried shiny
guides.summary: Paints and washes that dry with an unwanted sheen can be matted down with matt varnish or a little paint in the wash.
body: Some washes, inks and one-coat paints dry satin or glossy, which looks wrong on cloth and skin. Heavily thinned paint and some reds do it too, even after a good shake.
Brush matt varnish over the shiny areas only. Dry it and check under a lamp. Going from gloss to matt often needs two or more coats.

Mixing a little of the base paint, or some matt medium, into the wash makes it go on more evenly and dry flatter. For inks and one-coat paints, mix in some matt varnish, up to about a third. A satin paint can be flattened with a matt paint of a close colour; mix each tone in its own small cup so later touch-ups match.
A tiny drop of washing-up liquid in these mixes helps them spread into corners instead of pulling away.
If flat panels look shiny or blotchy after a heavy wash, paint thinned base colour back over the raised flats only, stopping at the edges so the shading stays in the gaps.

A matt varnish over the finished, fully dry model evens everything out in one go and makes washed and drybrushed areas sit together. Varnishes differ: a standard one dulls only a little and a satin one adds shine, so use an ultra matt last for a truly flat finish. Add gloss back afterwards to anything meant to look wet.
Varnish before painting metallics, then add the metal on top so it stays shiny.
On a grimy scheme, a little uneven sheen or streaking from a wash can help the look.

guides.title: Thick varnish or primer filling detail
guides.summary: Let it cure, ease small pools out of recesses, and strip and redo it if thick coats have buried the detail.
body: Stop and do not add more coats. Let it dry for a full day; varnish and primer shrink as they cure, and some detail often comes back.
If it is still wet, wick pools out of recesses with a clean, damp brush. Tilt the model so the excess runs off rather than into detail.
Where only a few recesses are filled, work the dried varnish out with a stiff fine brush and a drop of water or its own thinner, a little at a time. Then repaint any shading you lost.
A small lump on a flat area can be sanded flat with very fine abrasive, then given one thin new coat to even the sheen.
If thick coats have buried detail all over, stripping is the cleanest fix. Strip, wash and dry the model, then prime and paint again. The second time is usually faster.
Prevent it next time. Shake the can well, spray light misty passes from about 20 to 30 cm, and let each pass dry. Brush varnish on thin and spread it, never flood it.

guides.title: Highlights that went too bright
guides.summary: Glaze the colour from the step before back over an over-bright highlight, then redo it smaller.
body: It is easy to jump too bright too fast, especially on skin and pale colours. Let the highlight dry before you judge it, as paint dries a little darker.

Thin the base or previous colour into a very wet glaze, test it on your nail or the palette, and pull it lightly over the over-bright area. Let it dry and repeat if needed. It tones the highlight down and smooths the join.
Then redo the highlight more carefully, in a smaller area.
If a step looks harsh while still wet, rinse the brush, take most of the water off on tissue and run it along the join to soften it.

Pick the glaze to suit the problem. Pale grey edges on black: thinned black. A cream highlight on yellow: the base yellow. Red gone orange or pink, or purple gone pink: a milky coat of the original base over the whole area.
If a whole garment looks stark, mix a dark wash with matt medium so it is weaker and brush it over everything. It ties the highlights back into the cloth without repainting.

If bright layers covered too much and the midtone is lost, glaze the midtone back over the transition a few times. Push the darkest areas back if contrast has faded, then repaint the brightest points.
Pale paints are mostly white and act fast. Add only a little to a mix, and test on your hand or the palette first.

guides.title: Transfers that tear, wrinkle or bubble
guides.summary: Most transfer trouble comes from a rough surface, a rushed soak, too much blotting or matt varnish straight on top.
body: Gloss varnish under the transfer prevents most trouble. Greyish see-through patches and a visible clear edge mean trapped air over a matt or rough surface. Gloss first, and trim the film close to the design.
If it curls in the water, leave it a little longer until it relaxes, or ease it flat with a damp brush. If it tears leaving the paper, it was forced: wait until it slides off on its own.

Keep it slightly damp so it can slide. Blotting too much makes it stick to the brush and dry out. If it grabs, add a drop of water around it and nudge it with the brush tip. If it lands in the wrong place, lift it while still wet and try again.

Once softening solution is on, the film is fragile. Use very light brush pressure and never scrub. Add softener in small amounts; a strong one helps on tight curves, but too much can melt the film or the plastic.
Press out bubbles while the softener is still working, or roll a damp cotton bud gently over them.

For a wrinkle, press the tip of a very sharp blade into the fold without sawing. The cut edges sink back into the solution; nudge them flat while wet. On big or curved transfers, make several small cuts so it follows the shape. If it dried crooked, rewet it with softener, wait, and ease it over.
Matt varnish straight onto a freshly softened transfer can leave white frosting. Seal it with gloss or satin first, then matt later. If the film edge or a shiny patch still shows, add more matt.
Put transfers on before weathering, so the grime ties them into the paint. Done well, they look painted on.

guides.title: Fixing wash tide marks and pools
guides.summary: Lift pools while wet, use enough wash and leave it alone to dry, and repaint the raised areas if marks dry in.
body: Wash collects on smooth flat areas, the low points of folds and robes, the bottom edge of banners and cloaks, and tips that stick out such as barrel ends and fingertips. Check every area while it is wet, before you reach for a hair dryer.

To lift a pool, keep a spare clean brush that is only damp. Touch it to the pool to wick the excess away, and move that wash into a recess that needs it. Repeat until even. A brush full of wash soaks nothing up.

Too little wash dries before it spreads and leaves blotches. Load enough to cover the area quickly, start away from tricky details and keep moving. Then leave it: brushing back into half-dry wash is what leaves hard rings, and brushing over it before it is dry lifts paint.

On large flat parts, thin the wash with medium, or add a drop of flow improver or washing-up liquid, and put it on in two thin coats. Lay the part flat and keep it still while it dries, one side at a time. On a slick metallic primer, a heavy flood slides off.
Where wash ends next to unwashed paint, pull the pigment towards the area that should be shaded. Feathering the edge like this stops hard rings.
Ready-made washes and one-coat paints can ring on smooth rounded panels. A normal paint thinned with plenty of water dries as an even tint instead, and you can stack coats for depth.

Give a heavy wash about 45 minutes to dry. Then layer the base colour back over raised areas, avoiding recesses. If the whole model was washed, tint the base slightly darker, with a little wash or a touch of mid brown, so the patch blends in. On textured areas a drybrush of the base fades blotches fast. Re-washing will not match.

If coloured wash pooled oddly where two materials meet, run a thin dark brown or grey along that seam instead. Wash heavily clogging fine detail can be lifted with a little paint stripper on just that spot, then repainted.

guides.title: Wet blends that look patchy
guides.summary: If the base shows through a wet blend, lay a solid midtone first, and keep paint workable with a little retarder.
body: Few paints cover in one coat, so a wet blend straight over a base coat often lets it show through. Paint a solid coat of the midtone over the whole area first. While it is wet, blend the darker tone into one end and the lighter into the other.
Acrylics dry fast. Work in small sections at a steady pace, and spread paint quickly after laying it down.

Stop as soon as the paint starts to drag. Brushing paint that has formed a skin lifts it and leaves a bumpy, peeling or blotchy surface. Let it dry fully, then make another pass. Two or three passes are normal, and a failed first pass does not need stripping.
If the light colour vanishes into the blend, you used too little of it. Strong midtones such as red swamp pale colours quickly, so load much more of the light paint.

A hard line or stripe usually comes from the bead of paint at the brush tip. Pull rather than push: point the tip towards the colour that is loaded on the brush, so the bead is not dragged across the other colour.

Use creamy paint, not watery. Paint that is too thin, often from a wet palette, falls apart in the blend. On larger areas, lay creamy paint on thinly, as thick paint gets scraped into stripes; do a second pass for strength. On tiny areas thicker paint is fine.
A small amount of drying retarder or flow improver extends the working time. Too much leaves a thick, glossy film.
If the blend is still stepped once dry, repaint the two colours with their edges closer and try again, or glaze over the join with a one to one mix of them. Stop glazing once it looks right.

guides.title: Removing wet paint slips
guides.summary: Lift a slip or flood of wet paint at once with a clean damp brush or a fingertip, before it dries.
body: Speed matters. These fixes only work while the paint is still wet, and stain-like one-coat paints set especially fast.
Keep a clean, damp synthetic brush, clean water and a lint-free cloth such as a glasses cloth beside you just for this, especially when painting eyes, lenses and small details.
On an open surface, wipe the slip straight off with a fingertip or the cloth. This also works on purpose: paint a shade slightly past the line, then wipe the raised areas clean before it dries.

In recesses, run the damp brush over the spot to loosen the paint, use it like a sponge to soak it up, then wipe it on tissue. Rinse and repeat. If water alone will not lift it, a little saliva on the brush often does without disturbing the layer below; soapy water is the last resort, then rinse.
For a flood, such as a clogged pot dumping one-coat paint on the model, soak up as much as you can with a large dry brush. Add a little clean water and soak it up again to lift more pigment.

Dark paint on yellow, white or a fresh light one-coat colour is the hardest slip to hide. Brush clean water, or the lighter colour, over it at once to thin and lift it, then soak it up. Leave the faint stain, finish the dark areas, then cover it with thin coats of a pale base and the original colour.
If flicked spatter spots land too large, run a wet brush over them while wet. They melt into a soft wash in the recesses.
Let the area dry, then paint over any faint mark with the colour underneath.

guides.title: Fixing a model that leans
guides.summary: Raise one foot on a rock or rubble so a model that leans too far stands upright.
body: Some sculpts lean so far forward that from the front you see only the top of the head.
Test the angle on the base before gluing anything.
Raise one foot on a rock, step or piece of rubble so the body tilts back upright.
If the model is pinned, bend or re-drill the pin to correct the angle.
Blend the raised piece into the rest of the base with texture or putty, then paint it as one.

guides.title: Fixing eyes that go wrong
guides.summary: Reline wonky eyes with the dark colour and try again, and use a dot of off-white for eyes you cannot reach.
body: Expect a few passes, often two or three. If the white floods over the dark outline, reline with the dark colour, let it dry and try again. Put the white on in small strokes from the middle outwards rather than outlining the eye.
Do not paint the iris as an outlined circle. A misplaced outline means starting over. A simple dot or short vertical line is easier to correct.

If the pupils look in different directions, let them dry, then trim a white back with the dark colour or add white to move a pupil. Make small changes and check from normal viewing distance. Putting both irises to the same side, so the figure glances sideways, hides small mismatches.
Eyes painted too large make a face look startled. Paint the skin colour back over the edges to narrow them, and tidy the surrounding skin.

A thick dark ring around the eye looks like heavy make-up. Paint the lids back in with shaded skin until only a hairline of dark remains. Off-white and a dark brown instead of pure white and black give a softer, more natural eye.
Judge the face once it is framed. Thin dark lines along the nose and around the sockets help features read, and blocking in the hair early stops a face looking unfinished.
For eyes hidden under a hat brim or in deep sockets, paint the face before gluing the hat on if you can, and tilt the model to find a clear line.
If you still cannot reach, or it is too fiddly, fill the socket with a deep brown or shade and touch in a tiny dot of off-white. In deep shadow that is enough.

guides.title: Flying stands
guides.summary: Make a strong, removable join between a flyer and its stand, and build sturdier or scenic stands for big models.
body: Plan the join before painting. A clear stand holds the model by a small peg that snaps or pulls out, so swap it for magnets or a pin early.

For magnets, fill the base's peg hole with putty to give a flat seat and glue a magnet on. Glue another to the top of the rod and hold it still until set. Check polarity first; if every rod faces the same way, models can swap stands.

Cut and sand the moulded pegs off the model. Put a blob of putty behind each model magnet and press it in place, then stand the model on its rod while the putty is soft. The magnets pull it into line; leave it to cure.

For a pin join, drill a socket in the underside the size of the rod and glue a stiff wire across it through two small side holes. An angled rod top rests against the wire, and turning the base changes the pose: level, banking or nose down.
For a scenic stand, glue a metal rod into a hole drilled in a rock, ruin or printed piece. Drill the model's matching hole at an angle so it banks and leans rather than sitting level.

Large flyers need a heavy base. Two layers of thin plywood glued with the grain crossing resist warping. Let the glue dry fully, then cut the circle with a jigsaw, tilting the blade for a tapered edge.

Drill a pilot hole at the centre, open it with a flat bottomed bit to fit the rod, and stop short of going through so the rod has more to grip. Pack a loose rod with putty and super glue, set it straight, and saw the top at about 45 degrees as a cradle.
A magnet or pin join lifts off, so the model travels flat and can go on the table without its stand.

guides.title: Foliage camouflage on vehicles
guides.summary: Glue small leafy sprigs to a finished vehicle with PVA, vary them on each one, and handle it gently after.
body: Paint and weather the vehicle first. The sprigs go on last.
Use small dry leafy sprigs, such as torn pieces of foliage clump or trimmed dried plant. Keep them to scale; a branch longer than a hatch looks wrong.
Glue them on with PVA where a crew would tie branches: turret sides, hull edges and the front plate. Keep hatches, vision slits and the gun clear.
Vary the amount and layout from vehicle to vehicle so a group does not look stamped out of one mould.
The sprigs are fragile. Let the glue dry fully, then handle and transport the model with care.

guides.title: Why copying a painting guide looks different
guides.summary: The same paints give different results depending on how they go on, so treat a guide as a starting point.
body: Knowing the exact colours is only a small part of a look. How thick the paint is, the order of the steps, the number of glaze passes and the method used all change the result far more.

Thick layers, thin glazes, wet blending and feathering all look different with the same paints. Highlighting with pale colours and then glazing the base back over looks unlike mixing the steps directly.
Neighbouring colours change how a colour reads. A mid grey looks nearly white beside black and dark beside white, so a colour copied onto a different scheme can look wrong.
Exact paints matter most for special effects and technical products. For an ordinary red or blue, any similar red or blue gets you close.

Read a picture guide all the way through before you start. Late steps can change early ones, such as priming one part a different colour. Check you have every colour and transfer, or pick close matches.
Zoom in on pictures to judge where highlights sit. Still images do not show how a stroke is made, so watching the same step being painted helps too.
Brush control, paint consistency and judgement come from practice with your own tools. Expect to adjust and experiment, and paint lots of models. A finished model beats a perfect copy.

guides.title: Filling gaps between parts
guides.summary: Fill join lines and gaps that show through paint with glue, putty or paint by gap size, then sand smooth before priming.
body: Let the glue set fully, ideally overnight, before filling or sanding; a fresh join goes stringy. Joins in sockets or under plates hide themselves. Joins across faces, scales or smooth panels show worst once washed or drybrushed.

Hairline seams on a close fit: brush plastic glue on both faces and squeeze so softened plastic beads out of the join. Once hard, scrape the ridge off with a blade edge and sand flush. Keep thumbs off soft glue.

Small gaps: dab in super glue with a pin, or sprinkle in baking soda or mix in talc and add glue for a fast, hard fill. It sets warm, so use little and ventilate. Sprue goo glues and fills plastic at once. UV curing resin sets in seconds but grips weakly, so use it in hidden spots and wear a mask and eye protection when sanding it.

Water based paste fillers suit gaps under about 1 mm. Lay a small blob in with an old brush, rinse the brush to damp, and draw it gently away along each side of the gap so the filler feathers to nothing. Glide rather than press. They shrink, so expect two or three thin coats, and sand them dry, as water dissolves them again.

Solvent tube putties grip plastic well and dry fast, but they shrink, soften nearby detail and give off strong fumes. Use them only on small seams, smooth them with a damp tool while soft, and work with fresh air.

Larger gaps: knead two-part epoxy putty to one even colour, press a thin sausage in and smooth it with a wet tool or rubber shaper. On fur or hair, use a softer putty and push matching texture in. Fill very deep holes first with foil, super glue or a mesh patch, then level with putty.

Overfill slightly, as most fillers shrink. Leave putty at least four hours, ideally overnight; thick fills stay soft inside. Shave flush with light knife passes, then sand from about 400 to 1000 grit, bending the paper round curves. If it dried into a dip, fill proud again and sand back.

On a painted model, run thinned base coat into a hairline gap again and again until it fills, then repaint. Check every model under a strong light before priming; primer shows any seam left, so fill, sand and prime that spot again.

guides.title: Gluing models to bases
guides.summary: Glue the model down before texturing so the feet blend in, or after painting with a wiped drop of super glue.
body: Check which base size the model needs before gluing anything, so you never have to cut a figure off later.

There are two good orders. On a plain base, glue the model down first: the ground blends into the feet and the base gives you something to hold. On a detailed sculpted, resin or printed base, paint model and base separately so the brush reaches every bit of texture, then join them at the end.

Before texturing: glue the model on, then apply texture paste with a small tool near the feet so detail is not buried. Dab the wet paste with an old frayed brush for roughness, and press small dips where you want puddles.
Thick texture can take two or three times longer to dry than usual. Leave it fully dry before priming.

On a finished base: glue holds poorly on paint, so scrape a small patch back to bare material where the feet sit. Put a little super glue on the feet, touch them down on a mat to take off the excess, then press onto the base. Less glue means no shiny bulges round the feet.
A figure on its own small integral base needs only two small dots of glue under it. Press it down firmly so a little glue seals the edge, then texture over the join.
Much of the base hides under the model, so do not spend time detailing what will not be seen. Once joined, add a little of the ground colour up the feet as dust or mud to tie model and base together.

guides.title: Gluing painted parts together
guides.summary: Scrape paint off the contact points so you glue bare plastic, then join painted parts with a little super glue.
body: Glue on painted parts only holds as well as the paint does, so heavy arms and weapons snap off easily.

Scrape the paint and primer off both contact points with a file, a hobby knife or a metal pick until bare plastic shows. On a ball joint, clean the ball, and use a pointed file tip to clear a ring inside the socket too.

Super glue is the safer choice, as plastic glue melts the surface and dissolves the paint around the joint. Plastic glue can work on bare plastic if you lay the tiniest amount on with a fine needle applicator, but any overspill marks the paint.
Apply a very small amount to the contact points only, so nothing squeezes out onto finished paint. Touch the part on a mat first to take off any excess, then hold it still while the join sets.

For heavy painted parts, add a pin as well. When painting in sub-assemblies, keeping the contact points free of paint saves the scraping later. If your gluing tends to be messy, assemble first and paint after.

guides.title: Gluing small parts
guides.summary: Put glue on a scrap and apply tiny amounts with a pin, so small parts stay neat and nothing floods.
body: Squeezing super glue straight from the bottle floods small joints. Only a thin film is needed; extra glue sets slower and can fog nearby detail. Wick away a little excess with the corner of a cotton bud, but never mop a big puddle that way, as soaked cotton can get hot and smoke.
Put a drop on scrap plastic card, then pick up a tiny amount on the tip of a straightened paper clip, pin or short wire and touch it to the contact point only.

Pick up tiny bits like buckles and rivets by lightly spearing them on a craft knife tip or with tweezers. Touch them into the glue; it holds them and pulls them off the blade. To test an angle first, hold the part on a blob of putty on an old brush handle.

Plastic glue needs bare plastic, so scrape primer off the contact point. An extra thin plastic glue needs only a dot touched to the join; capillary action pulls it in. Put it on the part that is not moving, then seat the other.

Shave the leftover sprue nub off tiny joints with a sharp knife so they sit flush. On small models with many legs, glue one leg onto every model in the batch, let them set, then add the next. Gluing all the legs at once leaves a wobbly model and fingerprints in the glue.

Thin parts like sword blades often snap at a weak point. A clean break lines up well: glue it with a tiny drop, hold it straight, and smooth the join with a fine emery board. If a part gets squashed, cut it at an angle that looks like a natural break.
Fill small gaps at the back with stretched sprue melted in with glue. If a tiny part will not stay put, a dab of UV curing resin set with a UV torch locks it in.

guides.title: Getting a strong, neat glue joint
guides.summary: Clean and roughen the contact faces, use only a little glue, hold the joint still and let it cure fully.
body: Dry fit every joint first. File or sand anything that rocks or leaves a big seam; faces that meet flush bond far better than glue bridging a gap.
Clean the faces of dust, oil and mould release. Wash resin and metal parts in warm soapy water and let them dry. Scrape off any paint or primer, as glue is only as strong as the paint it sits on.

Super glue holds poorly on smooth, flat faces, especially metal and resin. Score small nicks across both faces with a hobby knife so the glue has something to grip. On many small resin and metal parts this is enough to avoid pinning.
Use plastic glue for plastic to plastic, as it welds the parts together. Use super glue for metal, resin and mixed materials.

Put a small amount on one face only. Too much super glue sets slowly, turns brittle and fogs detail; too much plastic glue melts detail. Thin plastic glue that squeezes out can be left to melt into the seam. Wipe super glue ooze away before it sets.
Press the parts together straight away in the dry fit position and hold them still. Use tape, rubber bands, small clamps or a helping hands stand for awkward joints.
Set time is when you can let go; full cure is when the joint can take weight. Do not prime, pose or stress it until it is fully cured, then fill any seam left with putty.
Glue with fresh air in the room and keep paper towel or cotton buds handy for spills.

guides.title: Head swaps
guides.summary: Pick a head that fits the neck, seat it at a natural height, and hide the join with a tiny ball of epoxy putty.
body: Gather spare heads of roughly the right scale. Neck width matters most: a head that fits the joint blends in, one that does not looks stuck on. Try each with a little tack at different angles; judge horns and crests on the model, not in your hand.
A new head often sits too high or leaves a gap at the neck. Trim the neck peg or socket, and the back of the head if needed, until it sits at a believable height.

Where the body has a block and the head needs a socket, drill a pilot hole in the middle of the collar and carve outwards with a knife, or work up through bigger bits. Twist by hand; a power tool melts plastic. Set the hole slightly back so the face sits behind a high collar.
To put a new face in an open helmet, carve out the old head, then shave the new one down, mostly at the back and sides. Test fit often; it takes many small cuts.

Roll a very small ball of two-part epoxy putty and press it where the neck meets the body. Push the new head in so the putty fills the gap. Angle it to look where the weapon points or where the action is.
Tacking the head with a little thin plastic cement lets you nudge it while the bond is soft. A tiny dot of super glue stops it falling off while you sculpt the neck.
Smooth or shape the putty with a fine tool, wetted or lightly greased so it does not stick. Ridges like armour joints blend the join in. Leave it at least four hours, ideally overnight.
A head slightly smaller than the kit one makes the body look larger and more imposing. Leave the head loose for painting if you can.

guides.title: Making transfers look painted on
guides.summary: Hide a transfer's shiny film with gloss under it and thin matt varnish over it, then shade and chip it so it looks painted on.
body: Put transfers on early, before washes and weathering, so they get the same treatment as the surface around them. Lay them on gloss varnish so the film sits flat, and use a thin coat of softening solution so they mould to curves. Soaking them makes them fragile and they tear.

Let the transfer dry completely; a hair dryer can blow it out of place. Then brush thinned matt varnish or matt medium over it and its edges in two or three thin coats with a soft brush, blotting any that pools. The varnish settles around the film edge and hides it. A thick coat can dry milky.

Varnish the whole panel in the same sheen so it matches. Without this, later washes gather along the raised film edge and outline the transfer. When washing, blot off any liquid that collects around the edge.

Glaze very thin black or shade over the lower part so it darkens with the panel, and add a few fine chips and a little grime across it, painted on or scratched with a needle tip. They also hide any wrinkles.

Paint the area under a dark transfer lighter so the design stands out. Thin transfers take on the colour beneath, so one laid across two colours looks patchy; once set, paint over its coloured part with a matching colour.

If a transfer is the wrong colour or vanishes into the paint, seal it and paint over the design itself in a colour that stands out, using it as a guide. Shiny metallic transfers that clash with painted metal can be painted over lightly in matt colours.

If no transfer comes in the colour you need, paint one of the right shape with an opaque colour while it is still on the backing sheet. Let it dry, then cut it out and apply it as normal. Handle it gently, as the paint stiffens the film.
Seal one transfer before stacking another on top, and seal the finished transfers so they do not rub off. A non-yellowing varnish is safer over light colours.

guides.title: Beating hobby burnout
guides.summary: Take a break without guilt, paint one model just for fun, and keep quick one-sitting models to hand.
body: Long projects, especially big hordes, can feel endless, and motivation comes and goes for everyone. Taking a break is fine, and long projects drag less when they are models you really like.

If one area will not come right after hours of trying, stop for the day, eat and rest. Tired painting makes it worse. A few glazes with fresh eyes next session often fix it. When you run out of steam on a whole piece, put it aside and work on something else rather than forcing it.

Keep a small box of simple one-off models you can finish in a sitting, or swap between a quick batch of army models and one slow display piece. Finishing something lifts motivation for the big project.
Keep a model you like but do not need, just to experiment on. Try a new basing idea, a glow, a cartoon or comic style, or a different kind of paint. If it fails it does not matter.

For a low-pressure session, pick a model that builds quickly, get colour on straight away with a coloured shadow from below and a bright light from above, then start with the part that drew you to it and follow whatever catches your eye next.
When nothing appeals, look through your unpainted models until one sparks an idea or a scene. That is often enough to start.

On an army, set a lower standard on purpose so it gets finished. Spend real time on the parts you enjoy, such as skin or fur, and move faster on small details. Varying tones across a group keeps it interesting.
Pair desk time with things you enjoy, such as audiobooks, music or comfort films, and break dull jobs, like repeated trim, into short sessions.

guides.title: Keeping hobby kit safe from pets and children
guides.summary: Blades, glue, solvents, resin and small parts go in a closed box out of reach, and lids go back on before you leave the desk.
body: Treat blades, superglue, solvents, strippers, resin and spray cans as the dangerous group. Keep them in a closed box or cupboard, up high or locked, never in an open caddy on the desk.
Most hobby acrylics are low risk on skin, but they are not food. Some pigments contain heavy metals, and metallics, inks and washes can contain alcohol or other solvents. Keep all paint out of reach.
Put the lids back on pots and the rinse cup when you leave the desk. A cat knocking over a rinse pot is a stain. A cat drinking from it is a trip to the vet.
Count blades and pins back into their box at the end of a session. A dropped blade or sharp sprue offcut in the carpet is a hazard for paws and bare feet. Sweep under the desk.

Liquid resin, fresh prints and resin wash alcohol are the worst for pets and children. Keep the printer and wash station behind a closed door, and wash and cure prints fully before anyone handles them.
Small parts, bases and magnets are choking hazards. Magnets are dangerous if two are swallowed, since they can pinch through the gut. Keep them in sealed tubs.
If something is swallowed or splashed in an eye, rinse with water and call a doctor, vet or poison line straight away. Take the container so they can read the label.
Wash your hands after painting and before touching food, pets or small children.

guides.title: Saving money in the hobby
guides.summary: Cut costs with home-made washes, the right brush for each job, fewer duplicate paints and less waste.
body: Get only the colours the current scheme needs. A small core set plus mixing covers a lot. Keep paints in a rack where you can see every colour, so you do not end up with doubles.

Mix your own washes and glazes. A simple base is matt varnish, a drop of flow aid and water, tinted with any paint you already have. Match paint to the base: oil paint in oil-based washes, watercolour in water-based ones.
Use cheap synthetic brushes for priming, base coats, drybrushing and texture. Save fine natural-hair brushes for detail and blending, and clean them well so they last for years.
A tiny dab of oil paint goes a long way, so a tube lasts far longer than a pot of acrylic.

Waste less paint. Put out small amounts, keep lids closed, and use a wet palette so mixes stay usable between sessions. An airbrush uses nearly all the paint in its cup, while a brush loses some in the bristles.
Basing does not need kits. Sand, grit, cork, twigs and kitchen spices make good ground, rocks and texture for very little.

guides.title: Types of hobby paint explained
guides.summary: Base, layer, wash, one-coat, dry, technical and air paints are all acrylics made thicker or thinner for different jobs.
body: Most hobby paints are acrylic. The labels mostly describe how thick the paint is and how much pigment it holds. They all mix with each other and thin with water.
Base paints are thick and opaque, made to cover in one or two coats over primer. They suit big areas and solid starts. Thin them a little so they do not hide detail.
Layer paints are thinner and less opaque, made to build highlights in smooth steps over a base. Light colours may need several coats to cover.

Washes, also called shades, are very thin, see-through paints that run into recesses. Contrast-style one-coat paints sit between a wash and a base: over a light undercoat they colour and shade in one coat.
Dry paints are thick and paste-like, made for drybrushing texture. Technical paints cover special effects, such as base texture, crackle, rust, blood, gloss for gems and clear glowing liquid.
Air paints are thinned ready for the airbrush. By brush they work as glazes or smooth thin layers. Inks are strong, bright and thin, good for glazes and for tinting your own washes.
You do not need every type. A few base colours, a wash or two and a good white go a long way. Thick paint can always be thinned; thin paint is hard to make cover.

guides.title: Safety with paints, fumes, solvents and dust
guides.summary: Ventilate, wear a sealed mask with the right filters, keep solvents and resin off skin, and do not lick brushes.
body: Work with a window open or good airflow, and take breaks. Spray cans and airbrushes belong outdoors or in a spray booth that pulls the mist out of the room.
Wear a respirator for spray cans, airbrushing, solvent paints and thinners, plastic glue, sanding and resin dust. Paper dust masks, even good ones, only stop particles and do nothing against fumes.

For general hobby use, pick a combined filter rated A2 for organic vapours and the top particle class for fine dust. Uncured printing resin gives off a wider range of vapours, so it needs a filter that also covers inorganic vapours (B2 or higher), and ventilation alone is not enough.

The mask must seal against your face, as any gap lets unfiltered air in. Choose one comfortable enough to wear for a whole session; a mask left on the desk protects nothing. A half-face mask with replaceable cartridges works out cheaper for regular use.
Wear disposable nitrile gloves for uncured resin, solvents and cleaning prints, and wash any splash off skin straight away.

Enamel thinners and white spirit are toxic to breathe, so keep lids on jars when not in use. Rubbing alcohol is flammable with a flame that is hard to see; keep it away from heat, including hair dryers. Some glass cleaners used as thinner contain ammonia, so do not breathe them in.

Do not lick brushes. A non-toxic label covers normal use, not swallowing paint, and a colour name does not tell you which pigments are in it. Metallics and pigments containing chromium, cadmium, cobalt, manganese or lead need extra care. Point the brush on the palette or a damp cloth instead.

Flow improvers are harmful if swallowed or breathed in, so only spray them with strong ventilation. Keep drinks and food well apart from the rinse water, and read the safety data sheet for any product you are unsure of.

guides.title: Making a model hover
guides.summary: Fix a model to a tall piece of terrain on its base so it looks airborne without a clear flying stand.
body: Find a tall scrap of terrain, such as a wall corner, tree stump or small rock, and hold it against the model to check the height.
Cut the terrain piece fully off its frame first, then saw it to shape. Sawing it while still on the frame goes badly.
Trim it so it sits inside the edge of the base, and push it to one side to leave room for the model.
Choose a hidden contact point on the model, such as the back of a pack or a trailing foot, to join to the terrain. Scrape the joint flush.
Pin the joint with wire for strength, as the model will be held at an awkward angle.

For a ghostly figure with no legs, drill a long brass rod into the body to act as a handle and later as the support. Bulk out the lower body with putty and cover it with chain or trailing cloth. Wear eye protection if grinding metal.

guides.title: Do you need an airbrush
guides.summary: Not to paint well, but an airbrush makes base coats, priming and smooth light fast when much of a model is one colour.
body: You do not need one. Everything an airbrush does can be done by brush, only slower, while the reverse is not true. Brushes cost less, need less upkeep and travel easily, and brush skills make the airbrush easier to learn later.

The biggest gain is fast, smooth base coats and priming in any colour you can mix, even with paints that brush on patchily. An even white base coat can take five to ten minutes a model by brush and about two by airbrush. Spray cans come in only a few colours.

It also makes a light sketch or pre-shade in minutes rather than an hour, ready to cover with translucent one-coat paints. Smooth fades, glows, thin filters, stencil and masking work, and controlled varnish coats are all easier too.

It saves time when a big share of each model, roughly 40 percent or more, is one colour or smooth surface: armies, vehicles and large armoured models. Busy models with many small colour areas suit a brush. Setting up just to spray something small costs more than it saves.
Faces, fine detail, dark lining, edge highlights, drybrushing and small points of light still need a brush.
A budget airbrush and a small compressor are enough to start. A cleaning pot is handy but not essential. Good kit looked after lasts many years.

It is one more tool to learn and maintain. Paint drying in it during long sessions clogs it, and clearing a clog can take longer than the time saved. Spray in a booth so you do not breathe the mist. With water based acrylics, wear a filter mask and gloves; solvent based paints need much stronger ventilation.
If you do get one, practise pre-shading on lots of models. It teaches distance, angle and paint consistency faster than anything else.

guides.title: Keeping and disposing of solvents and strippers
guides.summary: Keep solvents sealed, labelled, cool and out of reach, and never pour them down a drain; take the waste to a hazardous waste site.
body: Keep solvents and strippers in their original labelled containers with the lids done up tight. If you decant some, use a glass or solvent-safe bottle and write what it is on the side.
Keep them somewhere cool, dry and dark, away from heaters, flames and the boiler. Many thinners and alcohols are flammable, and their vapour can drift a long way.
Put them up high or in a locked cupboard, away from food and drink. Never reuse a drinks bottle for a solvent, and never leave an open jar of stripper on the desk.
Work with a window open and gloves on, and put the lid back on as soon as you have poured. Keep jars of soaking models covered between checks.
Rags and paper towels soaked in oil paint or solvent can heat up as they dry. Lay them flat outside to dry, or keep them in a sealed metal tin with water before throwing them away.
Never pour solvent or stripper down a sink, drain or toilet, or onto the ground. Let used stripper settle, pour the clear part back for reuse, and let the sludge dry out in an open tub outside.
Take used solvent and dried sludge to your local recycling or waste centre as household hazardous waste. Local rules vary, so check them first.
If a bottle has lost its label or turned gooey, do not guess what it is. Treat it as hazardous waste and dispose of it the same way.

guides.title: Keeping white clean
guides.summary: White shows every trace of another colour, so use clean water, fresh paint and paint white areas last.
body: Even a trace of another colour visibly tints white. Red in the rinse water turns it pink.
Change to clean water before painting white, or keep a separate rinse pot for it, as you would for metallics.
Red pigment lingers in bristles even after rinsing. Rinse the brush, dip it in a little black paint and rinse again. Any tint left is grey, which hurts white far less than pink.
If the white on the palette gets tinted, replace it. Clean the mixing area well; fibres and dried flecks show on pale surfaces.

Paint white areas last where you can, since mistakes on white are hard to fix. Shade the white first with a light grey wash, then wash dark details next to it with a small brush and very little wash so nothing splashes.

Keep a high-coverage off-white for corrections. One coat usually hides a dark spill, where a weak white needs three or four thin coats, each left to dry. Over red, use the same off-white and patient thin coats; the first will look pink and see-through.
Avoid wet blending into white. Darker colours overwhelm it easily.
Seal finished white areas with varnish. Handling rubs paint off, and marks show badly on white.

guides.title: Kitbashing
guides.summary: Combine parts from different kits into a new model by starting with a strong pose and changing the outline.
body: Start simple. A head swap alone makes a big difference; next try a hand or weapon swap, such as trimming the head off a spear to make a staff. Kits from the same maker and scale often share neck and shoulder joints, so parts swap with no cutting.

For a bigger build, start from a core model you like for its pose and size. Pick parts that match its scale, style and level of detail. Parts from much bigger kits look comic, and from smaller ones like a pinhead.
Do not assemble it yet. Swapping parts is far easier while pieces are loose, such as cutting out a chest plate before the body halves are joined.

Dry fit bits from your spares with tacky putty until ideas come. Let the model's story steer what you pick. A theme helps: list the few visual signs of it, such as a round shield and a crested helmet, and look for parts that carry them.

Change the outline. A new head, helmet or shoulder shape does most to make it read as something new. New arms change the whole pose, and turning the head the other way makes a known model read differently. Avoid neat symmetry in repeated parts.

Remove unwanted parts a little at a time with clippers, then a knife and file. Slice the surface flat where a new part sits, as glue holds far better on flat faces. A weapon made for the wrong hand can be cut at the hilt and pinned into the other. Glue the main body first.

Spread small themed details over the whole model rather than relying on one or two big swaps. Blend joins with putty so add-ons look built in; neat sculpting at the joins makes a conversion. Spare cloaks, plates and chains hide rough joins.

Clear shapes read better than subtle additions. Keep loose elements like hair, tails and cloth flowing in one direction. Prime the whole model one colour to judge it and spot gaps, as mixed plastic colours make it look worse than it is.

guides.title: Kitbashing terrain from junk and kits
guides.summary: Turn old toys, packaging and spare scenery kits into new terrain by hiding their old shapes under kit parts.
body: Old plastic toys, playsets, packaging, wooden toy blocks and spare scenery kits make good starting shapes. Charity and bargain stalls are good places to look. Wash toys in warm soapy water and let them dry.

Empty your spare parts box and lay everything out. Look for shapes that suit a new job: a tank becomes a boiler, floor panels a deck, a gun barrel a chimney. Cleaned sprue makes walkway supports and ladder sides, with plastic card strips as rungs.
Lay pieces out dry first, then build a flat, braced, stable base and add everything else to it. Hot glue joins blocks and foam quickly and can be pulled apart to redo a mistake.

Replace plain, toy looking parts with detailed kit parts, and cover large blank areas with thin plastic panels cut to size. Parts can go on upside down or inside out to hide details that would look wrong. For vehicles, keep a real machine's length and width, or it looks like a toy.

Flat laser-cut wooden buildings gain depth from coffee stirrers glued on as beams and doors, nicked with a knife so they look hand hewn. Coat bare walls with grit texture, and replace warped roof parts with plastic card.
Run small wires and cables across walls and machines. They add detail and hide messy joins. Watered filler brushed over joints and stabbed with the brush gives a rough stone texture.
Check that bases fit on stairs and ledges before painting. Playsets made to be seen from one side suit a display shelf or the back of a board.

Prime the whole piece one colour. Kitbashes look rough until primed, then suddenly read as one object. Paint it in the same scheme as your other terrain. In a hurry, matt varnish and a little grime round vents make a toy usable as it is.

guides.title: Lengthening and shortening weapons
guides.summary: Join two copies of a weapon to make it longer, or cut a section out of a barrel to shorten it.
body: To lengthen, take two copies of the weapon. Cut the end off one and the start off the other at the same slight angle so details line up.
Brush plastic glue on one cut face, line the pieces up and check they are straight. Run a little more glue into the join so the plastic melts together.
When fully dry, scrape the seam with a hobby knife so it reads as one surface.
To shorten a barrel, saw off the muzzle end, then cut the barrel near its base with a knife where a saw would catch other detail.
Trim the faces so the muzzle sits level and straight, then glue the ends together. Repeat the same cut on matching weapons so they agree.
Test fit on the model before gluing. Longer parts can clash with other parts in ways you did not plan.

guides.title: Lighting and magnification
