guides.summary: Even daylight lamps stop colours looking different the next morning, and a cheap magnifier makes fine detail easier to see.
body: Good light comes right after brushes and paint. It shows true colours, reveals rough blends and stops your eyes tiring. Even a basic lamp is far better than room lighting, and it matters most if you paint in the evening.

Pick daylight bulbs, about 5000 to 6500K, and use the same in every lamp; mixed colours muddy what you see. Warm bulbs tint everything orange. Look for a colour rendering (CRI) of 90 or more, and about 800 to 1000 lumens per lamp so it stays bright once diffused.

Diffuse the light. A bare point of light throws hard shadows and glare spots, which hide detail as badly as dim light. A lamp with a white cover, several bulbs or a wide panel spreads it evenly. Never cover a hot bulb with paper.

Place lamps so your hand does not shadow the model; two, one over each shoulder, work well. Old fluorescent tubes often flicker, which causes tired eyes and headaches, so use a steady flicker-free LED. LEDs also run cooler, so your palette dries out less.

A magnifying visor, reading glasses or a magnifying lamp makes fine vents, faces, eyes and small edges much easier. Try an inexpensive option first. Glass lenses are clearer and less tiring than cheap plastic ones over long sessions, and a visor must sit firmly without tilting your head.

About 2 to 3 times magnification suits most work. Stronger lenses shorten the gap to the model, roughly 25 cm at 2 times and 15 cm at nearly 3, and blur anything that moves. If the brush handle bumps the lens, drop a step.

Magnifiers help at every stage, not just final details. Seeing exactly when the brush meets an edge stops you pressing too hard and flooding paint. Good light and magnification help more than any special brush; bracing your hands and loading the brush well do the rest.
Judge final colours away from the magnifier too, at normal viewing distance and ideally in daylight.

guides.title: Loading the brush
guides.summary: Load paint halfway up the bristles, then roll off the excess on a damp towel so the brush comes to a sharp point.
body: Rinse the brush and blot it on a towel so it is damp, not wet.
Dip only the tip, carefully, and load until the bristles are about half full. Keep paint well away from the metal collar, or it dries there and the brush splays.
Do not go straight to the model. A loaded brush acts like a sponge and lets go of far too much on contact, flooding detail or leaving a raised blob with its own texture.
Roll and drag the brush on a slightly damp paper towel or tissue, or twist it on the palette, to take off the excess and reform the point. Hold it on the towel longer to wick off more.
Keep the towel damp. A dry one sucks the brush dry and leaves a splayed tip. Thick, slow absorbing mechanics towels give more control and do not shed fibres.

Test on your thumb, nail or a spare base: it should give tiny dots and fine lines on demand. If it floods, wick more off; if paint will not leave the brush, add a touch of water. A wet palette can make paint look thinner than it behaves on the model.

Inks, one-coat paints and fine metallics rush off at the lightest touch, so blot before every stroke. The same unloading keeps a wash where you want it, and lets a thinned highlight go on slightly see-through so you can build it in a few passes.
If the brush starts to drag or bend and you find yourself pressing, stop. Rinse, reload and test again; small brushes dry quickly in a warm room. Load gently, then use the brush with confidence.

guides.title: Magnetising models
guides.summary: Small magnets in joints let you swap heads, weapons and options on one model.
body: Magnets let one model carry several options, such as a helmet or bare head, or different weapons, and let a big model come apart for painting. Magnetise only what you will really swap, usually heads and weapon hands. If a part never changes, glue it.

Plan it before the main halves go together. On ball joints, cut the ball off flush and glue a magnet where it was, or drill into a small ball for a smaller magnet. Odd locating pegs and holes often need filing flat before a magnet will sit.

Drill a hole sized to the magnet so it sits flush; a magnet glued to a bare flat face pops off. Pack hollow parts with two-part putty and press the magnet in. Thin solid parts split when drilled, so thicken them with glued plastic sheet first.

Glue a magnet into the body first and let it set. Before gluing each matching magnet, stick it onto the body magnet so it faces the right way, and mark its outer face. Glue it in marked face out, then test the fit on every option.
Keep magnet sizes and polarity the same on every mount, so any weapon fits any mount and parts can move between models.

Heavy weapons need big magnets. Small ones in thin plastic let arms droop and fall; going from 1 mm to 1.5 mm thick discs in load-bearing joints makes a big difference. Set a large magnet flush into solid plastic, and key the joint with a short slot or square tube so it cannot spin.

For light parts like shields, a small ball of reusable tack works without magnets; black tack hides better than blue. A snug socket can also hold an unglued option. Sand the contact faces slightly first, as paint and varnish add thickness.
Fill the seam on the fixed side with putty so the swap point is hidden, and paint the options separately. Paint several shield designs and one squad in neutral colours can serve different sides.

guides.title: Making barbed wire for bases
guides.summary: Twist thin wire into a strand, add short knotted barbs, and run it along posts and wall tops with care for your fingers.
body: Use thin, soft wire, such as fine craft or florist wire. Clamp two lengths together at one end and twist them evenly, by hand or with a hand drill, until the strand is tight.
Keep gentle tension on the wire while twisting so it does not curl and kink on itself.
For barbs, knot a short piece of wire round the strand every few millimetres and snip the ends short. Pull each knot tight with pliers on both ends rather than your fingers, as the wire cuts skin.
For a safer version with fewer spikes, use the twisted strand alone and skip the barbs and cutting. At table distance it still reads as wire.
Gather every offcut as you go. They are small, sharp and easy to step on or lose in carpet.
Wrap it round fence posts and stumps for a rural fence, or run it along wall tops and wire fences for an urban look. Let it sag a little between posts rather than pulling it straight.
Fix it at the posts with a dot of super glue, then paint it a dark metal and add rust with a brown wash or a few dabs of orange.

guides.title: Making casualty models
guides.summary: Pose spare bodies lying down with limp arms and a turned head, building only for the view from above.
body: Look through spare frames for bodies with a bend in the knee; they lie naturally on the front or side. Straight, stiff poses suit figures lying flat on the back or front.
A casualty is only seen from above. Cut away arm parts or shoulders that stop the body lying flat, even if it looks wrong from below.
Try several left and right arms in place, matching the sleeves to the body. Relaxed, loose arms look best. Hands made to grip a gun still pass if they are half hidden.
Cut the head off and reattach it turned to one side so it rests against the ground.
Test fit with poster putty for a rough idea, but remember the putty lifts parts and changes the angle slightly.
Fill gaps around the head and under the body with super glue set with accelerator, or with filler. Sand or texture on the base hides the rest of the joins.
Casualties make good markers for wounded figures and objectives, or scenery for an ambush or a display base.

guides.title: Making your own transfers
guides.summary: Print designs on waterslide decal paper, seal inkjet ink before use, and use white sheet for dark surfaces.
body: Waterslide decal paper comes for inkjet or laser printers, in clear or white backed sheets. Clear shows only the printed image, so it suits light surfaces. Dark surfaces need white backed sheet.

Make a page the size of the sheet in an image editor; a vector editor gives crisper edges. Use images with transparent backgrounds. Scale with the proportions locked, then zoom in and clean up rough edges, as the decal stays on the model for good.
Repeat the design many times across the sheet so nothing is wasted, keeping clear of the edges your printer cannot reach.
Inkjet ink runs in water unless sealed. Follow the sheet's instructions, usually a sprayed decal film that sets the ink and strengthens the paper. A matt varnish may not be enough.
On white sheet, cutting round a complex outline leaves rough white edges. Put the design on a simple shape like a circle, ideally in the colour of the surface it goes on.

Apply over gloss varnish. Use setting solution, then press out liquid and bubbles with a makeup sponge, repeating as bubbles return. Softener helps over panel lines but can wrinkle very thin decals, so use it only where needed.
Home printing suits flat, matt colours. Shiny gold or silver transfers need a different process.

guides.title: Handling metallic paints
guides.summary: Keep separate water and brushes for metallics, use them barely thinned, and move them to a dry palette if they split.
body: Metallic paint carries tiny flakes that linger in rinse water, brushes and palettes, then show up as glitter or a dull haze in matte colours and washes.

Use a separate rinse pot for metallics, or change the water before going back to other colours. Use separate, older soft synthetic brushes too; the flakes lodge in the bristles, gum up near the collar and wear brushes out faster.
The flakes settle fast, so shake or stir the pot hard before use and again in long sessions. If you can, paint all the metallics in one session and clean the palette afterwards.

Thin metallics only a little, with a drop of water to about the feel of milk, or wet the brush and dip it straight in. Too much water breaks up the flakes and leaves runny, blotchy coverage. Thick, paste like metallics can go on almost neat with a damp brush. Alcohol-based metallics need their own thinner and synthetic brushes.

Build two or three thin coats, laying each across the direction of the last to hide brush strokes, and let each dry fully so the flakes lie flat. Metal shows every ridge of thick paint, and varnish will not hide it. A lumpy part can be stripped with a cotton bud and isopropyl alcohol and redone.

Very fluid metallics run into recesses and can flick specks off a springy brush. Wick the brush on a towel first, use a thicker metallic for chains and rivets, paint them slowly, and check nearby areas for silver specks.

Some metallics separate into flakes and medium, or turn to goo, on a wet palette within minutes. If yours do, use a dry palette or glazed tile and stir the puddle often. Others are fine there; the flakes do not travel through the paper, so just keep them apart from other colours.

Shade with a matching metallic, a dark wash or a thin glaze, and highlight with a lighter metallic, so the area stays reading as metal. Let metallics dry fully before handling. A satin varnish evens a patchy sheen but dulls the shine, so test it first.

guides.title: Mixing your own wash
guides.summary: Any paint thinned with water or medium becomes a wash, so you can make a shade in exactly the colour you need.
body: A wash is just paint with less pigment and more water and binder. Thin an ordinary paint with water, acrylic medium or both to get a wash in any colour. It helps when ready made shades are too dark or have too much black in them.

Medium is the better base. Water alone lets the pigment split and spread unevenly. Medium keeps it bound so it dries smoothly with fewer tide marks, and stays workable longer so you can lift mistakes. A drop of flow improver helps it run into recesses.

Put a good puddle of medium on the palette, about five drops, then pull in a small dab of one or two related colours until the tint looks right, counting drops so you can repeat it. Roughly equal paint and medium is a strong wash; more medium makes it a glaze. For pale colours, a slightly darker version of the base shades softly without turning grey.
A weak ready made wash can be strengthened with a dot of matching paint. Balance it with medium rather than lots of water, which causes tide marks.

Inks in medium make smooth washes too, but neat ink is very strong, so add it a drop at a time. More brown gives a warmer tone, more black a cooler one. A little matt medium cuts the shine some inks dry with. About 8 parts medium, 3 to 4 parts ink and 2 parts flow improver gives a home-made one-coat staining paint.

Medium mixes are thicker than ready made washes, so use a medium brush and do not overload it. End each stroke in a recess so colour gathers there, and add a second pass only in the deepest ones. Test on a spare piece first, and add medium if it is too strong. Two light washes are safer than one heavy one.

Instant coffee dissolved in water makes a cheap, grimy brown wash for bone and undead flesh, and food colouring shifts it red, green or blue. It stays tacky for up to a day, so dry it gently and seal with spray varnish; a brushed varnish can lift it.

A coat of gloss varnish underneath helps any wash flow into the recesses cleanly instead of staining the raised areas. Let it dry for about half an hour before layering over it. Mixes can turn jelly-like if left standing, so check before reusing one.

guides.title: Modelling battle damage
guides.summary: Drill shallow holes, carve cracks and tear thin plastic before priming, then paint the damage dark inside.
body: Do damage before painting. Plastic is the easiest to cut and bend; resin allows less. Drill shallow craters with small bits in a hand drill, using a few sizes to suggest different weapons. A short row reads as a burst of fire.

For heavier hits, press a knife tip into the armour and twist to carve a shallow pit, then scribe a few short lines out from it in an uneven star. A drill alone makes a clean hole without the torn edge. Vary the depth. Young painters should ask an adult to do the knife work.

Take small bites out of armour edges with clippers, and scar the surface with a ball burr in a rotary tool where shots did not punch through. Keep bites small; big forced cuts can damage the clippers.

For torn panels, make lots of small nibbles with clippers inside a hatch, then bend and tear part of it back. Bend mudguards up or down with the smooth part of the plier jaws so they leave no marks, and damage one side more than the other.

Brush thin plastic glue over worked areas to melt away fuzzy shavings. Hold back: one to three big hits on a vehicle is usually plenty, and more looks fake. Damage should season the model, not cover it.

For arrows or spears stuck in a model, drill a small hole where each one enters and glue in a trimmed shaft, varying how much sticks out. For a spear through a body, drill right through so the two ends line up.

Open extra hatches to tell a story: cut the closed one out before the hull halves are joined, file the edges and build an open one from plastic card, checking reference for the hinge. Fix loose chain by gluing the end links, clipping to length and touching tiny dots of glue along it.

Paint holes with thinned black inside, then a chip colour just under the rim, with a touch of grey or silver in the very middle for depth. Add a fine highlight of the armour colour round the outer edge, and stipple a little black round it for scorching.

guides.title: Removing mould lines
guides.summary: Find the thin ridge where the mould halves met and scrape, file or sand it off before priming.
body: Mould lines run round each part in one plane, like an equator, usually in line with the frame it came on. Turn the part side on under good light and follow that line all the way round. On faces that glue together, they also stop parts sitting tight.

Scrape with the knife edge held steeply across the line, in light strokes towards you, using the part of the edge near the handle. Do not slice. A slightly worn blade chatters less than a new one, but change it once it skips or tears. A triangular seam scraper is comfortable and gouges less. Rotate curved parts as you go.

A foam backed sanding stick or fine sanding sponge flexes round curves and is often quickest. Cut narrow strips of sponge to pull across rounded parts. Sand in one direction only to keep a sharp point, and check often, as over-sanding changes the shape.

Small metal files suit resin and metal but can scratch plastic. Washes and one-coat paints pool in sanding scratches, so finish with fine grits: around 600 to 800 for tight spots, 1200 or finer for smooth surfaces. Wet paper clogs less, and a mask keeps the dust out of your lungs.
Brush a little thin plastic glue over fuzzy, scuffed patches and stuck shavings. It softens the surface and settles smooth. Use it sparingly near fine detail.
Spend the time where it shows: faces, weapons, smooth curves and anything facing up or forward. Undersides can wait. Where a line crosses texture like hair, take off a little and accept the rest.
Large flat panels can carry faint swirl marks that only show after priming. Buff them with very fine sanding sponge and dust on a filler primer in a well ventilated room.

Run a fingertip over the line: if it feels smooth, you are done. Brush parts with an old toothbrush, then check from several angles under a strong light; drybrushing and washes pick out every line you miss. Second hand models often hide them inside thighs and along jaws. A line spotted after priming can just be scraped and touched up.

guides.title: Press moulds and casting
guides.summary: Make reusable stamps or silicone moulds to repeat base textures and inserts across many models.
body: Press stamp: spread fine epoxy putty on a small wooden block and let it cure. Draw a pattern in pencil, then carve it with a fine tool such as a brass rod filed to a chisel. A square split into quarters with a shape across them gives a repeating tile. Press it into fresh putty on a base; the stamp lasts for years.

Rock textures: paint several layers of liquid latex onto a clean, interesting rock and peel the mould off when dry. Fill it with fine casting plaster. The flat backed casts glue down easily and break and sand cleanly, so one mould can supply a whole army.

Fine sand in the plaster makes casts stronger, and tinting the whole mix means chips still look finished. Uneven moulds such as egg cartons give a varied set from one pour. Plaster sets fast, so measure everything first.
Never pour plaster or plaster water down a sink, as it sets in the pipes. Keep spoons and tubs just for plaster, cover the work surface, and handle set pieces with care, as they shatter if dropped.
Cast inserts: cut thin plastic discs to fit the base recess and build textures on them, such as scraped balsa planks or wavy lines in putty for sand.

Avoid undercuts. Every detail should taper inwards or the mould will tear. Seal the masters with thin super glue. Build a box from taped card, space the masters out, pour slow curing silicone, then cast resin copies in it. Heavily filled resin sands and drills easily but is brittle.

For small press moulds, firm oven-bake clay gives crisp casts; modelling dough shrinks and air-dry clay distorts. A reusable hot water moulding plastic also works: soften it, fill a small box in batches, press the part in and leave it until fully hard. Epoxy putty pressed into it cures in up to 8 hours and peels out.

Always mould inside a container, overfill and clamp. Ease casts out with a cocktail stick rather than pulling. Expect failures and keep the best. Trim flash, wash resin in soapy water and prime as normal.

guides.title: Mounting models on plinths
guides.summary: Blend a model's base into a display plinth with putty, or use magnets so it can lift off for games.
body: Keep a display plinth simple so the model stays the focus. For a single figure, placing the head over the centre of the plinth usually looks balanced. Pin a test hole first to see where it will stand.
For extra height, trim a busy kit base down to its best section and glue it to the plinth at an angle so its top sits level. Build rocks and rubble underneath it.
To make a model part of the plinth, glue it on first, then press epoxy putty around its old base edge and smooth it into the plinth top.
Texture the putty to match the ground and add a few small rocks, then paint the whole ground area as one so the join disappears.

To keep the model removable, glue a small magnet under its playing base and set a matching magnet or a disc of metal flush into the top of the plinth. Double sided tape is a cheap way to sit a model on a square plinth and fix its front.

To line magnets up exactly, glue them into one part, press small balls of putty on the other where their partners sit, push those magnets into the soft putty and bring the halves together so the magnets find each other. Check they pull, not push, before it cures.

For a whole group, fit foam into a cheap picture frame with the glass removed, adding a raised step at the back for leaders. Cut a hole for each base a little larger than it, and line each with a socket made from the inner ring of a paint pot lid so models lift in and out.

Paint the plinth top to blend with the base, such as a dark outer area fading lighter towards the middle. Paint sockets to match the base rims, with a little matt varnish in the paint, as they get handled often.

guides.title: Organising your hobby space
guides.summary: Set up the desk so paints, tools and kits are easy to see and reach, and you start painting faster.
body: Every barrier between sitting down and painting, such as hunting for a bottle or setting up a lamp, makes you less likely to start. Aim to be painting within a minute or two. A spot you can leave set up beats packing away each time; a desk corner or a portable box works if a room is not possible.
Keep the paints and tools you reach for most within arm's reach, and keep only the tools you really use out. Basing supplies, spare frames and bits can live in labelled drawers further away.

Wall racks meant for nail varnish hold standard dropper bottles neatly by colour, and shallow spice racks take inks. Measure your bottles first: droppers want slots of about 28 mm, wide pots about 36 mm. Offset stepped rows so the labels behind stay visible.

Keep a small desk rack for the paints in the current project, grouped in runs such as skin tones, and put them back when it ends. Squeeze tubes flat from the bottom and dab a little colour on each cap so you can find it from above.

At the end of each build, clip every unused part off the frame, glue obvious pairs such as arm halves together, and sort bits by type into divided bead boxes labelled with tape. A bigger tub takes wings and cloaks, and a lidded box keeps empty sprue for spare plastic.
Keep loose frames in labelled card magazine holders so part built kits stay together. Stand boxes on their side with labels out. Small clear tubes hold tokens and tiny bits.

On the desk: a strong light, a painting handle, a comfortable chair, a few tools, a wet palette kept made up and clean water to hand. Keep it clear: never stack bottles, as they tip and spill, and keep brushes in a pot or flat rack. If you can, do gluing and sanding on a separate table so dust stays off wet paint.

Give unfinished models their own shelf and finished ones a closed case. Keep paints cool and out of direct sun. Take tall models off handles before leaving them overnight, as handles can tip over. A whiteboard in view helps track projects and next steps.

guides.title: Details that look the wrong scale
guides.summary: Remove, repurpose or repaint parts that look too big or too small beside your models.
body: Check terrain and accessories next to the models you will use. Oversized furniture or controls make a whole piece look like a toy.
Cut off parts you cannot save and cover the scar with panels, pipes or rubble.
Repurpose a giant part for a bigger model, such as an oversized chair for a large walker.
Or paint it as something else. A chair-shaped block with glowing lights reads as a machine.
On models, details that are too chunky, like huge buckles, can be painted dark so they recede.

guides.title: Paint beading or sliding off primer
guides.summary: If paint or wash beads on a slick primer, work it in, add another thin coat, or brush a grippy layer over first.
body: Some primers dry very smooth or slightly water repellent, and metallic sprays are especially slick. Thin paint, washes and one-coat paints then pull into beads, slide off or dry patchy.

On a plain smooth primer, let the first thin coat dry and add another. Paint grips much better the second time. Build weak colours such as orange in several thin coats rather than forcing one heavy one; the smooth surface then gives a very even finish and makes wet blending easier.
If paint keeps pulling away, brush it over the spot a few more times to break the surface. Or wipe it off with a tissue or fingertip and reapply. The area usually takes paint the second time.

Over a metallic spray, brush one thin coat of a matching metallic paint over the whole model with an old brush. It gives washes and base coats something to grip, evens out colour shifts and fills missed spots.
Another way is to wash the whole model first, including parts you will paint other colours. Once dry, later coats stick better. On gold, a warm brown wash shades the metal at the same time.
Change your rinse water before moving on to non-metallic colours, or metal flakes will spoil them.
On glossy coated surfaces, such as a sealed print, let the coating cure fully and prime before painting, or paint will slide and pool.
It can hit only a few models in a batch. Shaking the can well before spraying helps.

guides.title: Paint consistency for each technique
guides.summary: Each technique wants its own thickness, from nearly dry for drybrushing to mostly water for glazes and washes.
body: Drybrushing: barely any water. Keep the brush just damp and wipe most of the paint off before you start.

Base coats and layers: from straight out of the pot to about half water, like thin cream or full fat milk. Thin enough to level flat, thick enough to cover in two or three coats. Neat paint is fine if you brush it out thin rather than flooding the model; several thin coats beat one thick one.
Edge highlights: thin less than for layers. The paint should flow off the tip in a clean line without being watery, giving a strong, opaque line in one pass.
Highlight stages: thinner for early, broad stages built over a couple of coats; less water as you go up to the final small highlights.

Glazes: over half water, up to about nine parts water to one of paint, almost tinted water; they also hide small imperfections. Washes and shades: thin as much as you like, as long as some colour remains.

Blending: thin on a wet palette, with a touch of glaze medium for very smooth blends. Stroke the brush on the palette and blot it so it looks wet but carries almost no visible paint. More, thinner layers give smoother blends; fewer, thicker ones are faster but grainier.

Mix a little at a time and add water a drop at a time. Strongly pigmented colours need more thinning than weak ones. Test on the palette or a thumbnail first: dry, scratchy lines mean the paint is too thick, and paint that floods off the brush is too thin.
These are ranges, not rules. Slow, smooth display work uses more water; quick work can use paint nearly neat. Move between layering and glazing freely as the area needs.

guides.title: Paint drying too fast
guides.summary: Keep paint in compact blobs, refresh it every few hours and add a little retarder when it dries on the brush or before blending.
body: Paint spread thin over the palette, or pulled into long strings, dries fast. Keep each colour in a tight blob, mix only what you need now, and put out more than a tiny dab. A little extra paint costs far less than the time spent remixing.
A wet palette slows drying a lot. It keeps the consistency you set rather than thinning paint for you.
After about three hours, paint loses much of its medium. Water makes it flow again but brush strokes show more. Put out a fresh blob.
On tiny brushes for eyes and fine lines, paint dries on the tip in seconds. Water does not slow drying; a drop of flow improver or drying retarder does.
For blending, retarder can double the working time. Use it sparingly, as too much leaves a sticky glossy film.

Heat speeds everything up. In a warm room or under hot lamps, paint drags, will not leave the brush or leaves a gritty line. Rinse the tip often, reload with small amounts and work in smaller sections.
Leave the finest detail, such as eye dots, for a cooler time of day if you can, or cool the room first.

guides.title: Paint markers
guides.summary: Felt tip markers filled with one-coat paint work like colouring in and give fine control.
body: These markers hold a one-coat, contrast-style paint, so prime white or another light colour first.

Shake the marker well, then prime the felt tip by pressing it down repeatedly on scrap or the upturned cap until paint soaks into it. Markers can spit when first opened, so do this away from finished work. A nib that has dried after weeks unused can be reloaded the same way.
Holding a pen feels familiar, so many people get more control on mail, helmets and straps than with a brush. They are also quick on large areas such as tunics, base rims and terrain.
The nib is not very fine, so keep stripes broad and fill tight gaps with the same colour from a pot and a brush. Touch it along edges and into panel lines with light pressure.
Paint comes out at full strength. For softer coats, thin it on the model with a damp brush. Let each coat dry before going over it.
Tidy slips with a brush and the base colour, and finish with an all over wash for a grimier look.
A chrome effect marker run along painted blades gives a brighter, mirror-like shine than brushed silver, and is quick across a whole unit.
A brush is still faster for large, loose coats and needed for curved fine detail and colours the set lacks.

guides.title: Flow improver and glaze medium
guides.summary: Glaze medium thins paint without breaking it down and flow improver helps paint leave the brush, but use both sparingly.
body: Glaze or thinning medium is binder and water with no pigment. It spreads the same pigment over more binder, so paint becomes more see-through but still goes on evenly.

That makes it ideal for glazes, and it is safe to use in fairly large amounts. Most named glaze and thinner products are mainly plain acrylic medium, and a large art bottle costs far less. Some dry slightly glossy, which a matt varnish evens out at the end.
To blend with it, brush a little medium on the area, put paint on a dry spot nearby, then pull the paint into the wet medium so it fades.

Water evaporates and leaves only pigment. Too much water in a weak, pale paint can break it into blotches and coffee-ring stains; medium keeps it even but leaves a thin clear film that builds over many coats. Water is a fine place to start, and medium gives the same result every time. Try both.
Flow improver breaks surface tension so paint leaves the brush and spreads more easily. A little helps fine lines, eyes, freehand and edge highlights, and turns thinned paint into a wash.

It is strong. Dilute it about one to ten with water first, then add less than a drop at a time. Too much stops paint setting, so it runs and stains. A few drops in your rinse water also helps clean brushes.
For ink, a few drops of isopropyl alcohol act as a flow aid for fine lines. It evaporates fast, so reload often, and never leave neat alcohol sitting on painted acrylic, as it can lift it.

A cheap glaze mix: 2 drops matt varnish, 1 drop flow improver and about 10 parts water, kept in a dropper bottle and mixed about one to one with paint. Any additive that is not paint reduces coverage, so keep mediums for glazes, washes and blends rather than first base coats.

guides.title: Paint spilled on clothes
guides.summary: Rinse acrylic paint out of fabric with cold water straight away, as heat sets it.
body: Acrylic paint sets into fabric when heated, and once dry it is very hard to remove.
Rinse a spill with cold water as soon as you can, working it out from the back of the fabric. Do not use warm water.
A little washing-up liquid helps lift it while it is still wet.
Do not put stained clothing in a hot wash or dryer until the paint is gone.
Wear an old shirt or apron at the desk, and keep paint-covered drybrushing cloths for painting rather than washing them hot.

guides.title: Looking after paint pots
guides.summary: Stop paint drying out: keep pot rims clean, open tall pots with two hands, shut lids straight away and keep paint cool.
body: Tall flip-top pots are top heavy and tip easily, especially narrow wash pots. Open them with two hands with the pot steady on the table, rather than flicking the lid up with one thumb.

Dried paint in the rim stops the lid sealing, so the paint dries out, and it makes you press harder to close it, which tips the pot. Wipe the rim and lid groove with a damp cotton bud at the end of a session.
Shut each lid as soon as you have taken what you need. Paint left open for an hour starts to skin over.
A stand or rack that holds the pot steady while you open it saves most spills. Sticky tack under the base works only until it gets dusty. Work over a plastic tray.
Act fast on spills. Scoop small spills on hard surfaces back into the pot, and blot wash spills with tissue before they dry.
Keep paints upright somewhere cool and dry with lids shut tight. Freezing makes paint lumpy, and heat can make it separate or go thin, so keep it out of direct sun and hot cars.
Shake pots well before use. If a paint has thickened, add a few drops of water and shake again; a small glass bead or steel ball dropped in helps it mix.

guides.title: Making paint swatch cards
guides.summary: Swatch every paint on primed card to see its true dried colour, keep track of your collection and plan schemes.
body: Dried paint often looks quite different from the pot, so a swatch of every paint shows its real colour, finish and coverage at a glance.

Use textured plastic card with a grid pattern, cut to sheet size. The texture shows how paint behaves over raised and recessed surfaces. Avoid paper: it soaks paint up and changes the finish, so the swatch will not match the model.
Prime one sheet in a neutral mid grey, or in your usual primer colour. Prime a second sheet white just for washes, shades and one-coat paints, which look very different over white.
Paint a small block of squares for each paint, adding a coat to each square in turn and a tally mark per coat, until the coverage is solid. You can then see how many coats it really needs.
Next to each block, write the paint's name and the coat count with a fine waterproof pen.
Keep the sheets grouped by colour family. When planning a scheme, lay candidate swatches side by side to compare colours and contrast before painting anything.
Swatch new paints as soon as you get hold of them, and add favourite mixes with their ratio noted.

guides.title: How see-through a paint is
guides.summary: A quick test over black and white tells you whether a paint covers well or lets the colour underneath show through.
body: Paints vary a lot in how much they cover. Knowing which of yours are opaque and which are transparent tells you which jobs each one suits.
Make a test strip with black and white side by side, such as a tile with a stripe of black paint.
Spread a little paint thinly over the black. If the black still shows, the paint is transparent. That is not a fault, just a property.
Brush a little over the white. A paint that glows bright like a highlighter pen is ideal for glazing over a light undercoat.

Paints with a lot of white in them cover well but can look chalky over a gradient. Clean, pure colours cover poorly but let the shading underneath show. Weak or transparent paints need more thin coats; let each dry rather than piling on one thick coat that softens detail.
An undercoat or zenithal only changes the result under thin, see-through paint. After two or three opaque coats it is hidden, so with strong paints the undercoat colour matters little.
To build a gradient, thin paint to between a glaze and a layer and stack coats: more where you want the new colour solid, fewer where the base should show through, such as shadows.

Strong, opaque paints suit early coats, clean mixes and crisp final dots, but overpower a mix, so add them a little at a time. Weaker ones suit subtle blends. For a bright highlight, place an opaque layer and soften its edges rather than glazing up in many coats.

guides.title: Painting the base rim
guides.summary: Paint the base edge last in a dark colour, with thinned paint and an angled stroke, for a clean frame round the model.
body: Paint the rim after texture and drybrushing, so any mess from those steps gets covered, but before grass or tufts, which stick in wet paint.
Black is the safe choice and suits every scheme. Brown gives a natural step down to most gaming boards, grey suits ruins, concrete and ash, and a darker version of the ground colour also works.
Thin the paint just enough to flow. Stroke along the side at a slight angle, or hold the brush bristles up from underneath, so the colour stops cleanly at the top edge.

Start and finish at the back of the base so any join is hidden. Go in two or three thin coats; trying to cover in one pass causes most slips. A satin black levels more smoothly than matt and covers faster.
Stand the model on a holder, such as a block with tacky putty, so your fingers never touch the rim while it dries.
Clean sand and texture off the edge first, or the rim never looks sharp. On a black-primed base, a cotton bud damped with alcohol can wipe the rim back to primer.
Take care with superglue for tufts near the rim, as thick glue can fog the paint white. Pick one rim style for a whole army and keep to it.

guides.title: Painting handles and holders
guides.summary: Grip the model by a handle, not its body, so fingers stay off wet paint, and make holders from cork and paper clips.
body: Holding a handle keeps your fingers off wet paint and gives you something bigger and steadier to grip. Pinching a model cramps the hand and makes it shake, and skin oils left on the surface can stop paint sticking.

Fix the model's base to a handle: a spring clamp holder, a cork, a short length of dowel, an old paint cap or spray can lid. Double-sided foam mounting tape grips heavy models better than tacky putty; slide a knife underneath to pop the model off.
Get comfortable before you start. Brace your elbows on the desk and rest your hands against each other. Tension in the shoulders shows as wobbly lines.

For loose parts, glue a cork to a heavy spare base so it stands, and push a straightened paper clip into it. Drill a small hole in a hidden spot on the part, such as a neck socket, and fix it on the wire with a dot of super glue.

Super glue is brittle, so parts twist off cleanly once painted. For small feet you would rather not drill, a drop of super glue on the feet and accelerator on a scrap of sprue gives a weak bond that snaps off later. Ventilate well.

To reach under cloaks and robes, leave the model off its base: pin paper clips into the feet and push them into a cork so it stands about 2 cm up. Paint the base separately, then push the same wires into holes in it and glue. For a big kit in pieces, put each part on a skewer with tape and stand them in dense foam.
For thin parts with nowhere to pin, paint the hidden side and what it covers first, glue it on, then paint the outside.

Very large models are often too heavy for a clamp; rest them on the table or paint them in parts. Wear a thin disposable glove when you must touch them. One-coat paints rub off where fingers go, so varnish an area you have to hold. Repaint a fingerprint rather than scrubbing it with a damp sponge.

guides.title: Painting in sub-assemblies
guides.summary: Leave parts that block your brush unglued, paint them on holders, then assemble and tidy the joins.
body: Dry fit the model first and ask: could I reach every visible detail if it were all glued? Shields across chests, heads deep between shoulders, weapons across the body and riders on mounts are common blockers. On vehicles, tracks, doors and exhausts are easier in hand, and anything sealed in, such as a pilot or interior, must be painted first.

It is not always worth it. Every piece needs a holder, and you paint areas nobody will see. If you cannot see an area once built, you rarely need to paint it. For a quick batch of game pieces, build them whole with only the head or rider loose; for a model painted to your best, split it.

Also keep parts apart if they want a different primer or main colour, such as helmets or pads in a contrasting colour. Each group can then be sprayed on its own with no overspray or masking. Parts awkward to keep apart, like wings, can be glued and masked with tape instead.

Glue parts together where detail flows across the join, like a chin whose folds continue onto the chest, so they paint as one surface. Read the build steps ahead, and mark skipped steps in the instructions so you remember them.

Fix loose parts to holders with a tiny dot of super glue on the gluing surface. Old flying stand stems glued to spare bases make good handles, and riders or heavy weapons can sit on short pins pushed into a cork.

Do not split a model further than you need. A few groups, such as body with backpack, arms with weapons and the head, keep it easy to judge where light falls. Too many loose bits stops models getting finished.

Before assembly, check every part for missed spots. Dry fit, then hold each part in tissue, snap it off the handle and scrape paint and old glue off the contact points. Plastic glue only bonds bare plastic and can melt paint, so use super glue where paint remains. Fit parts that slide under others first.

Once together, look again. Shade new joins with a glaze, lift areas that now look dark against their neighbours, and touch up highlights worn by handling. Brush a little matt or satin varnish over any glue shine.

guides.title: Painting on the sprue
guides.summary: Tiny figures joined to the frame at their bases are often faster painted before clipping off.
body: Usually it is better to build first, but very small figures attached only at the feet are easier to paint while still on the frame.

Clean the mould lines first, then cut the frame into small pieces that are easy to hold, grouped by the colour each will be sprayed. Prime pale items with a pale spray and dark ones with black, so each starts close to its final colour.
Turn the piece to reach each part and work in a production line, one colour across every figure.
Clip off when painted, trim feed marks with a knife and touch up the small bare spots. Join painted parts with super glue, as plastic glue needs bare plastic to bond.
Small add-ons such as pouches and holsters, and parts that fit on later, such as vehicle tracks, can be painted on the frame too. Parts that end up hidden make good test pieces for a new effect.
Large separate pieces, such as a big beast, are better assembled first. Mould lines should still be removed before priming.
On a big squad, finish two or three models completely before batching the rest. Seeing them done keeps you going through the long production line.

guides.title: Cloaks and banners from tape and paper
guides.summary: Masking tape and paper make thin cloaks, wraps, pennants and banners with no sculpting needed.
body: Cloaks: sketch a rough shape on paper masking tape, tapering to the neck with strips at the top to wrap it, and leave it oversize. Cut it out with a sharp blade and peel it off carefully.

Stick it on and work it into folds with tweezers or a knife tip, tucking the strips under the collar. Tear or nick the bottom edge before fitting for a frayed hem, as tearing it on the model can pull it off. Tape can be lifted and moved until glued.

Wraps and bandages: trim any brim off a helmet first, then wrap strips about 4 to 5 mm wide, twisting them back on themselves each turn so they bunch like cloth. A plain wrap looks like a paper crown.

Pennants: fold tape back on itself, leave a loop to slide over the shaft, and cut a V in the free end. Back banners: bend brass rod into an upside down L, lay it on the sticky side of tape cut with tabs, fold the tabs round it, and fit it in a hole drilled behind a backpack.

Paper banners: cut paper with a sharp blade and steel ruler, glue it round a brass wire pole, then bend it into a droop while wet with varnish. Bent dry, it creases. Thin paper soaked in watered PVA drapes into flags and tarpaulins that dry stiff.

Foil flags last longer and bend to look windblown. Cut the flag with about 5 mm extra on the pole side and roll that strip round the pole. Spray the base coat, as brushed paint cracks at the folds, paint the design while it is flat, then check the pose and fold it gently by hand.
Prime or varnish tape to kill its stickiness. Brushed on thinned PVA glue makes it rigid and locks the shape, with a dab of super glue on a pin tip under key folds.
The paper soaks up paint like fabric. Tape bends without cracking its paint, unlike foil that is folded after painting.

guides.title: Spotting mistakes with a phone photo
guides.summary: Take a close phone photo and zoom in to find missed spots, stray marks and flat areas your eye skips over.
body: Your eye fills in gaps on a model you have stared at for hours. A close photo in even light, zoomed in on the phone, shows what is really there.
Use it after fine detail such as eyes, lenses or a symbol. Blobs, uneven lines and stuck fibres stand out at once.
Use it to find missed areas too, especially in recesses and underneath. Gaps in a base coat or drybrush are easy to see in a photo.
To check contrast, step back and take one shot under a frontal light and one under soft overhead light, which flattens things. Areas that look flat in both need darker shade or brighter highlights.
When a piece feels finished, photograph it and list what you dislike, such as a highlight that stops at a hard angle instead of following the shape.
Fix only what the photo shows before moving on. To hide a stray brush line, stipple either side of it rather than brushing over it again.
Then decide whether to stop. Repainting the same tiny area again and again fills in detail, extra tweaks cost time and add little, and good enough on an army model usually is.

guides.title: Photographing your models
guides.summary: Soft front light, a plain backdrop and a steady camera fix blurry or yellow photos far more than the camera itself.
body: Stand the model a little in front of a plain, matt backdrop: white, mid grey or black. Curve a sheet of paper or card from the wall down under the model for a seamless background. Black velvet gives a clean black with no editing. Busy backgrounds confuse focus and colour. Lift models into place, as sliding bases marks the backdrop.

Use daylight LED bulbs, roughly 5000 to 6500K and rated for good colour rendering, all the same colour. Avoid yellow household bulbs, switch other lights off and close the blinds. Turn the flash off; it wipes out the light and shade you painted.

Light from the front and slightly above: two lamps at about 45 degrees either side, or a main light with a second at 30 to 50 percent as fill. A white card on the shadow side bounces light back. Diffuse bare bulbs with baking parchment. A lamp straight overhead blows out the top and casts shadows that hide your painted ones.

Fix the phone or camera on a tripod about 30 cm away and use the self-timer so pressing the button does not shake it. Avoid digital zoom; shoot from a distance where it focuses well and crop afterwards. A matt varnish cuts glare, and photos show every slip, so tidy the model and base first.

On a phone, turn off automatic adjustments if you can, or use a camera app with manual settings. Tap to focus on the face, then drag the exposure down until the highlights are not blown out and the contrast matches the real model.

On a camera, use manual mode with ISO as low as it goes, around 100 to 200, and an aperture of about f/8 to f/16 so the whole model is sharp. Then lengthen the shutter until the exposure is right; on a tripod a slow shutter is fine. Use optical zoom only and save raw files if you can.

For true colours, set a custom white balance from a shot of a grey card under the same lights. Auto exposure darkens the model against a white backdrop, so expose for the model; the backdrop should look slightly grey before editing. Take a few shots a little lighter and darker and keep the best.

For big models and groups, take several shots focused from front to back, overlapping, and merge them with focus stacking. Shoot groups from slightly above, in landscape. Keep one camera angle for a collection: tilt until the top of the base looks as deep as the rim is tall. Compare the photo with the model and adjust.

guides.title: Picking a model that is good to paint
guides.summary: Choose a model you like with crisp, moderate detail, few materials and an open pose your brush can reach.
body: Above all, pick a model you like. You are about to spend hours on it, and liking the design keeps you going.

Look for crisp, sharp sculpting with clear edges, which takes washes, drybrushing and one-coat paints well. Soft, blurry detail on cheap toy figures teaches little. If 3D printing, print at the best quality you can.
Aim for a moderate amount of detail. Smooth, featureless surfaces give little to work with beyond gradients, while models covered in trim, pouches and trinkets are slow and tiring.
Fewer materials is faster. A model that is mostly one material, such as armour or robes, lets you paint most of it with one method.
Check access. If a weapon or cloak blocks the chest, you will struggle to reach it. Leave that part off while painting, or plan to keep the hidden area dark.

For practice, low cost plastic figure sets let you try a new scale or technique without risking an expensive kit. Pick sets with lively poses, or use the spare heads and arms to add movement to stiff ones.

guides.title: Pinning parts
guides.summary: Fix snapped or heavy parts by drilling matching holes and gluing in short lengths of wire so joints will not break.
body: Pinning strengthens joints on heavy parts, metal and resin models, models standing on one foot and anything that gets handled. Glue alone rarely holds heavy metal arms and weapons for long. Use paper clip wire or brass rod.

Plan where the pin goes so the hole is hidden and there is enough material round it. Pick a drill bit the same size as the wire or slightly bigger, and drill into the first part with a hand drill, straight and with light pressure.
Two pins stop a joint from twisting round and falling off.
Glue a long length of wire into each hole with super glue, then snip it so it stands out a little less than the depth of the hole it will go into.
Dab a little paint on the pin ends and press them against the other part. The paint marks exactly where to drill.

Drill the marked spots and test fit before gluing; if the fit is poor, shorten the pin or widen the hole. Then add super glue, push the parts together and check alignment before it grabs. Use super glue, not plastic glue, for metal or resin to plastic. Cut wire with rough old cutters, not your good ones.

Where a new part has a peg, drill out a matching socket so it is held in the hole, not by glue on a flat face. A second contact point, such as an elbow glued to the body, also strengthens thin limbs. A snapped spear or lance can be drilled and pinned through both halves.
Glue the biggest parts first, then the small ones, and let every pinned joint cure fully before handling.

guides.title: Pinning models to bases
guides.summary: Pin the feet into a scenic base so the model sits firm, marking the holes with short pins first.
body: Light plastic models often hold with glue alone, but heavy metal and large models need pins, or the joint snaps when handled. If the model has a cast-on base, cut it away carefully with pliers, knife and file without nicking the feet.

Dry fit the model in its final spot and check the pins will not show. If you are building up the base, dab strong paint on each foot and press the model in place. The prints show where rocks, putty and pins go. On soft putty or clay, a wetted foot leaves a matching print.
Start a hole under the foot with a knife tip, check the angle against the leg, then drill slowly and straight.
Push short pins into the foot holes, set the model on the base and press so the pins mark where to drill.
Drill the marked spots, then glue longer pins into the feet only with thick super glue. Pointed pins push into cork well.
For a leaping model or one handled a lot, use thicker wire. It lets you bend the model slightly to get the angle, and a little putty round the foot hides the pin.

On a large rock, shave the top flatter so the figure stands firm, fill gaps under the feet with epoxy putty and carve it to match the stone once hard. If base slots miss the feet, use a solid base and cut holes where the tabs land.
Let it cure fully. Paint model and base separately where you can, and fit them together at the end. If a dropped model tears out of a clay base, glue the feet back into their own footprints.

guides.title: Planning a diorama
guides.summary: Test the layout with sticky tack and sketches, pick one main viewing angle, and finish the centrepiece first.
body: Start with the scenery, as the space decides how many figures fit. Sketch it on paper first, even with stick figures, showing backdrop, figures, roads and focal point. It is quicker than building and easy to redraw.

Hold models on the base with sticky tack and try different placements and heights before gluing anything. Photograph a layout you like so you can put figures back in the same spots. Dry fit again each time you add new structure.
Pick one main viewing angle where the whole story reads at a glance. Decide early where the light comes from and give it a believable source, such as a fire or furnace, then build round it.
In a two figure scene, avoid both facing each other side on. Turn them so both still show their faces to the viewer.
Balance the layout. If one side is high, raise the other so the eye travels round the piece. Keep background parts simple and spend the time on the focal models.
For a competition, check size limits and look at strong past entries. Pick an idea that plays to your strengths.
Paint the main model first, so a finished centrepiece exists if time runs out. Keep hard to reach figures separate until the end.
Expect to add or remove things as it develops. Leave small final extras until near the end.

guides.title: Planning a conversion
guides.summary: Gather reference and parts, sketch the idea, and dry fit with tacky putty before any glue goes on.
body: Start with a picture or a short story for the character. Gather reference images and keep a theme in mind rather than a fixed final look.
Pick one core kit whose size and pose suit the idea as an anchor, then list what must change: head, hands, weapons, pack. Kits where arms, head and pack fit the usual way are easiest to swap.
Sketch the finished figure, front and back, especially areas you will rebuild. It is quicker than building and helps you decide.

Go through your spare bits and judge shapes, not what a part was made for: a pipe can become a smokestack. Mixing genres is fine, but parts from the same maker match scale and style best. Clean mould lines before you cut.

Leave arms on the frame until you are ready to pose them, and trim locating pegs so they turn freely. Hold parts with tacky putty, look from all sides and try flipping a part. Choose what keeps the face visible.

When fittings do not match, clip away detail and shave contact faces flat, testing often. Shoulder plates hide small gaps. If a part you will remove holds the model together, glue the rest first, then cut it away.
Get the big shapes right first and add chains, spikes and extras last. Fit the head last, as its angle sets the character, and leave head and pack loose for painting. Let putty cure before handling.
Keep new parts in the same style as the rest of the figure. A single coat of grey primer at the end shows weak joins and lets you see it as one piece.

guides.title: Planning a large model project
guides.summary: Break a big model into written stages, build it in sub-assemblies and paint shared colours across every part at once.
body: Before you start, write out the stages in order: clean and build, the sub-assemblies, painting each part, the base and final assembly. It is easy to forget the base on a big project. On a model built round a large scenic base, start with the base and build up.

Decide which build option you want before cutting anything off the frame, and note which spare parts could become separate models. Magnetise parts you may want to swap, such as a rider that also fits its own base.

Look at artwork and other painters' versions first to find a look that excites you. Under each stage, note the methods you will use, such as metal, then a wash, then details. Make sure you have enough of each colour for the whole model, as a colour remixed halfway rarely matches.

Leave riders, crew, cloaks and large armour plates off the main body so every surface is reachable. Crew figures can sit on a spare base, held by one heel with a dot of super glue so they snap free later. Building it whole instead shows how light falls and skips hidden areas, at the cost of reach.
Prime each part in the colour closest to its finish, such as a pale bone under pale wings and black under metal. Mask nearby areas with reusable putty before airbrushing next to them.
Paint the biggest areas first, right through to highlights. Once those are done the model is more than half finished, which keeps you going. Then do the figures, then the small details.
Do each shared colour, such as a glow or a metal, on all parts in one sitting so they match.
Finish the base before final assembly, as a fully built large model is fragile and awkward to handle. Join painted parts with super glue, since plastic glue melts paint.

guides.title: Plinth backdrops and display pieces
guides.summary: A small painted picture or scene on a plinth's back wall can add a story to a display model.
body: Plinths with a flat back wall give room for a backdrop that adds story or setting to a display model.
For a simple picture, cut thick card into a torn paper shape and glue it to the back wall. Paint it as old parchment: a pale tan with darker, browner edges.

Sketch the picture lightly in soft brown pencil, then go over the lines with thin dark brown paint and a very fine brush. A small red mark or circle on the picture that points to the model ties the backdrop to the figure.
Keep the backdrop quieter than the model, with fewer colours and less contrast, so it supports rather than competes.

For a built scene, cut a floor and a back wall from thick plastic sheet, sizing the wall to the tallest feature, such as a door. Thick sheet cuts with a craft knife; thin sheet with scissors. Cut openings for doors and windows, frame them with thin strips, and back them with mesh and a second sheet so you cannot see through.

Cut metal mesh with proper metal shears, as hobby clippers struggle. Pin and glue the wall to the floor, then add vents, floor tiles and small junk. Lay the extras out and rearrange them before gluing so the scene does not look cluttered.
For a quick stage, stand a sturdy small box on its side, build a ground level inside like a little theatre and fill it with flat props cut from card and thin plywood, edges sanded.
Match the props to the models: simple, cute figures suit simple cut-out shapes. Leave props unglued so you can rearrange them for different photos.

guides.title: Sculpting in polymer clay
guides.summary: Smooth unbaked polymer clay with a little odourless solvent, cutting key wrinkles deeper first so they survive.
body: Over a cured putty armature, glue very thin sheets of clay with super glue spread on a patch slightly smaller than the sheet, so it does not squeeze out, and roll them down with a smooth rod. Re-glue any lifted patch.

Press each added volume on firmly. Trapped air does no harm in the oven but squashes flat when you sculpt over it, leaving a smaller form than you meant. A dusting of talc stops clay sticking to the table.
Blend the main shapes with a rake or smoothing tool to even out bumps. The surface will still look grainy or show fine grooves.

Dip a soft old brush that holds a point in a little odourless white spirit or turpentine substitute, blot most off on tissue, and stroke it over the clay so the top layer softens and tool marks melt away.
Work in the direction of wrinkles and folds. Do one pass, let it evaporate, and add a second only if needed.
Smoothing erases shallow detail, so cut deep wrinkles deeper than you want before smoothing, and re-cut any that faded.
Add fine wrinkles last by dragging a textured tool or a pair of very fine wires across the skin, then smooth lightly. Stippling with a stiffer brush adds skin texture and dulls a shiny surface.
Let the solvent dry off before baking. Work with the window open.

guides.title: Paints that cover badly
guides.summary: Patchy, streaky base coats and weak yellows, reds and greens need an opaque undercoat and more thin coats, not thicker paint.
body: Acrylic paint is partly see-through, so one coat over black always looks patchy, and light colours can look murky or green-tinted at first. That does not mean the paint is bad. To test a paint's coverage, paint a stripe over something black.

Saturated yellows, greens, oranges and reds are often especially translucent. Do not use them thicker; thick paint leaves brush marks and hides detail. Keep them thinned and apply three or four coats, letting each dry. Going back over wet paint drags it and builds texture. A drop of flow improver helps weak greens level out.

Under a weak colour, use a light grey or white primer, or two or three thin coats of a dense, chalky colour close to the target but lighter: a strong orange under red, a pale stone or cream under yellow. A thin, glossy undercoat covers no better than the top colour.

Over that undercoat, red usually covers in about two coats and yellow in one or two more. The whole job is then four or five layers instead of eight or more straight over black, so detail stays crisp.

For bright colours, you can also base with the colour mixed with a high-coverage pale such as bone, or about a sixth of a khaki or sand colour for yellow. Then put a thin coat of the pure colour on top. It looks vivid because the layer below did the covering.
For a base coat that mostly sits in shadow, a little strong black mixed in boosts coverage and rarely spoils the colour. Mix plenty for a big model, and keep a little back to match a second batch.

If a highlight colour goes patchy on its own, add a little paint that has some white in it, plus a little of the base so the step is not too big. White steps up fast, so go carefully. Put messy pale colours such as off-white on early, before the neighbouring areas are finished.
The same see-through quality makes these paints good for glazing. Metallics need less water; a damp brush is enough. Try any unfamiliar paint on a spare part first.

guides.title: Pre-mixing custom colours
guides.summary: Mix a batch of a custom colour once and keep it in a spare bottle so every model matches.
body: When a colour needs two or three paints mixed in set parts, mix a larger amount once instead of every session.
Count drops from dropper bottles so the ratio is exact, and mix thoroughly.
Keep it in an empty dropper bottle or pot with a lid. A small mixing ball or bead inside helps it stay mixed.
Write the ratio on the bottle so you can make more later. Note ratios even for small mixes, such as two to one, and keep a dried dab of each step on card to match against.
This saves remixing and stops each model ending up a slightly different colour, which shows across a unit.
Washes drift in strength when mixed fresh each time. Mix a batch and keep it in a small lidded glass jar, which also suits oil washes. Test it on a spare piece first.
If a mix covers badly as a base coat, look for a single paint that matches it closely and covers well, and save the mix for highlights.

guides.title: Cleaning and checking before priming
guides.summary: Wash off grease, check for lines and gaps under bright light, and fix anything priming reveals before paint goes on.
body: Work in order: clip and clean up the parts, wash them, assemble, fill gaps, then prime. Each step is far harder to do once paint is on.
New models carry release agent from the factory, and handling adds skin oil. Both make primer and paint bead or slide off.

Scrub the model with a drop of washing-up liquid in warm water and an old toothbrush, or use an ultrasonic cleaner. Super glue joints survive this. Rinse, then let it dry fully, ideally overnight. Hold it by the base or a handle from then on.
Just before priming, wipe large smooth surfaces with high strength isopropyl alcohol on a makeup sponge to lift oils from handling.
Check the model under a bright lamp with something white behind it, turning it slowly, for mould lines, gaps, flash and undrilled barrels.

Priming the whole model in one colour shows a few more flaws. Go back now: scrape lines, drill barrels and fill gaps, then brush primer over just that spot. If you can see it, others will, and it is far harder to fix under paint.
For a tiny gap, plastic shavings dissolved in plastic glue make a filler that hardens in minutes. Pots of liquid filler tend to dry out within a few months of opening, however tight the lid.
Very thin paint grips poorly. If paint still beads on a clean model, use a primer or a fairly thick, well spread first coat.

guides.title: Preparing 3D printed models
guides.summary: Trim support nubs, smooth them with a fine file, clean the print of every residue, then prime in thin coats.
body: Before printing, check the height of the figure itself in the slicer against your target scale. It is easy to scale by the wrong axis and print it too big.
Wash resin prints in isopropyl alcohol, or in water if the resin is a water-washable type, then cure them fully under UV light as the resin's instructions say. Wear gloves until the print is cured.
Clip supports off with flush cutters, then slice the leftover nubs level with a sharp craft knife, cutting away from yourself. Smooth the spots with a fine emery board or sanding stick.

Clean off every trace of residue before priming. Wipe resin prints with a lint-free cloth dampened with isopropyl alcohol and water, and wash filament prints in warm soapy water. Oil and dust left behind stop primer gripping.

Faint layer lines are normal and very fine ones usually vanish under primer. For stronger lines, sand with 600 grit or finer, or build up thin coats of a self-levelling primer, alternating dark and light so any lines left show as shadows. If detail looks soft even at good settings, another resin may hold it sharper.

Prime in two or three thin coats rather than one thick one. Resin is semi-transparent, so detail is hard to judge until it is primed. Thick filler primer suits rough filament terrain but buries fine detail on small figures.

On filament printed terrain, drybrushing and washes catch the print ridges. Prime dark, sponge a lighter colour over with a dense makeup sponge, add the main colour, then edge highlight and line recesses by hand.

guides.title: Preparing metal miniatures
guides.summary: Metal models need careful cleanup, super glue and pins on heavy joints, and a varnish to stop chipping.
body: Check each casting for holes, shifted mould halves and soft detail before you start. Makers usually replace a badly miscast part; small missing areas can be rebuilt with two-part epoxy putty.

Metal casts have mould lines and flash, the thin webs left by the mould channels. Clip flash away, then clean lines with a needle file or a sharp knife. Start with long thin parts such as weapons, hands and spikes, where lines show most.
Cut parts off casting tags or thin metal links carefully. Bend metal as little as possible, as it tends to crack or snap.
Wash the parts in warm soapy water to lift grease, and let them dry fully.
Plastic glue does not work on metal. Use a strong super glue, and file contact faces so parts meet snugly, as loose fits make weak joints. Plugs and sockets hold far better than flat joins.
Pin heavy arms and weapons, since glue alone will not hold them for long. If the base has a slot under a foot, push a lug through it for extra hold.
Look again under a bright light once primed. Primer shows up lines you missed on bare metal, and they are far easier to fix now than halfway through painting.
Paint chips off metal much more easily than plastic, and heavy figures knock together. Once transfers are on, seal the whole model with a matt varnish.

guides.title: Preparing resin models
guides.summary: Check every part, wash off mould release, cut casting blocks away in small bites, and glue resin with super glue.
body: Lay out every part under good light and check nothing is missing or short, looking hardest at thin spikes, horns and claws. Note any warped pieces early. Makers usually replace missing or badly cast parts.

Resin parts often carry mould release that stops primer and paint sticking; a waxy or oily feel gives it away. Scrub them in warm soapy water with an old toothbrush, leaving the casting blocks on as handles. A little fine rubbing compound on the brush helps. Rinse well and let dry fully.

If a part still looks shiny or feels tacky after cleaning, the resin was probably badly mixed or cured. Paint will not hold on it for long, so ask the maker for a replacement rather than painting over it.

Resin is more brittle than plastic. Cut feed blocks in small bites, a little away from the part, with the flat of the cutters towards it. Too big a bite can crack the piece. Always cut away from yourself, and young hobbyists should ask an adult to do knife work.

Take the last stub off with a sharp knife, bracing flat parts like feet on a cutting mat and slicing level. Sand with a medium then a fine stick, wetting the spot to check it is smooth. Wear a mask when sanding, as resin dust is harmful.
Thin webs of resin, called flash, mostly pop off with a knife. Resin gouges easily, so file and scrape gently and only where a line really exists. Small metal files suit it well.

Look in folds and weapon ends for air bubble holes. Fill tiny ones with a drop of brush-on surfacer or liquid filler, and larger ones with epoxy putty smoothed with a wet tool. On rotten or ancient subjects, small pits can stay as wear.
Dry fit every joint, even where there are locating pegs, and trim pegs that leave gaps. Glue resin with super glue only; plastic glue will not bond it. Pin heavy joints and fill gaps before priming.

guides.title: Keeping a photo record of your progress
guides.summary: Photograph every model the same way at each stage so before-and-after pictures show your painting, not changes in the light.
body: Use the same set-up every time: the same spot, the same lamps, the same plain grey or white background and the same distance. Then old and new photos compare fairly.
Mark the camera and model positions with tape on the desk. Shoot the front, a three-quarter view and the back, in that order, every time.
Turn off phone filters and beauty modes. Tap and hold on the model to lock focus and brightness. Afterwards only crop and adjust brightness, and do the same to every photo.
Take a quick photo at each stage: built, primed, base coats, shading, highlights, base done. These show where your time went and make good before-and-after pairs.
Name files by date and model, for example 2026-03 knight front, and keep one folder per model or per month. Back them up somewhere other than the phone.
Every few months, put a new model next to an old one, on the desk and in a photo side by side. Seeing the gap is better motivation than any single compliment.
Keep a few early models as they are, even the rough ones. They are fixed markers for how far you have come, and they are hard to argue with on a bad day.

guides.title: Keeping painted models safe
guides.summary: Keep finished models behind closed doors to cut dusting, and varnish anything that gets handled.
body: Open shelves gather dust and pet hair quickly, and dusting painted models risks snapping parts.

Glass door cabinets suit whole armies. Pick one whose doors close fully, or stick brush-style draught strip round the door edges to keep dust out. Most figures fit in 13 to 15 cm of height, so extra glass shelves fit far more in, with one taller level for big models.
Small wall cabinets with lights suit display pieces. Plastic pull out drawers suit older models and spares.

Keep models out of strong sunlight, which fades colours and can heat resin enough to warp it. Do not leave them in a car: heat softens plastic and resin, and cold makes glue brittle. Ease warped parts straight in hot water, never over a flame.
Models used for games wear where fingers touch. Varnish once painting is fully finished, paying attention to the base if that is where you hold them.
Magnets glued under the bases keep models still in a metal-lined case. To clear dust, use a soft, dry makeup brush or a gentle puff of air.

guides.title: Raising a model for uneven ground
guides.summary: Trim the support under the feet and glue the model a little high, then build rough ground up round it.
body: Thin legs on push fit models are hard to pin, so keep part of the moulded support under the feet.
Cut it down and glue the model slightly above the base surface.
Fill around it with glue and sprinkle on fine earth, adding a second layer near the feet.
The result is uneven ground that looks better than a flat layer of sand, and it hides the support.
For a bigger lift, glue flat slate or cork under the soles first, then fix it to the base so the feet sit properly.

For a striding pose, dry fit slate under the model to find an angle where every foot touches. Press warmed two-part epoxy putty where feet need raising, then push slate chips in from a random spot so it does not look planned.
Let gravity guide you: loose stones settle at the bottom of a slope. Keep everything a little back from the base edge, and seal it with spray varnish once dry.
Build putty ground up to meet low parts such as a belly, as a gap underneath stands out. Very dry twigs, bark and stones pressed into soft putty grip without glue.

guides.title: Adding real chain to models
guides.summary: Wrap or hang fine chain on a model, lock it with thin super glue, and pre-shape floating chains on wax paper.
body: Use scale model chain or fine jewellery chain, and check the link size against the model. Coarse chain looks out of scale. Cut it with old cutters.
To wrap chain round a model, glue one end in a hidden spot such as an armpit with a drop of super glue.
Wrap it tightly. Crossed, X-shaped wraps look better than straight loops. Finish the other end out of sight, under an arm or behind another part.
Touch thin super glue along the chain. It wicks through every link and locks it rigid, so it does not shift or scratch the paint later.
Hang a plate, tag or other small bit off the chain to hide a join and add interest.

For stiff, curving chains that seem to float, oil a sheet of wax paper, lay cut lengths on it in the bends you want and touch thin super glue to each link. Once dry they pop off as fixed shapes. Fit them at varied heights and lengths.

guides.title: Rebasing a model
guides.summary: Cut a model off its cast-on, scenic or old base in small bites, protect the feet, and fix it firmly to the new one.
body: Scenic bases cast with the model can look repetitive across an army, and older models may need a new base size. Keeping the feet intact matters more than saving the old base. Decide on the final base before painting, as cutting a model or print free afterwards chips paint.
For a cast-on base, never try one big snip. Clip away chunks well clear of the feet, then nibble small bites towards and around each foot.
Trim closer with a sharp knife, scoring along the line of the sole rather than cutting in one go, until the underside is flat. Cut away from your body and fingers.

To move a figure from a square cast base to a round one, saw most of the old base away with a fine razor saw, leaving a thin slab under the feet. Glue the slab to the centre of the new base, blend the step with epoxy putty and texture the whole top as one piece of ground.

For a model already glued down, use an old blade and old clippers, as grit ruins good tools. Slide the blade under the basing first; glue under sand often gives way. Then nibble the old base away. Hold the model by its sturdiest area while levering, never by fragile sculpted parts.
Glue the figure to the new base with super glue, as feet give only small contact points. Fill gaps under the feet with slate or a small rock, or keep a little platform from the old base.
On a slotted base, line the model up with the front mark and cut only as much slot as the tab needs, so there is no large gap to fill.

guides.title: Removing sculpted details
guides.summary: Clip off the bulk, shave down in thin layers, scrape and sand smooth, then fill any holes left behind.
body: A smooth surface takes transfers or freehand and often looks larger and more real. Decide early, before other parts and putty go on. Cutting off a fussy back banner can also clean up the outline.
Clip the bulk off with flat faced cutters, staying clear of the surface you want to keep. Do this before gluing halves together so you can reach.
Shave a thin sliver at a time with a fresh blade, changing it once it drags. Brace the blade against your thumb and cut with the part near the handle; the tip wobbles.
Near the surface, switch to scraping with the blade upright, following the curve of the form. Use a curved blade in hollows, do not roll over panel edges, and clean off the burr that builds up.

Finish with a file or fine wet sandpaper, around 800 to 1000, which keeps dust down. Brushing thin plastic glue over the area melts away fuzz. A small diamond burr in a rotary tool gives control up to edges.

Fill engraved symbols and dips with sandable two-part putty, or water-based filler pushed in with a damp brush and wiped level with a damp cotton bud. Sand putty with a hard-backed stick, as a soft sponge sinks into it and leaves dips.
If removing a part leaves an empty socket, fill it with putty and press in a trimmed spare piece, such as a bit of armour plate, so it looks intended. Keep spare parts for this.
Where a detail cannot come off, change it a little to suit the new theme. Dips that still show can be painted by layering rather than drybrushing, or turned into a scar or rust patch.

guides.title: Repainting toys and pre-painted figures
