guides.summary: Clean a factory-painted figure well, prime thinly over the old paint, then rebuild colour in thin coats.
body: Factory paint is often thick and fills fine detail, so a careful repaint can bring the sculpt back. Gather more than one reference picture first, as printed and screen versions of the same art often differ in how dark they are.
Clean the figure well to lift oils and grime, in warm soapy water or a few minutes in an ultrasonic cleaner, then dry it with a soft cloth. New paint will not grip a greasy surface.

Priming over the factory paint is usually better than stripping it. Stripping is slow and rarely complete, and harsh solvents can pit soft plastic and vinyl. Sanding is only needed if you want a model-grade surface.

Brush on one or two thin coats of a water-based surface primer, adding a little water if it is thick. Keep it thin over printed eyes or markings you want to trace later, and work it into hair texture so it does not pool.

Soft, rubbery plastic is hard to cut or convert, and one-piece figures cannot come apart, so plan to paint them whole. Pressed-together vinyl parts pull apart with firm, steady force; being too timid bends the soft parts.

Where the factory colour is close to what you want, keep it as your first layer. Build the rest in two or three thin coats of water-thinned acrylic, letting each dry. Pointed round brushes in sizes 1 to 4 suit this.
Start with the area that bothers you most, usually the face and head, as that is where people look and where a repaint changes most. A new base is an easy extra upgrade.

guides.title: Replacing snapped spears, ankles and thin parts
guides.summary: Pin clean breaks, and swap snapped spears and poles for metal rod or wire so the new part bends instead of breaking.
body: If the broken piece is still there and the break is clean, pin it: drill a small hole into both faces, glue in a short length of wire, then superglue the joint. A pin makes a thin joint far stronger than glue alone.

Spears, staffs and lances: cut away the broken shaft and replace it with brass or steel rod of the same thickness. Drill into the hand and the spear head and glue the rod in. Next time it bends instead of snapping.
Ankles: drill up through the foot into the leg, add a pin, and fix the model to its base through that foot too. A second pin from the base into the other foot helps a lot.
Antennas, banner poles and thin blades: thin plastic rod suits straight parts that need to stay light. Wire is better for anything that sticks out and gets knocked.
Match the new rod to the old part by eye against the break or with calipers. Add a grip with a wrap of thin putty or thread so it fits the sculpt.
On painted models, scrape the paint off both faces of the break so the glue meets bare material. Touch up the paint over the joint afterwards.
Fill any gap around the joint with a little putty, smooth it with a wet tool, then prime and paint the repair to blend in.

guides.title: Reposing a model
guides.summary: Cut limbs at the joints, trim the faces to a new angle and reglue them to change how a model stands.
body: Decide the new pose first, for example sitting instead of striding, and look at reference. A simple change that captures the feel is often enough. On a big model, work from the ground up: legs, hips, torso, then arms and head.
Cut through limbs at knees, hips, elbows or shoulders with a fine razor saw or sharp knife. Clippers pinch the cut and waste material. Keep cut faces flat and file off the burr.
Trim the cut faces, or a little plastic out of the joint, until the part pivots to the new angle. Separate knee or shoulder pads are handy, as they hide the cut once glued back.
Pin larger joints: drill both halves, glue an oversized pin into one, then trim it until the other sits right. A paper clip wire core can also be bent to angle or lengthen an arm.
Hold parts with poster putty or a tack of super glue and check from every side. Expect to adjust several times, and make sure the feet sit flat and the stance looks balanced.
Fill gaps with two-part epoxy putty and let it firm for 10 to 15 minutes before sculpting folds. Small gaps can take super glue and accelerator, smoothed with a file. Priming shows any lumps.
Swap hands between kits if yours lack the pose. To flip a weapon grip, cut the shaft off both sides of the hand and refit it reversed. Hide awkward joins with cables or cloth.
Small cuts go a long way: a foot turned inwards at the ankle and arms lifted forward give a shambling walk. It is fiddly work, so take your time.

guides.title: Resin or filament printing for miniatures
guides.summary: Resin prints the fine detail figures need but brings fumes and messy kit; filament is cleaner and suits terrain.
body: Resin printers harden liquid resin with light, one thin layer at a time. They give the fine detail miniatures need, such as faces, chainmail and small lettering. Layer lines are almost invisible at this scale.

Filament printers melt a plastic strand through a nozzle. Layer lines show on small figures and fine detail goes soft, but large prints are cheap and the plastic is tough. They suit buildings, scenery, bases and carry trays.
Resin smells and its fumes irritate. It needs a well-aired room or extraction, ideally a spare room, garage or shed, not a bedroom or kitchen.
Resin also needs gloves, eye protection, an alcohol or wash bath, a curing lamp or sunlight, and careful waste handling. Uncured resin on skin can cause an allergy that does not go away.
Filament needs much less: the printer, spools and a level surface. The common plant-based plastic gives off little smell, and there is no liquid to spill, so it is easier in a family home.
Size: resin build plates are small, fine for figures and small vehicles. Filament printers usually build larger, which suits hills and buildings.
For figures, pick resin. For terrain, or if you have nowhere to vent fumes, pick filament. Many hobbyists end up with one of each.
Either way, expect a learning curve. Failed prints, settings and supports take a few weekends to get right.

guides.title: Looking after a resin printer
guides.summary: Check the vat film, clear failed print scraps, level the plate and soften cured resin off the screen with alcohol.
body: Check the clear film in the bottom of the vat often. Even a pinhole lets resin through onto the screen, and a slack or scratched film also spoils prints.

After a failed print, cured flakes can float in the vat and ruin the next one. Run the printer's tank cleaning mode, or expose a single blank layer, so a thin skin cures across the film. Peel it out with the bits stuck to it using a plastic tool, never metal. Stop the exposure yourself if there is no timer, or the skin gets thick and hard to lift.

To replace a torn film, fit the new one over the alignment pegs, clamp it under the bottom frame and tighten the bolts evenly. Uncut film needs bolt holes punched and must be large enough to cover the frame.
If resin has leaked and cured on the screen, lay a cloth soaked in isopropyl alcohol over it and wait. Once the resin softens, rub it away gently. Never scrape the screen with anything hard.

To level the build plate, loosen its bolts, lay the levelling card or a sheet of paper on the screen and lower the plate onto it. Tighten the bolts with the plate pressed flat. On a solid machine this holds for many prints.
Resin gathers round the plate bolts and runs along the plate if you set it on its side. Wipe it off with paper towel, and wear gloves whenever you handle liquid resin.

guides.title: Resin printer settings and scaling
guides.summary: Find the shortest exposure that prints reliably, and scale printed parts to fit your kit before the final print.
body: Each layer is cured by UV light for a set time. Too much or too little exposure both soften detail, so aim for the shortest time that still prints reliably.

If your printer can run a test that exposes zones of the plate for different times, print the small test card and compare the zones. Otherwise start from settings others use with the same resin, then print one model with the same supports three times, changing exposure by one second each time.

Every resin cures at its own speed, so test again whenever you change resin and note the settings that work. Many printers let you change exposure and lift speed on the machine without slicing again. A sharp, high resolution screen may need shorter exposures than you are used to.
Room temperature, the resin itself and a clean, tight vat film all affect quality, so check those before blaming exposure.

Check the height of the figure itself in the slicer against your target. Printed bits are often sized for a bigger model: measure where a part that fits meets the model, work out the difference as a percentage and scale by that.
Print one test set to compare arm and weapon lengths before the final batch. Mirroring parts in the slicer lets you test which side looks better in a pose.
Pour thick resin slowly and let it settle, as trapped bubbles can leave holes in the model. Wear gloves with liquid resin and work in a well ventilated space.

guides.title: Pouring resin water effects
guides.summary: Choose the right clear resin for the depth, seal the edges, tint sparingly and leave it alone to cure.
body: One part water resin or gel suits small, shallow puddles but shrinks and leaves a dip, so pour several thin layers. It stays rubbery if poured deep.

Two part clear epoxy shrinks much less and suits pours deeper than a few millimetres. Mix more than you need, as the ratio is easier to hit and a wrong ratio may never set. Stir slowly to avoid bubbles. Deep pours can take days to harden.
UV curing resin is thick, easy to push around and sets in seconds under a UV torch or sunlight. Use it for puddles, drips and streams built in thin layers, not big deep pours.
Paint everything that will sit under the water first; you cannot reach it afterwards. Leave the upper parts of the base until after the pour. Real stones look natural under resin even unpainted.

Where resin meets a base edge, wrap at least three tight layers of tape. For deep pours, build a wall of plastic card lined with acetate, sealed outside with hot glue that peels off cleanly. Set it at the final water height, or resin climbs it.

Tint with a single drop of transparent ink in a lot of resin, or swirl in a brush that has touched the ink. Too much kills the depth. Clear layers over a tinted bottom layer look deep. For ripples, brush tinted gloss gel along the flow.

After pouring, lift bubbles out with a skewer, then leave it at least 48 hours, longer for deep pours, without poking. Work over a cover, as uncured resin spreads like honey. A clean tap with a metal tool means UV resin is hard.

To fix cloudy sides, sand from about 400 up to 1000 grit and restore the shine with gloss. A thin top pour levels resin that climbed the edges. Keep glue accelerator away, as it leaves a white film. Satin varnish helps paint grip resin.

guides.title: Reusing leftover sprue
guides.summary: Spare plastic frame becomes rod, spikes, girders, terrain bits, filler and handy workshop helpers.
body: Spare frame is the same plastic as the kit, so it glues with plastic glue, carves, sands and takes primer like any other part. Keep a box of offcuts: long straight lengths, round sections and junctions all have uses.

Stretched sprue: trim a clean straight length and turn it above a candle or low flame, never in it, until it softens. Pull the ends apart gently and steadily, lay the strand flat to cool, and use it for cables, aerials, bowstrings or slices for rivets.

Cores and spikes: bend or cut sprue to the rough shape of an arm, pole or blade and sculpt putty over it, so the putty does not snap. Slice long thin triangles off a rod and scrape them smooth for quick spikes on armour or hulls.

Terrain: glue long lengths into low walls, fences and girders behind card walls, cross equal lengths into tank traps, cut round sections into pipes with thin slices as clamp rings, and cut small rectangles into staggered brick rows.

Workshop helpers: a painting handle with a cork or old base glued on top, a drying rack for brushes, a gluing jig of two parallel sprues that holds a pole straight, a flying stand post, and a test panel of glued-on sprue to practise techniques on.
Chopped sprue dissolved in plastic glue makes a filler and gap-filling glue of the same plastic as the model.
Cut sprue spread thin between baking parchment and pressed on the lowest heat of a hobby-only press flattens into a rough plastic sheet. Never use equipment that will touch food again.

Heating, melting or dissolving plastic gives off harmful, flammable fumes. Work on a heatproof surface with good airflow, gloves and eye protection, keep batches tiny, and stop at once if it smokes or chars. Grinding sprue for base texture needs a dust mask too.

guides.title: Old, thickened or separated paint
guides.summary: Most old paint just needs a hard shake or a little medium, but paint that has set into chunks cannot be saved.
body: Look through the side of the pot before opening. Paint that has settled into a solid layer, or gone into hard chunks, will not mix back. Replace it with a close colour.

Settled paint splits into sludge under a runny liquid, and old whites come out thin and watery until mixed. Shake hard for a good while, or open the pot and stir with an old brush. Stainless steel mixing balls in the pot, or a small vortex mixer, do it faster. Stir a stuck ball free first. Never rig a mixer from power tools.
Textured effect paints, such as rust, hold heavy grit that sinks. Unstirred, they go on thin and flat with no variation, so stir then shake well.
Paint that splits on a wet palette after a while is normal. Stir the puddle with the brush and carry on.
One-coat paints lose water as they age and get thicker and stronger; staining your skin is a sign. Test on a hidden spot and add medium a little at a time until it flows and tints as it used to.
Old washes separate and can dry gritty or shiny. Shake or stir well and test on a spare piece. A matt varnish knocks back any shine later.
Ordinary paint that has thickened but is still smooth can take a few drops of water or medium. Stir well and check it on the palette.
To prevent it, wipe the rim and thread before closing, as dried paint can glue a lid shut. Close lids firmly and keep paint somewhere cool.

guides.title: Keeping rinse water clean
guides.summary: Change rinse water before smooth stages and never let the pot dry out, so grit and fluff stay out of your paint.
body: A little colour in your rinse water does no harm. Floating dust, fluff and loose sludge are the problem, as they end up stuck in smooth finishes.
Check the water before a smooth stage such as base coating, glazing or stippling, and change it if it looks dusty.

Never let a pot dry out with paint in it. A crust forms on the bottom, and rinsing loosens bits that end up in your brush and on the model. Empty and wash the pot regularly. Glass jars and ceramic mugs clean more easily than plastic; soak a crusted plastic pot in household degreaser.
Many painters keep two pots: one for rinsing, and one kept clean for thinning paint and wetting the brush. A separate rinse for metallic paint keeps glitter out of other colours.
Never leave brushes standing bristles-down in the pot, as the tips bend for good. Keep the water pot well away from your drink so you never pick up the wrong one.
A few drops of flow improver in the rinse water helps paint leave the bristles.
If a hair or fluff lands on wet paint, flick it off with the brush tip, or lift it with a blade once dry and touch up.

guides.title: Scratch-building small details
guides.summary: Make armour plates, belts, wheels and handles from plastic tube, card, rod and spare bases.
body: Plates: halved plastic tube makes curved plates, and a slightly larger piece laid over gives a banded look. For rough plates, cut thick plastic card and shave the edges at random angles. Score thin sheet with light knife lines and bend along them to shape a shield or panel; score, do not cut through.

Tubes: a short length of narrower tube with bevelled ends makes a band that hides damage. For a tube of any size, wrap thin card round a handle with super glue run between the layers, never onto the handle, and it sets hard. Paper wrapped the same way round plastic tube makes barrel shrouds.

For a flanged wheel, glue a small solid round base onto a slightly wider clear flying base with super glue. For a feed belt, bend a thin brass strip into place and glue on tiny plastic card rectangles one at a time from a knife tip, leaving even gaps.

For a handle or haft, use brass rod, which is stiffer than copper, and file two opposite flats pressing with one finger. A plastic tube wound with fine chain along a line of glue makes a rougher haft.

For straps, glue a strip of thin plastic card about 1 mm wide at the hip, take it over the shoulder and pinch the ends together. Thin brass sheet makes banners and parchment strips that flex rather than snap.

Rivets: mark spacing on tape and drill shallow pits, then set beads or punched plastic card discs on dots of super glue, lifted on a damp knife tip or a needle tipped with sticky putty. A hole punch squeezed over plastic card with a scrap shim beneath presses a raised dimple instead. Dab away excess glue, as it shows once primed.

Pipes: bend plastic coated wire to the route, strip the ends and glue them into drilled holes, sliding a short piece of plastic tube on as a coupling. Guitar string makes scale cables; bend it round something round to avoid kinks.

Keep rods and strips longer than needed while working so you have something to hold, and trim at the end. Folded card boxes with glue tabs make stowage. Model a part's most recognisable shapes; a clear silhouette matters more than every detail.

guides.title: Scratch-building vehicles
guides.summary: Build a card core clad in plastic sheet from a template, carve tracks from plastic card and borrow kit parts for detail.
body: Expect a scratch build to take three or four times as long as the kit, about the effort of a heavy conversion. It costs little: plastic sheet is cheap and a mostly card build is nearly free.

Work from a pattern, your own drawing or a printed papercraft template, so sides match and corners stay square. Check it against a real kit and rescale it if the hull comes out large. You need scissors, a sharp craft knife, a steel ruler, a cutting mat, super glue, PVA, a glue stick and small hole punches.

Build the main box from thick card, such as template card backed with cereal-box card, then clad it in plastic sheet for the armour. Plastic sheet cuts and drills easily and takes glue and paint like kit plastic. Card alone is too weak once heavy parts go on; a plastic core is heavier and stronger.
Check the box is square, then add plastic armour plates and detail with rod, tube, putty and spare parts. Fill unwanted openings by gluing sheet behind them.

For tracks, stick the template to 1 mm plastic card with a glue stick, score between plates with a razor saw in a mitre box and shape each score with a triangular needle file. Glue on detail plates, then bend the strip round the hull, starting with a full plate at the front. Card tracks are cheaper but need sealing.

Scissors twist thick plastic and side cutters leave a sloped edge, so score and snap, or use anvil-style cutters, for square ends. If a scored strip snaps while bending, glue the pieces on one by one.

Spare kit parts close most of the gap between a hand-made hull and a moulded kit. Split kit tracks between the kit and the scratch hull, leaving hidden top runs bare, and borrow weapons and lights. Raise track guards on short rod spacers so the tracks look free to move.
Add stowage, damage and weathering details last, before painting. Plastic sheet can be cut or drilled afterwards to show battle damage.

guides.title: Scratch-building terrain
guides.summary: Plan a building from reference, build it from plastic card with braced walls, then detail it with spare parts.
body: Start simple. Rocks, hills and standing stones forgive wobbly cuts and need few tools. For a building, gather reference and give it a purpose. Angles and varied heights look better than a plain box. Work from big shapes to medium ones such as steps and overhangs, then details, stepping back to check the whole.

Rigid extruded insulation foam is the usual core; avoid beady white packing foam, which crumbles. A hot wire cutter gives rough natural shapes. Spray paint and super glue melt bare foam, so clad it in plastic card or use PVA where foam shows.

Cut walls from plastic card with a fresh blade against a steel ruler, scoring and snapping. Use angle guides at joints and plastic strips inside to keep walls straight and square. Cans and plumbing parts make quick tanks and pipes.

Cardboard and foam board make cheap cores. Cut them with a sturdy utility knife with snap-off blades, snapping off a fresh section often, as card blunts it fast. Hot glue joins big shapes in seconds. Brush finished card with one part PVA to two of water to harden it, and clad weak panels in plastic card.
Score panel lines with a light second cut, then deepen them with a triangular file. Back gappy corners with mesh or card so filler grips, then fill, sand and rescribe any lines you lost.

Give each piece a rigid base that will not warp, such as two layers of plastic card glued together or thick board. Cut an irregular outline, bevel the edge to sit flush with the table, and blend the foot in with filler.

Leave room for play. Test a model on its base through doors, on steps and along walkways, keep gaps wide enough for two medium bases side by side, and floors flat. Terrain should support the models, like a stage set.

Add detail with spare kit parts, wire cables, tiny rivets and the clutter of daily use, such as stacked logs or a ladder, but know when to stop. Wash the finished shell in soapy water to remove grease and dust before priming.

guides.title: Sculpting proportions and anatomy
guides.summary: Measure the whole figure from one head unit, place skull and face landmarks by thirds, and build muscles piece by piece.
body: Learn a few measurements by heart so the anatomy stage runs like a checklist, leaving your attention for pose and expression. Check landmarks again after every big change of pose.

Counting heads only works for a figure standing straight, and the classic eight heads is idealised; most people are nearer seven. A better unit is the head width, about five eye widths, which also equals crown to base of nose.

From the base of the nose, one unit down finds the top of the breastbone. One unit is also each collarbone and the shoulder blade. The next unit finds the bottom of the rib cage, and the next the front point of the hip.

The thigh is three units to the middle of the kneecap and the shin three more; the foot is about half a unit tall. The upper arm is two units to the elbow, the forearm two more to the knuckles. Measure along each limb, so it works in any pose.

Block a skull as a big ball at the back with the face added on. From the side its length roughly equals its height to the jaw; from above it is wider at the back. On a bust, get the skull width right first, as shoulder width is measured from it.

Mark a centre line and split the face from hairline to chin into thirds. Press eye sockets in just under the top line, starting large as smoothing shrinks them. Cheekbones are the widest point, and temples dip behind the sockets.

The mouth line sits halfway down the lower third. Treat the jaw as a sphere split into upper and lower halves, and keep the bulge at the back base of the skull. For teeth, cut a bite line and press small triangles between them.
Build muscles from small pieces of putty shaped like each muscle, placed from reference. Blend edges with rubber tipped shapers, smooth with metal tools, and add creases once the putty is part cured.

guides.title: Building a sculpting armature
guides.summary: Bend soft wire to a scale drawing, bulk it with foil and a thin putty skin, and set a natural pose before sculpting.
body: You need soft aluminium armature wire, round nosed pliers, side cutters, a cork block to stand it in and a body diagram printed at the exact figure height. For a first sculpt, a blob-like creature is far kinder than a human.
Fold a long wire in half: the fold is the head and the doubled strands the spine. At hip height bend each strand out to hip width, then down for the legs. Bind the hip tightly with thinner wire.

For arms, bend a small U into the spine below the collarbone, seat a second wire in it and bind it. Mark shoulders and elbows from the diagram, bend one side and copy the other. Lock joints with super glue and keep bindings slim.

A straight spine looks stiff, so add a gentle S curve. Tilt the shoulder and hip lines opposite ways: if one shoulder drops, that hip rises. Decide the pose before pushing the legs into the cork, one at a time, and avoid stray kinks.
For a bust, glue a thick upright wire into a wooden block, bind a shoulder crossbar to it and lock it with super glue. Winding thin wire over a film of glue gives clay far more grip than smooth wire.
Bulk the chest and back of the skull with scrunched kitchen foil glued in place. Keep it slim if the design is not settled, and leave room at the front of the skull for the face.

Clay grips bare wire badly and thin wire can slice through it, so cover the armature in a thin skin of two-part epoxy putty, mixed until no streaks remain and wrapped fully round. You need grip, not volume.
Leave shoulders, elbows and hips bare so the pose can still change, and give the head a solid rounded block, not a thin rod. Check the size against a normal model of that scale early.

guides.title: Sculpting cloth, cloaks and banners
guides.summary: Roll putty thin, half cure it for clean cuts, and press in folds that follow how the cloth would hang.
body: Roll two-part putty flat on a wet tile with a wet brush handle, to the thickness the cloth needs. Two thin rails such as toothpicks either side keep the sheet even.
For a banner or strap, leave the sheet one to two hours to half cure. Soft putty drags when cut; half cured putty cuts cleanly.
Cut by pressing a loose blade straight down rather than dragging it, and keep it wet. Trim the edges square, press out small triangles for a ragged hem, and fold the top over for a pole sleeve.
For a cape or cloak, lay a thinner sheet onto the model while soft and press in folds with a rounded tool, following how the fabric would hang from the shoulders and gather where it is caught.
Add overlapping folds and hems as further thin layers, letting each cure before the next so you do not squash your work.
Press a line with the back of the blade for a seam. Tiny pieces of a rolled strip, dipped in super glue and placed with a pin, make stitches.
Let it cure fully, about a day, before working the other side. Light sanding of the cured edges sharpens folds and makes the cloth look thinner.

guides.title: Sculpting pustules and fleshy texture
guides.summary: Craft half beads or putty balls make boils, and thick filler stippled with a brush gives rough organic skin.
body: Half round craft beads in mixed sizes make convincing boils and pustules. Place them on dots of super glue with tweezers, or press them into a flat sheet of putty for a cluster behind an opening.
Blend their bases into the surface with a thick, water based filler brushed on with an old brush. Wipe the bead tops clean.

For putty boils, roll epoxy putty into a sausage about 1 mm across and slice pieces as long as they are wide. Smooth plastic gives little grip, so dot super glue on the back with a pin, then press the edges flush with a rubber tipped shaper.
For a burst boil, open the top with a needle in small circles, then press the hole wider with the shaper.
For rough organic skin, paint the filler onto an area and stipple it with a damp drybrush while wet.

For ribbed skin, work in small patches: press on a flattened piece of putty, trim it, score gentle parallel lines with a wet tool, and nudge the edge back to leave a clean edge for the next patch. Thin rolled strands draped over the shapes make vines or tendrils.
Lumpy mutated flesh is forgiving and hides awkward joins. Push small amounts of putty into bulges and ripples with a wet tool, let it firm for an hour or two, then shape growths on top.
Vary the sizes and leave some smooth areas between clusters so the texture reads clearly. Next to flesh, flat pressed facets with a few cut scratches read as hard shell.

guides.title: Hiding gaps and damage with sculpted cloth or fur
guides.summary: When a gap or break is too awkward to sand flat, cover it with a sculpted scarf, cloak edge or fur, or rebuild the part on a wire core.
body: Some gaps are too wide or awkward to fill and sand flat, such as an angled neck or waist join. Cover them instead. A scarf, a cloak edge, a fur collar or a belt hides the join and looks deliberate.
Fill the deepest part of the gap first with a little putty and let it cure. Then lay a thin sheet of fresh putty over the join and shape that into folds or fur.

Cloth: flatten a thin strip, drape it over the join, and press in a few folds with a rounded tool, running the way gravity would pull. Thin the edge with a wet blade so it does not look like a sausage.
Fur: lay a thin layer, then drag a pointed tool in short strokes in one direction, overlapping like roof tiles. Vary the stroke length a little so it looks natural.
Broken detail: rebuild the missing part, such as a nose, a hand guard or a horn tip, around a small wire pin. Bulk out the shape first and let it cure, then add the fine shape in a second thin layer.
Match the sculpt nearby. If the model has big soft folds, do not add tiny crisp ones. Copy a matching part on the same model, or on its other side.
Prime the repair and check it under a lamp held low to one side. Side light shows bumps and ridges that overhead light hides.

guides.title: Sculpting with putty
guides.summary: Mix epoxy putty evenly, block in a rough shape, then refine it with a few small, fine tools.
body: Mix the two parts until the colour is completely even. Discard the strip where they touched in the packet. Take less than you think you need. A hard sandable putty mixed with a softer one holds detail and still smooths well.

Keep fingers and tools wet, or lightly coated in hand cream or petroleum jelly, and top up when the putty drags. Keep tools spotless, as old cured putty tears fresh putty. Work on a glazed tile or baking paper so cured parts release. If putty smears, let it firm a while; it holds sharp detail better.
Putty is weak on its own. Build tall shapes round a glued core of sprue or plastic card, and roughen wire pins so putty grips them. Thin wire gives sharper horn tips than paper clip.

Plan the order: sculpt the deepest layers first, then parts that lie over them, such as eyelids or armour rims. Press each piece's edges down and let a stage cure before working beside it. Turning a head upside down shows lopsided features.

Block in a simple shape, press it into place and trim the excess. For hard parts like an axe head, make it oversize in a hard curing putty and file it once cured. For a hood, roll a thin wet sheet between two rails, let it firm, then cut and drape it.

For fur, dig the tool's edge in and flick away, over and over in the direction it grows; fill a gap in fur the same way, following the fur either side. For mail, press a thick needle in row after row. To hide a messy join, wrap a thin roll round it and press in matching ribs or texture.

Small parts are easier made off the model. Slice a cured thin sausage into discs for rivets. Press balls of putty into points with wet fingers for spikes, let them cure, then fix them with a little fresh putty smoothed over the join. Build chains in two layers, letting the first cure before the second.

Small, fine tools beat big sets: a rod filed to a small bent blade, a firm rubber tipped shaper, a needle and a ball tool. Leave putty at least four hours, ideally overnight, before priming. Wear a dust mask when sanding.

guides.title: Smoothing stepped or stripy blends
guides.summary: Hide visible layer steps with a halfway mix, thin passes of the darker colour, or a glaze over the whole area.
body: Some steps are normal after layering, especially with pale highlights or see-through colours like purple. Get the lights and darks in the right places first, on a solid, even base coat. If a jump looks stark before the next step, mix the two colours half and half and paint that first.

To soften a line, thin the darker of the two colours until it only tints, test it on your thumb and take almost all of it off the brush. Start just over the line and pull away from the highlight into the shadow. Leave it to dry, do not go back while wet, and repeat several times. Then do the same with the lighter colour back towards the light.

Make glazes with water, glaze medium, which dries slower, or matt varnish, which avoids the shine some mediums leave. If a glaze pools, the brush was too loaded; wick it off and use less. A wet glaze looks darker than it dries, so judge it dry.

If a light glaze will not hide a hard edge, add a drop of the shadow colour so it sits between the two, then pull from light into dark. Or stipple the lighter colour over the border with a small, barely damp drybrush.

For stripy edge highlights, glaze the main colour once over the whole area, then again where the steps meet. Over-highlight slightly first since the glaze tones everything down, then sharpen the brightest point with one more fine layer.

A thin glaze of the midtone brings back saturation and masks many lines; on red, a deep red glaze pulls the steps together and makes it richer. A very thin glaze of a different hue, such as violet in blue shadows or a red ink on skin, also hides steps. For highlights, use the light tone with a touch of off-white rather than pure white.

You do not always have to fix it. A crisp edge highlight or light drybrush draws the eye from the blend. Scattered dots of varied size, like freckles, hide a patchy blend on skin. On metal, feather a little silver over the join; roughness looks natural.

Tide marks in a layer come from too much paint on the brush or paint that is too thin; about one to one with water is a good limit. Stippled areas can look grainy; a thin glaze restores colour. Uneven sheen evens out under clear medium. Do not fix a step the next layer will cover.

guides.title: Speeding up drying
guides.summary: A hair dryer on a gentle setting dries thin layers quickly, but keep it moving so the plastic does not warp.
body: Lots of thin layers and glazes means lots of waiting. A short blast from a hair dryer dries each one fast.

Use a low heat or cool setting, keep it moving and do not hold it on the model for long. Too much heat can soften or warp plastic, and resin softens sooner still, so use less heat on it. Hold it well back from fresh paint so the liquid is not blown around.
Make sure a layer is fully dry before glazing over it, or you will lift the layer below. Wet paint looks darker than dry, so dry a glaze before judging it.

Let a wash settle into the recesses before drying it. Then let the model cool, or finish with cool air, before the next wash, glaze or one-coat paint. Runny paint on warm plastic dries on contact and leaves hard rings and tide marks.
A small heat gun on its lowest setting works too. Gentle heat also speeds up oil paints and enamels.

Do not heat wet glue, PVA and sand, or poured resin, as it can crack the basing or warp the model. Never dry brushes with it either: heat makes natural hair brittle, loosens the ferrule glue and bends synthetics. Keep rinse water and paint pots clear of the dryer.
Working on another model or part while one dries is the simplest way to keep going.

guides.title: Splicing kits together
guides.summary: Cut two models at clean lines in small bites, file the faces flat, test fit often, and hide gaps.
body: Look at where each kit's detail sits. If belts or pouches run across the join, cut above or below them, not through them.
Keep halves separate while cutting. Glue only the half you need, so the unwanted part is easy to clip away.
Clip well away from the line you keep, creep closer in small bites, then finish with a file or sanding stick so both faces meet flat. Test fit after each small adjustment, keeping curves smooth.

Watch proportions: a natural figure is about two parts waist down to one part waist up. If a kit looks squat, try legs from a slightly taller kit, cutting away the hips so they slide up into the torso. Build one test model first.
Test fit heads and shoulder pieces before gluing, and trim necks or beards where a collar stops a head sitting. A very distinctive shape can make the model look like the wrong type.
Riders made for slimmer mounts leave gaps at the saddle; fill them with putty and shave off clashing detail. To join two weapons, cut matching L-shaped steps so the halves overlap and lock.

Hide small gaps behind pouches, badges or spare parts, and fill larger ones with putty pressed to match the texture. On creatures, a thin roll of putty wrapped round a limb join and pressed with even lines reads as a natural segment. Wedge crooked panels with plastic card and putty. A riveted plate covers a hole cut too big.
Old painted models can be stripped and spliced too. Prime the result one colour to judge the shape.

guides.title: Setting up and using a spray booth
guides.summary: A booth's fan and filters pull overspray and fumes away so you can spray indoors; keep the filter clean.
body: A spray booth is a hood with a fan and filters that pulls overspray and fumes away from you. Run its exhaust hose to a window adapter to send fumes outside; with no window, the filters alone may do for light use. Pick a size that fits the models you usually spray.
Switch the fan on before you start. Keep the nozzle inside the booth and your face outside it, and aim towards the back filter rather than the side walls.

Put a turntable inside so you turn the model, not the airbrush, and paint does not pool on big flat areas. Hold models on a clip stand, cork or stick, and clamp small parts so the airflow does not blow them away.
Do not crowd the booth: models in front shadow the ones behind, and small batches end up faster. Booths are dark, so use the built-in lights or point a clamp lamp inside.
Keep pressure low, around 25 to 30 PSI for priming. Needing more usually means the primer is too thick.
Leave the fan running at least 10 minutes after you stop. Freshly varnished models can sit inside with the fan on for 30 to 60 minutes, away from dust, bumps and pets.

Test the pull with a hand-length strip of tissue at the front edge: it should snap in towards the filter. If not, soak the filter about an hour in warm soapy water, rinse, dry fully and refit. With heavy use, replace filters every two to three months. If a clean filter barely pulls, the fan may be failing.
Never spray flammable solvents in a hobby booth, as the fan motor can spark.

guides.title: Spray priming
guides.summary: Shake the can well and spray short sweeping bursts from a sensible distance, stopping at a thin coat that keeps the detail.
body: Warm the can in warm, not hot, water for a few minutes, then shake it for at least a minute or two. Warm, well mixed primer sprays more evenly. A can that sputters or loses pressure usually just needs the same again.

Wash, dry and assemble the model first, then fix it to a stick, or with tack on its underside to a strip of card, so you never touch it. Spray outdoors or somewhere well ventilated, wearing a mask, on mild, dry days of roughly 10 to 27 C. Cold, damp or humid air gives fuzzy, grainy or orange peel results.

Hold the can about 15 to 30 cm away, following the can's advice. Too close floods detail; too far and the paint dries in the air and lands gritty. In hot, dry air move a little closer, in humid air a little further.

Start spraying beside the model, sweep across it and release past it, in short light passes. Turn the model, or stagger a batch on card so none shades another, and spray from all sides at a low and a high angle, underneath included.
Spray the back first, so any problem shows there before it reaches the front.

Two light coats with drying time between beat one heavy coat; if no hint of bare material shows after the first, it went on too thick. Bright colours like yellow may need two or three. Check spikes and edges from every angle, as thin primer there rubs through under drybrushing.

If one coat went on thick, leave it alone to dry; it often shrinks back. Grainy or fuzzy primer will not improve under paint, so scrub it off with isopropyl alcohol and an old toothbrush, which is quick before it cures, and re-prime.

Let it dry somewhere covered and ventilated, at least an hour, ideally overnight; dry primer looks flat, not wet. Fill missed spots with the base coat. Use a matt or satin primer made for models, never gloss. Car filler primer buries detail. Wood and MDF soak primer up, so give them a generous coat.

guides.title: Dissolved sprue filler
guides.summary: Plastic frame offcuts dissolved in plastic glue make a paste that glues and fills gaps in one go.
body: Chop spare plastic frame into small pieces and drop them into a half full jar or bottle of plastic glue, up to just below the liquid level.
Leave it overnight to two days until it becomes a thick grey paste. Add more plastic or glue to adjust it. Thick works best as a gap filling glue.

Use it like plastic glue but generously, spread on both faces so some squeezes out of the join, which matters on parts never designed to meet. Hold or prop heavy parts such as wings at the right angle while it sets. For hairline gaps, plain thin glue run along the seam often does the job alone.
Brush plain thin plastic glue over the squeezed out paste. It softens and levels, and the gap disappears. Never do this on a joint still taking weight, as it softens the paste and the part can slip.

It also fills small holes, adds rough texture and sets slowly, so you can nudge parts straight. It cures into a tough plastic weld rather than a brittle join. Leave 30 to 60 minutes before handling and overnight before sanding or scraping it flush.
Run it round the edge of added parts on organic models and it reads as flesh stretched over machinery.
It softens the plastic round the gap too, so use it sparingly near fine detail. Keep the jar sealed and the room aired while it cures.
It only works on plastic. Use super glue for resin, metal and mixed materials. Keep it in its own bottle, separate from your normal glue.

guides.title: Starter sets or separate paints
guides.summary: A starter set is a quick, simple start; picking paints one by one costs more at first but wastes less.
body: A starter box or paint set gives you a matched group of colours, often with a brush and sometimes a few models. It removes the guesswork and gets you painting the same day.
The catch is fit. Sets often hold colours you will never use and leave out ones your scheme needs. The brush in a set is usually basic, so plan on a better one for detail.
Picking paints one at a time takes more thought, but every pot earns its place. Start from the scheme you want to paint and list only the colours it needs.
A good middle road: start with a broad set of core colours, then add single pots as each new project needs them. A set built for mixing, with strong primaries, black and white, lasts longest.
Look at what a set holds before choosing it. Count the colours you would really use, and check for a white and a black that cover well, a brown, a metal and a wash.
Once you own a few paints, sets mostly bring doubles. From then on, single pots are almost always better value.

guides.title: A beginner's tool kit
guides.summary: A few cheap tools, the right glues, a lamp and a basic painting set are all a new hobbyist needs to start.
body: Space: any sturdy table and chair you already have, with the surface covered against spills, and a desk lamp close to the model. A daylight bulb saves your eyes. A spot you can leave set up saves packing away each time.

Building: clippers with a flat side so they cut flush, a hobby knife, fine sandpaper around 400 to 800 grit or sanding sticks, and tweezers. Hardware and craft versions work as well as hobby branded ones, and bulk scalpel blades cost far less.
Glue: plastic glue for plastic kits, super glue for metal and resin, and white PVA for basing and terrain.

Painting: a heavy water pot that will not tip, a few synthetic brushes including one pointed round around size 1 or 2, a palette such as an old tile or a home-made wet palette, paper towel, a primer and, later, a varnish.

Start with a handful of colours for the model in front of you rather than a full range. The well known miniature paint ranges are all good, and finer than craft acrylics. Shake each pot well before use.

Hold the model on a painting handle or anything handy, such as a pill pot or a block of wood, with a little poster putty. A helping hands stand holds small parts while glue sets. Paper clips make pins and clear blocked dropper nozzles.
A small hand drill lets you pin heavy joints and open up gun barrels. The bits that come with cheap drills are often poor, so a set of fine bits is worth adding.
Cheap extras that pay off early are magnifiers and brush soap used after every session. An airbrush is useful but not needed. Everything else can wait: add tools as you add skills.

guides.title: Staying motivated on big projects
guides.summary: Start with the model that excites you, set small regular goals, mix easy and hard work and track your progress.
body: Pick models you are genuinely keen to paint, not just what is strongest in a game, and start a big group with the one that drew you in. Before a long showpiece, make sure the idea itself interests you, and decide up front whether it is for the table or for display.

Do not wait to feel motivated. Keep your kit set up so you can start the moment you sit down, and use a short start-up routine: lamp on, water pot filled, something to listen to. A regular slot, even half an hour, beats waiting for a long free evening. Ten minutes or one base coat still counts.

Set small goals you can meet, such as one model or one colour across a squad, and raise them as you go. End a session partway through a simple, repeated step, so next time you know exactly what to do.

Large batches drain enthusiasm through repetition and creeping standards. Accept the level you set at the start, so every model does not feel like an exam. Keep a simple model on the go beside the hard one, swap in a vehicle or monster between infantry, and paint a standout model as a reward after each batch.

Most projects slump about two thirds through, so save a favourite job, such as basing, for then, and keep one favourite model as the finale. If you sense burnout coming, switch to something simpler for a while; that is looking after the hobby, not giving up.

Split the project or a complex model into groups, such as cloth, leather, metal and gems, and tick them off on a list. A target date, such as an event, helps, and photos of finished models show progress when motivation dips.

If a unit has stalled, sort the models by stage, bring the least finished up to the next stage and carry on as one batch. Once all are base coated and washed they already look like a unit. For a daunting centrepiece, get primer, base coats and a drybrush on first, and add detail later.

Pick one or two skills to push, and try them on leader models or a simple head or weapon swap. Share work with friends or hobby groups, ask for help rather than dropping a stuck idea, use painted models in games early, and only aim to beat your last model.

guides.title: Steadying your hands
guides.summary: Brace your arms and hands together, move only your fingers and pull the brush towards you to stop wobbly lines.
body: Rest your forearms or elbows on the desk or chair arms, and your wrists on the desk. The further your support point is from your fingertips, the more your hand shakes. Arms floating in mid air shake most. With a big model, put your elbows down and press your wrists together, or rest them on a raised knee.
Let the hand holding the model touch the hand holding the brush, or rest a little finger on the holder, so they form one rigid unit. A shake in one hand is then cancelled by the other.
Relax everything except your fingers. Only the finger and thumb joints should move. A fingertip resting on the model adds more stability. Breathe normally; holding your breath tenses the hand.
Pull the brush towards you where you can, as it is the steadiest stroke. Turn the model, not your hand, so you can run along an edge rather than trace round it, and keep strokes short.

Dab the brush on your thumb on the way to the model to keep the paint flowing and show the line it will make. Bring the tip in slowly and let it touch before you start the stroke. Do not hesitate at the model: a waiting tip starts to dry, pale paints fastest, so dab and reload if you pause.
Raise the desk, to around 90 cm rather than the usual 70, or lower the chair rather than hunching, and use a strong light so you can work close. Grip wrap on a detail brush lets you hold it looser.

Caffeine, alcohol, an empty stomach, recent exercise and vibrating power tools all make hands shake, so plan fine work around them. Work in short spells, such as 30 minutes on and 5 off, put the brush down in breaks, and stop as soon as your hand starts to shake.
Work top to bottom and leave the back for later, so fingers rest on unpainted areas. Expect to tidy up afterwards; a slip can always be painted over.

guides.title: Straightening bent parts
guides.summary: Warm a warped resin, plastic or soft metal part gently, bend it straight and hold it as it cools.
body: Thin resin spears, blades and staffs often arrive warped. Wash resin in warm soapy water first to remove release agent.
Dip the warped part in hot water, from about 70 C up to just boiled, for 30 to 60 seconds, or warm it with a hair dryer, until it flexes slightly. Take care not to scald yourself.

Ease it straight with your fingers, holding it against a flat surface if that helps, and keep it there until it cools. Dipping it in cold water sets the shape faster. The same method makes small pose changes to legs or necks.
For a spot you cannot reach that way, press the warmed tip of a pair of metal tweezers against the resin and ease it round.
Do not overheat resin. It can blister or give off fumes.

Thin plastic parts often soften enough under a hair dryer on its hottest setting. Thick plastic needs more heat; a heat gun works, but plastic goes from soft to melted quickly, so work slowly and check it often.

Soft metal parts such as swords, horns and spikes can be warmed with a hair dryer and eased back in small steps. Do not bend the same spot back and forth repeatedly or it will snap. Flattened details such as squashed teeth can be recut with the tip of a sharp craft knife.
Never leave models in a hot car. It can get hot enough inside to warp them.

guides.title: Stripping paint off a model
guides.summary: Soak a model in a stripper that suits its material, scrub the paint off, wash it and prime again.
body: Stripping is the cleanest fix for thick or grainy primer, clogged detail, a paint job you want to redo or old second hand models. Only paint over old paint that is sound and firmly attached. On a big model with many parts, a repair and re-prime may beat a full strip.

Check the stripper suits the material and test it on a hidden spot. Hobby paint strippers are made to be safe on plastic, resin and metal. Acetone strips fast but can soften or melt plastic and resin, so keep it for metal. Undiluted household degreaser works too but needs hours. Resin is the hardest to strip cleanly.
Wear gloves and work with good airflow. Strippers are harsh on skin, and very old metal models may contain lead.

Soak the model in a lidded glass jar, or a zip bag with the air squeezed out so it needs less liquid. Hobby strippers can work in minutes to an hour or two; degreasers need several hours or overnight. Thick old layers may need more than one soak. An ultrasonic cleaner speeds it up if the liquid is safe to warm.

Scrub with an old toothbrush over tissue. If paint goes tacky again, dip it back briefly. Clear stubborn recesses with isopropyl alcohol on cotton buds or the blunt back of a knife. Never sand or use a heat gun to remove paint.

Stripper often softens old glue, so parts come apart. Use the chance to clean joins or repose the model, and reglue with super glue. On second hand lots, clip awkward joints rather than prising, so arms do not snap.

Wash it in soapy water with a clean toothbrush and let it dry fully. Plastic may stay stained, which is fine as long as the detail is sharp. Small leftover patches are easier to prime over than to remove.

For one small area, paint the stripper on, or scrub isopropyl alcohol into the patch, with an old brush you do not mind ruining. Many removers can be strained through a filter into a sealed bottle and reused.

guides.title: Superglue mishaps and glue that will not set
guides.summary: Free glued fingers and tools with acetone, use thick glue on porous parts, and use less glue if it stays wet.
body: Superglue grabs in seconds and bonds skin quickly, so dry-fit and line parts up before any glue goes on, and keep fingers clear of the joint.
Glue on skin: do not pull. Dab on an acetone-based nail polish remover, wait for it to loosen, then peel gently.
Glue on tools: a cotton bud with a little acetone cleans it off. Keep acetone well away from painted surfaces, as it strips paint.
A clogged metal nozzle can be cleared by briefly heating the metal tip with a lighter to burn off the dried glue. Never do this to a plastic nozzle.
Thin superglue soaks into cork, wood, paper and other porous materials before it can bond. Switch to a thick or gel type for these.
Glue that stays wet is usually too much glue or a loose fit. Use less and get the parts closer together. Superglue needs a little moisture to set, so very dry air also slows it down.
An accelerator spray sets superglue instantly when you cannot wait or cannot hold a part in place.

guides.title: Supporting resin 3D prints
guides.summary: Tilt the model slightly, support every island layer by layer, and run supports from the plate for a clean resin print.
body: Supports carry the weight of soft, part cured resin and catch islands: parts that start printing before they join the rest of the model. A missed island prints as a failure or a blob.
Automatic supports on a model tipped back steeply, around 45 degrees, often pit the detail on its back. Tilting it back about 10 degrees usually keeps that side clean.
Step through the layers in your slicer and add a support at every new island. A top-down view helps spot tiny ones.
Run supports from the build plate, not from one part of the model to another, so cleanup is easier.
Add extra supports only on heavy parts or places that are easy to clean, such as under a base.
Island-checking software can find any islands you missed. The first model takes a while, but it gets much faster with practice.

guides.title: Taking apart old models and removing old glue
guides.summary: Cut plastic-glue joints, freeze or soak superglue joints, and pick out old putty and glue before rebuilding a model.
body: Plastic glue melts parts together, so those joints rarely come apart cleanly. Cut along the seam with a fine razor saw or a sharp blade rather than pulling. Expect to fill and tidy a little afterwards.
Superglue joints are brittle. A few hours in the freezer, then a firm twist or a tap with a blade along the seam, often pops them. Wrap the model in a cloth so parts do not fly off.
A soak in strong isopropyl alcohol or paint stripper also weakens superglue, especially on metal. Test on a spare plastic or resin part first, since some liquids soften them.
Metal models: once the glue has let go, pull pinned parts slowly with pliers. If a pin will not move, cut it flush and drill it out.
Old putty usually loosens in a stripper soak. Pick it out with a dental pick or blade, working from the edge inward so you do not gouge the model. Hard old putty may need careful carving or filing.
Old white glue and basing sand soften in a long soak in warm water. Scrub the loosened bits off with an old toothbrush.
Clean recesses with a stiff old toothbrush or an ultrasonic cleaner, rinse well, and let every part dry fully before regluing.
Wear gloves and eye protection, work over a tray, and put small parts into labelled tubs as they come off.

guides.title: Texture before priming
guides.summary: Dab crackle or texture paste into recesses before priming for crusty corrosion; it also hides glue spills.
body: After assembly, dab a little crackle or texture paste into recesses, round pipes and wherever rust and grime would gather.
Use only the tip of an old brush and rinse it straight away.
Smooth the edges with a damp brush or finger so the texture fades out instead of ending in a hard line.
It also hides a messy glue drip without sanding. On a large kitbash, a fine gritty paste brushed over joins hides seams and reads as grime once painted.

For pitted rust, mix a fine filler powder or sifted dirt with PVA and a little water and dab it on flat metal. Avoid baking soda, which can react under paint. Add a few cuts and scrapes on big flat areas.
For rough organic shells, mix soft filler putty with plastic glue into a paste and dab it on, adding crackle paint in places. It suits dark, grimy styles and takes drybrushing well.

Glue sand and texture to the base before priming too, and prime model and base together, so no glue or grit lands on finished paint. The primer locks loose grains in and seals twigs and other natural bits that could crumble. Add tufts at the end.
Let it dry fully, then prime over it. The primer seals the texture in, and washes and drybrushing pick it out.

guides.title: Thatched roofs
guides.summary: Fake fur soaked in watered PVA and combed downwards dries hard into convincing thatch for model buildings.
body: Fake fur fabric with a longish pile makes convincing thatch. Cut it to fit each roof panel with scissors, cutting from the back so you do not trim the pile, and leave a little overhang at the eaves.
Soak the fur in a mix of PVA and water until it is wet right through.
Comb the pile downwards with an old comb so it lies like straw, then glue it to the roof, pressing it down along the ridge and edges.
Let it dry hard, ideally overnight, before painting. Trim any straggly ends at the eaves once it has stiffened.
Prime it, base it a mid brown, then drybrush a straw yellow and finish with a light drybrush of pale cream on the top surfaces. A thin dark brown wash under the eaves and along the ridge adds age.
Expect the first try to be rough. Practise on a scrap panel before doing the whole roof.

guides.title: Thinning your paint
guides.summary: Paint from the pot is usually too thick, so thin it on the palette until it flows smoothly but still has strong colour.
body: Thick paint goes on lumpy, shows brush marks, fills fine detail and tears when you brush over half dry areas. Paint that is too thin runs off raised areas, turns into a weak tint and needs coat after coat. Blotches with dark rims, like coffee stains, mean too much water; use a little medium instead.

Use a plain white palette so you can see the paint, and never thin in the pot. Put down a blob as a reserve, then pull some to one side with a damp brush and mix in water a drop at a time. It is easy to add more water and impossible to take it out; if you overdo it, add paint.

Aim for something like thin cream or full fat milk: it flows off the brush, covers without brush marks and does not run into recesses like a wash. Paint thinned for an airbrush is far too thin for brush coats, and some dropper paints are right from the bottle.
Test with a stroke on the palette or your thumb. If it drags or forms ridges, add a touch of water. If it runs and looks weak, add more paint. A swatch over a black mark shows how well it covers.

There is no fixed ratio. Paints differ by colour, range, age and even the weather. Some colours, often reds and oranges, cover badly once thinned and work best nearly neat; if a colour goes streaky, thin it less. Tap water is fine.

Thinned paint may not cover in one go. Let each coat dry and add another. Two or three thin coats give a smooth finish and keep the detail crisp; yellows, reds and whites over a dark primer need the most. Touch the loaded brush on tissue first so it does not flood.

Spreading the paint out matters as much as thinning it. Paint pushed thin across the surface keeps detail; paint left in a pile fills the recesses. Never go back over a coat while it is drying, as that tears it into texture.
For lines that must flow and stay strong, thin with a matching ink instead of water, such as black ink in black paint for recess lines, so you need fewer passes. Ink tints the mix, so test it first.

guides.title: Transporting models
guides.summary: Magnets under the bases and a metal tray in a lidded tub make a cheap, safe carry case.
body: Foam trays work, but models shift in them, which can snap spiky parts and rub paint off raised edges down to the primer. Magnets avoid both problems.
Glue strong magnets under each base. Put a metal baking tray in the bottom of a lidded plastic tub, or glue thin steel sheet inside any sturdy box or old tin. Trays with handles lift straight out.
Tubs stack, so they also work as long term homes for an army.

Cases with removable steel shelves let you put models on the table straight from the shelf. Removable dividers make room for large models. Line the walls with soft fabric, and screw heavy plinths down through the shelf from below.
Foam trays cut to shape suit tall or fragile models. A little tacky putty under bases adds grip on bumpy journeys. Clip cases that grip only the base are kindest to paint but cost more.

To cut your own tray, use foam as deep as the models are tall on a thin firm base sheet. Mark slots about 2.5 by 5 cm for standard infantry with 1 cm of foam between. Saw straight down with a long snap-off blade, and pluck out the waste only after every cut is made.
For vehicles, glue thin foam strips into walls round the models themselves, using the models to hold the walls while the glue sets.
For terrain, leave clip-fit walls and roofs unglued where the joins are hidden, so buildings come apart flat. Test pack the box before you paint.

guides.title: Painting away from home
guides.summary: Pack a small, leak-proof kit and a lamp, protect the room you borrow, and clean up fully before you leave.
body: Pack only the basics: a few brushes, a handful of small paints, glue, brush soap, a small wet palette, tweezers and scissors. Leave the airbrush and spray cans at home and brush on primer instead.
Check travel rules on paints and glues before you fly. Close every pot tightly and pack them in large zip bags, as paint leaks in transit.
Cap the bristles or carry brushes in a tube, or leave your best ones at home. Unbuilt kits travel fine in a bag; painted models need a foam-lined case, since unvarnished paint rubs off.
Room lighting is usually too dim and warm for colour work. A small USB task lamp makes a big difference.

Cover desks and counters with a mat, as knives, solvents and glue can mark furniture. Keep the wet palette sponge damp rather than soaked so it does not spill when moved, and keep it closed between sessions.
Wipe brushes on paper towel or a cloth, not tissue, which sheds fibres into paint. Wash them with soap and lukewarm water after each session.

Before you leave, clean the desk and especially the sink, check the floor for paint flecks and pack everything back in its place. Expect to paint less than you plan; on a short trip it may not be worth it.

guides.title: Working with two-part putty
guides.summary: Mix equal parts of epoxy putty until the colour is even, and keep tools wet so it does not stick.
body: Two-part epoxy putty hardens once its two parts are mixed. Hard, sandable kinds suit gap filling and smooth armour plates. Softer, springy kinds suit faces, cloth and organic shapes, but blend and sand poorly, so joins show.
Cut roughly equal amounts. Discard the strip where the two parts touched in the packet, and any crusty bits, as they have already set and make lumps.

Knead until there are no streaks left; if both parts are a similar colour, knead longer. You get a few hours of working time. The ratio can shift: extra of the soft, sticky part holds finer detail but stays tacky and cures slower, while extra hardener gives a firmer putty that sets faster and keeps crisp edges.

Wet fingers and tools lightly with water, or rub on a little hand cream, so it does not stick. Keep them damp, not dripping, as too much water turns the surface slimy. Uncured putty can irritate skin and eyes, so wash it off your hands after mixing, and wear gloves if your skin reacts.
Rough out the shape while soft; it will look poor at first. Come back every half hour or so. As it firms up it resists the tool and holds sharper detail.
Trim edges with a sharp blade while the putty is still soft or just firm. Fully cured putty cuts and sands rougher and slower. Leave it to cure fully, ideally overnight, before sanding.

Old putty goes lumpy, brittle and stops sticking. Keep it airtight; many keep fresh putty sealed in a bag in the freezer, though results vary, and warm a piece in the hands before use. Use older putty to bulk out hidden areas and fresh putty for surfaces that show.

guides.title: Using an ultrasonic cleaner
guides.summary: Run an ultrasonic cleaner with water, parts in a basket, to clean figures and airbrush parts; never fill it with alcohol.
body: An ultrasonic cleaner shakes dirt loose with sound waves in a small tank of liquid. It lifts mould release and grime off new figures, deep cleans airbrush parts and sculpting tools, helps strip old paint and soaks dried paint off ceramic palettes.

Fill it to the maker's line with fresh tap water; overfilling makes it work less well. A drop of soap can help lift grime, though some soaps stop the cleaning bubbles forming, so see how yours behaves.
Hang parts in a basket rather than resting them on the tank floor, which dulls the vibration. Leave a few centimetres of liquid under and around them, and do not overcrowd the tank.
Warm water shifts oil and grease better, and many tanks warm up as they run. Use a low setting for fragile items if yours has one. Keep airbrush parts to about 15 minutes per run.

Never fill a standard unit with isopropyl alcohol or other flammable liquids, as the tank warms and the fumes can catch. Units rated for flammable liquids exist. Water-washable resin prints can go in with plain water.
Synthetic brushes can go in briefly, but do not leave them soaking. When stripping, use a stripping liquid that is safe for the plastic and safe to warm.
Empty and rinse the tank often, as dirty water pushes grime back into parts and grows mould. If residue survives a cycle, finish with warm soapy water and a soft brush, then dry everything.

guides.title: Clearing clogged dropper bottles
guides.summary: A thin metal pick pushed into the nozzle clears dried paint from a dropper bottle in seconds.
body: Dried paint often plugs the tip of a dropper bottle so nothing comes out when you squeeze.
Keep a thin, smooth metal pick about the size of the nozzle hole, such as a small metal toothpick or a pin.
Push it into the nozzle a couple of times to break the plug, then squeeze gently.
Wipe the pick clean straight away. A dip in water or alcohol removes anything stubborn.
Wiping the nozzle and snapping the cap shut after each use stops most plugs forming.

guides.title: Understanding miniature scales
guides.summary: Millimetre scales are rough figure heights, ratios like 1:56 are true reductions, and doorways show if terrain fits.
body: Millimetre scales such as 28mm describe a rough figure height, not an exact ratio, and makers measure differently, often from foot to eye rather than to the top of the head. A 28mm figure is often 32 to 35mm tall overall.

A ratio such as 1:56 is a true reduction: the real thing is 56 times bigger. To find a ratio, divide the real size by the model size in the same units. A person 1800mm tall shown by a 30mm figure is 1:60.
Rough matches: 28mm is about 1:56, 32mm about 1:48, 20mm about 1:72, 15mm about 1:100, 6mm about 1:285 and 54mm about 1:35.

To size terrain, convert the real size to millimetres and divide by the ratio. A 2 m door at 1:56 is about 36mm. Handy real sizes: a person about 180 cm, a door about 200 cm, a building storey about 300 cm.

Doorways are the best check. Stand one of your based figures by a door or window before committing to terrain. A door around 35 to 37mm tall lets based 28mm figures through; a 28mm door looks too small.

Kits from other hobbies can work: a 1:48 car or O gauge railway buildings suit 28 to 32mm figures, and about 1:64 sits close to 28mm. HO railway at 1:87 is too small for most, though it can suit 25mm.

Heroic scale figures have chunky heads, hands and weapons; true scale figures are realistically proportioned. Figures have also grown over the years, so old and new ranges, or two makers' 28mm, can look mismatched. Match new models to what you have.
In a diorama, smaller-scale pieces at the back and larger ones at the front fake extra depth.

guides.title: Making squad models look different
guides.summary: Head swaps, new hand items, gear and small pose changes stop repeated sculpts in a squad looking identical.
body: Lay the models out and decide what to keep and what to change on each one, so no two match. Keep the strongest pose as the base.
Swap heads between kits. A bare head instead of a helmet, a scar or an older face changes a figure's character quickly.
Change what the hands hold. Cut a hand off at the wrist with a sharp knife and glue on a different hand or weapon. Keep the old hand for another model.
Where a part is moulded onto the body, pare it away in small cuts until the joint is clear. Hide any scars or leftover grips with a pouch or another small bit.
Turn heads and arms to follow the action, such as looking down a pointed weapon. A small angle change makes the same sculpt read as a different moment.
With two boxes of the same kit, mix the sculpts so each group gets one of each pose rather than two matching sets.
