guides.title: Using inks
guides.summary: Inks are thin, strongly coloured and see-through, so they tint what is underneath rather than cover it.
body: Paint is solid pigment in a binder and usually hides the undercoat after a few coats. Many inks are dyes in liquid. They flow almost like water and stay see-through however many coats you put on. Some inks are made semi-opaque or opaque and cover large areas fast.

Ink is very strongly coloured, so a little goes a long way and you usually thin it a lot with water or medium. A careless stroke stains a finished area, so test on a spare piece first. Most inks dry satin to gloss rather than matt.

Tint an undercoat or a painted texture with ink. Over a zenithal undercoat, rough leather or cloth, you get strong colour while the light and dark below still show through. Ink flows well through an airbrush for this.

Heavily thinned ink makes a good glaze by brush or airbrush. Over matt paint, ink in the shadows leaves a slight sheen, which adds a second kind of contrast. Matt varnish takes it off if you do not want it.

Make your own wash from ink, water, a little flow improver and matt medium. The strong colour sinks into recesses well. For deep hollows a brush cannot reach, drip ink in from a dropper and tilt the model so it runs into every corner. Washes look blotchy on big smooth areas with no texture to catch in.
Thin a weak top colour such as red or yellow with a matching ink instead of water. It flows just as well but adds colour rather than diluting it. Too much ink makes the coat glossy and see-through.
Tint metal: mix coloured ink into silver for a coloured metallic, or glaze it over dry silver. Black ink darkens silver without killing the sparkle the way paint does.
Stir a drop of ink into stringy glue or clear water effects to colour them while keeping them see-through.
keywords: is ink the same as wash

guides.title: Real objects in scenes
guides.summary: Cut real items into a display and repaint them so they match the painted world around them.
body: Everyday objects such as brushes, cutters, pots or a cutting mat can become part of a display scene.
Cut them cleanly where they meet the scene. Very tough items may need power tools, so get help with those.
Harden anything soft before painting. Soaking brush bristles in super glue sets them solid.
Glue any moving parts in place so nothing shifts later.
Small odds and ends work as scatter too: brush tip covers as pipes, bent paperclips as twisted metal, stripped wire as cables and dried tea leaves as coarse ground. Fix them with thin super glue.
Repaint everything, even items that already look right, so they share the painted finish of the rest of the scene. Priming it all together helps it read as one.
Measure and paint any grids, labels or small text carefully. Neat detail copied by hand is what sells the effect.

guides.title: Varnish changing your colours
guides.summary: Gloss deepens colours and matt dulls them, so choose the sheen that keeps the look you painted.
body: Varnish gives every paint the same sheen, and sheen changes how colour looks. Gloss makes colours darker and richer; matt makes them flatter and more muted. The shift is most noticeable if you mixed paints with different finishes.

Gloss is fine for the wash and transfer stage, but it can make pale armour look dull or muddy. Finish with satin or matt to bring the highlights back. Roughly four parts matt to one part gloss gives a satin.
A very flat matt suits a dusty, gritty military look. Skip it on bright reds or anything you want to keep vivid.

Airbrushed paint often dries flatter and duller than brushed paint, because it lands as fine droplets. A light satin or gloss coat brings much of the depth back. Judge colours once dry, not while wet.
A satin coat can also lift a model that looks dull and over-matt.
Matt varnish kills the shine of metallics. Give metal areas a brushed gloss coat afterwards to keep them bright.
Models that get handled are worth a matt coat even with a small shift. Display pieces on a plinth rarely need varnish. Try a new varnish on a spare painted part first.

guides.title: Varnishing models
guides.summary: Varnish protects paint from handling and sets the finish, with tough gloss under matt or satin to hide the shine.
body: Varnish is a clear coat that protects paint and sets how shiny the model looks. If you game with your models, varnish them, base included, as handling rubs paint off edges. Display pieces are often left bare, as varnish can shift subtle colours. Use varnish made for models; furniture varnish can tint.

Gloss is shiny and hardest wearing, and suits metal and wet looks. Matt is flat and suits cloth and skin but can deaden metals and bright colours. Satin sits between. Do not leave a whole model gloss or satin, as shine fights your highlights. Finish matt, then brush gloss back onto gems, eyes and wet effects.

For a tough finish, coat the whole model in slightly thinned gloss, then matt or satin over it. Over gloss, matt usually needs two thin coats. A mix of about three parts very flat matt to one part satin is tougher than pure matt and still looks flat.

Wait until every layer of paint is fully dry, not just touch dry. Dust the model with a soft dry brush or a puff of air first; fibres and dust get sealed in for good. Keep loose static grass away from wet varnish.

Brush on: shake well, pour some into a palette well, and coat the model with a large soft brush like an all over wash, moving pools away before they clog detail. Never go back over an area as it dries, as that tears the forming skin.

Spray: shake the can for longer than it says, test on card, hold it about 20 to 30 cm away and sweep past in thin passes. Cold or damp air, much above 50 percent humidity, gives a white frosty finish. Turn the can upside down and spray until clear afterwards. Check it is varnish, not a similar primer.

Airbrush: put two or three drops of thinner in the cup first so varnish cannot dry at the nozzle. Spray thin, even coats; if it pools, stop adding varnish and push it thin with air alone. Let it dry, ten minutes to an hour depending on humidity, before a second coat. Never leave varnish sitting in the cup.

Varnish also works as a save point part way through. Seal delicate glazes, and a later slip can be wiped off with water without lifting them. Matt varnish takes paint well; gloss is less grippy. Many painters add metallics after the last matt coat. Leave it a day before heavy handling.

guides.title: Varnish dulling metallics
guides.summary: Matt varnish turns metal grey and gloss looks wet, so varnish before the metals or put shine back afterwards.
body: Matt varnish over metallic paint flattens the shine so steel looks grey and gold goes dull. A strong matt removes every bit of gloss. Gloss keeps metal reflective but can look wet.

Option one: varnish first, then paint the metallics over the top so they keep their shine. A matt coat at this point also evens out the patchy sheen left by washes and mixed paints. Brush it on thinly, and do not miss spikes and tips or they stay shiny.

Option two: after varnishing, thin the original metallic until slightly runny and brush one coat over the flat central areas that catch the light, stopping short of recesses. Then add a paler metallic on the top edges, the very centre and a few fresh chips.

Option three: brush slightly thinned gloss or satin onto the flat and raised metal surfaces only, keeping it out of recesses so corners stay darker. On a model that is handled a lot this also adds protection.

If candy or tinted metallic armour looks too shiny and toy-like, mix a satin of about four parts matt to one part gloss and spray it over. Painting leather and cloth very matt next to it adds contrast.
If every colour, not just the metal, looks dull after varnishing, the matt coat went on too thick. Use thinner coats next time, and repaint the worst areas.
A very flat varnish mixed about half and half with clear medium gives a near-matt finish that keeps colours lively.
If you airbrush varnish, thin it with water only. Some thinners add shine.

guides.title: Swapping weapons
guides.summary: Cut weapons at a band or ridge, fit the new one straight, and hide the join with putty or a colour change.
body: Cut at an existing bar, ring or notch so the new part lines up and the join looks designed. For a hand swap, cut along a cuff, bracer or glove edge so the seam reads as the edge of the clothing.
If a new weapon will not sit in the hand, there is usually too much plastic behind it. File a little away, test the fit, and repeat. Small cuts can be added to; one big cut cannot be undone.
File both cut faces smooth and check the parts are straight from several sides before the glue sets.

To fit a new weapon or a brass rod pole into a fist, cut the old one out, drill through slightly oversize so you can adjust the angle, slide the new haft through and fill the gap with putty. Keep your fingers out from behind the drill.

To put a new blade or axe head on an existing haft, cut both cleanly, drill a short hole in each with a pin vice and glue in a short piece of paper clip. It is far less likely to snap than glue alone.
A slow setting glue such as dissolved sprue paste gives time to nudge a weapon level as it starts to grab.
Shave off small bolts or rings if you want a cleaner look, or add a thin ring of plastic rod around a shaft to hide a join. Different coloured plastics look odd until primed.
When painting, put a colour change right at the join so the eye reads it as a design line, not a seam.

guides.title: Using a wet palette
guides.summary: A wet palette made from a tray, damp paper towel and baking paper keeps thinned paint workable for hours.
body: A palette is where you thin paint, test it and take excess off the brush. Paint straight from pot to model skips all of that.

On a dry palette, thinned acrylic skins over quickly and you end up painting with thick, half dry paint. A wet palette keeps it fresh and the same consistency for hours, which helps blending and glazing and wastes less paint. Keep two drops of one colour side by side: plain for crisp edges, thinned for layers.

To make one, fold paper towel into a shallow tray or lidded tub, about four layers, and soak it until almost floating. A kitchen sponge works too. Use plenty of water so it does not dry out mid session.

Lay non-waxed baking parchment on top and press it flat, smoothing out bubbles. Paint sits on the paper and draws moisture up from below. Pour off any water pooling on top. Wax paper will not work, as it blocks the moisture.
A ready-made one seals better and lasts longer, but the homemade version works well. Kitchen parchment often beats the paper that comes with kits for thin miniature paints.
Keep paint in small, compact blobs, as spread out paint dries faster. With the lid on between sessions, paint often keeps for a day or more.
Keep a dry white tile as well. Washes and inks behave poorly on a wet palette, paint for sharp edge highlights can turn too runny, and metallic flakes can get into the sponge and taint other colours.
You do not need a wet palette to paint well. Any smooth, hard surface works; the wet one just buys time, and a dry palette can be quicker for fast speed painting.

guides.title: Wet palette problems
guides.summary: Stop curling paper, watery paint and mould with the right water level, blotted droplets, clean water and regular cleaning.
body: Baking paper works well. Some supplied membranes are not porous enough for hobby paints. Cut the paper smaller than the sponge so it cannot lift at the edges, soak it so both sides are wet, and smooth out air bubbles and creases. Replace it often; worn paper sheds fibres into your paint.

Keep the water level with the top of the sponge and top it up at the edge of the sheet as it evaporates. If paint turns watery or spreads, the sponge is too wet; squeeze some out. If paint still dries fast, the sponge has dried or the paper has lifted.

Blot every droplet on top. Stray water is a main cause of over-thinned paint. Press a paper towel on any puddle so it cannot run into other colours, keep paint in compact blobs, and stir paint that separates before loading.

A closed lid keeps paint usable for a day or two, but if paint soaks up water overnight and turns runny, vent the lid slightly or drill a few small holes. In a very humid room, waxed paper slows the water. In a very dry one, a humidifier helps.

Mould can appear within one to three days, as black, green or blue-green spots. Use distilled or boiled and cooled water, and put a drop of washing-up liquid, a few drops of hydrogen peroxide or a palette anti-mould additive in the water. A coil of bare copper wire helps, but test it, as too much metal can stain paint.
Keep bleach and alcohol out of the water. Bleach dulls colours and alcohol makes paint dry much faster. Never keep brushes inside the palette; damp warps handles and loosens the bristle glue.

Once a week, or as soon as mould shows, empty the water, throw away the paper, and wash the tray and lid in hot soapy water. Deep clean the sponge in boiling water or a one to one mix of vinegar and water, then rinse well. Synthetic sponges resist mould better than old yellow foam or paper towel.
Do not leave a sealed palette for weeks. If you will not paint for a while, empty it and leave it open to dry.

guides.title: Setting up a wet palette well
guides.summary: Keep the water level with the sponge, pick the right paper and keep paint dots compact so the palette stays useful.
body: Fill with water until it is level with, or just above, the top of the sponge. Top it up through the session by squirting water into the edge of the sponge from a small squeeze bottle, not onto the paper. Bright, hot lamps dry it faster.
A sponge alone can hold its water so the paper dries out. Two or three sheets of paper towel over it pass water up evenly. In a very dry room, stack two sponges or use a thicker one.

Cut the paper clearly smaller than the sponge, about a centimetre or two clear on every side. It grows when wet, and paper creeping up the walls dries out and wrinkles. It curls until both sides are wet, then settles; smooth out every bubble.

Plain baking parchment works. In a humid room, a slightly waxy paper lets less water through and stops paint going runny. Wrinkles, bubbles and running paint all point to too much water, so blot stray drops off the paper.

Put paints down as small, compact dots along one side and do not thin those. Pull paint into a new spot to thin or mix it. Fresh paint is as thick as from the pot; the palette does not thin it for you.
Roll the brush on the paper to shape the tip and shed excess paint. Keep a paper towel beside the palette to dab off a brush that is too wet.
Put the lid on during any break, even a short one, to keep paint wet and dust out. Overnight, leave it slightly open; sealed tight, paint keeps drawing in water and is watery by morning.
Swap the paper often and rinse or replace the sponge regularly to stop mould. If both dry out, soak them in hot water for about ten minutes.
keywords: how to use a wet palette

guides.title: What acrylic paint is made of
guides.summary: Acrylic paint is pigment, binder and water, and too much water breaks the binder and causes tide marks.
body: The binder is acrylic medium. It sets into a tough film as the water evaporates, which is why acrylics dry fast and cannot be rewetted once dry.
The solvent is water, so the paint thins and cleans up with water. It has little smell and is gentler on skin and lungs than oils or enamels, which suits indoor painting.
Pigment gives the colour. Most hobby paints blend several pigments; artist paints often list single pigments, opacity and finish on the label.
Acrylics grip plastic, metal, resin and porous materials like cork and foam, come in finishes from flat matt to gloss, and mix freely to make new colours.
Add too much water and there is not enough binder to hold the pigment together. The result is tide marks, blotches and coffee ring stains.
For very thin mixes, use some medium instead of only water, so the binder keeps up with the pigment. Other mediums slow drying or add texture.
Hobby paints contain additives so a range behaves evenly. Artist paints vary more from colour to colour.

guides.title: Which tools to upgrade first
guides.summary: Upgrade what holds you back: light first, then a good detail brush, a wet palette, magnification, then an airbrush.
body: Upgrade what holds you back right now, not what looks impressive. If you cannot see the detail, or the paint will not go where you want it, fix that first.
First, light. A bright daylight lamp over the desk shows true colour and fine detail. It helps more than any brush.
Second, one good detail brush. A quality brush with a sharp point that holds its shape makes eyes and edges far easier. Keep the old ones for rough jobs like drybrushing.
Third, a wet palette. Paint stays workable for hours, thins evenly and wastes less. You can make one from a tray, a sponge and baking paper.
Fourth, magnification and comfort. Head magnifiers or a lens lamp help tired eyes. A good chair, a rest for your wrists and a model holder that keeps fingers off the paint help long sessions.
Next come sharp clippers, good files and an extractor or booth if you spray indoors. Add more paints only for the schemes you actually paint often.
An airbrush comes later for most people, once brushwork is steady. It speeds up priming, base coats and smooth fades, but needs a compressor, cleaning time and practice.
Leave rare paints and special tools until you know you need them. Many painters do their best work with a short kit used well.

guides.title: When a wash will and will not work
guides.summary: Washes suit deep detail over mid-tone colours and struggle on big smooth areas and very pale or dark bases.
body: Washes work best on sharp, deep detail such as fur, hair, chainmail and textured surfaces.

Large smooth areas such as cloaks and bare skin tend to collect tide marks and blotches. On layer-printed scenery, washes run along the print ridges and stain in stripes; airbrush thinned one-coat paint into the shadows instead.

Over white or very pale colours, even a weak wash stains the whole surface, and covering the stains takes many coats that build texture. Shade pale colours with an oil wash or a fine line of thinned paint in the recesses instead. Over very dark colours, a wash barely shows.
The best results come over mid-tone reds, blues, browns and similar. A wash will not fix the wrong base colour: a green wash over pale blue just leaves green in every recess. Repaint instead.

Washes differ. Very runny ones flow into cracks well but barely tint raised areas and can dry glossy, so layers over them show. Thicker ones tint more and stay workable longer. A wash that dries satin-matt like your paints is easiest to layer over. Opaque inks cover paint rather than shading it, so check the type first.
Heavy dark washes darken and dull every colour. Dilute black and other dark inks before using them on most models.
A wash darkens every recess equally regardless of light direction. If the model went too dark or flat, re-layer the midtone over the raised areas, leaving the wash in the recesses, then highlight.
A wash plus a quick drybrush is fast and ideal for bases and gaming pieces, but rarely enough on its own where quality matters.

guides.title: Wire details
guides.summary: Thin wire makes lightning bolts, energy arcs and tiny candles that add life to a model or scene.
body: Lightning: bend several short pieces of thin, soft wire into random zigzags. The thinner the wire, the more convincing the bolt.
Drill a small hole in the barrel, staff tip or hand where the bolt starts, glue the main wire in and add the extra zigzags so it branches.
Paint it white at the core fading out to a bright colour, and add a soft glow of that colour on nearby surfaces.

Candles: cut wire or thin rod about 1 to 1.5 mm across into pieces 3 to 6 mm long, at slightly different heights. Glue them upright in a cluster on a table, altar or ledge, or push them into small balls of putty.

For wax drips, dab white glue thinned with a very little water down the sides with a toothpick. Let it dry and add more on the same spots for fatter, longer drips. A short piece of fine thread stiffened with super glue makes the wick.
Paint them off white with an orange yellow tip, and glaze a soft warm glow on the surface round them.

guides.title: Zenithal priming
guides.summary: Prime dark, then spray a light colour from above so the model starts with its lighting already in place.
body: Prime the whole model black or a dark colour. Then spray white or pale grey straight down from above. Turn the model so every upward facing surface gets some, but keep the spray coming from overhead.

Recesses and undersides stay dark, so the model already looks lit from above. Stop once the tops are white: piling on coats leaves a chalky surface that makes later paint fuzzy. White over black still reads greyish, so brush heavy white onto the face, shoulders or other focal points for extra punch.

For a front-lit piece, spray mainly from about 45 degrees above the front, then add a light dusting from straight above. Photograph the result under your lamp and keep it by you. It shows where highlights belong, even if opaque paint will cover the undercoat.

Thin one-coat paints, glazes and washes over this undercoat pick up the light and dark for free; a thin satin varnish first helps them flow evenly. Thin other base colours until they stop streaking but still let the undercoat show. Finish with your usual washes, highlights and drybrushing.

You can spray in colour too: dark, mid then light shades of one colour, each from a higher angle. A dark brown prime with warm pale tones above suits one-coat paints. For quick metal, spray silver or gold from above over black or deep red. For fur, spray black, a mid colour from below, then off white from above.

A top-down spray wipes out the thin dark lines between upward facing parts, such as armour panels. Put them back with a thin dark line or recess wash. If white reached the undersides, turn the model over and mist a little dark back in. If a big part blocked the spray, re-spray white there or spray that part separately.

An airbrush gives the most control and lets you add passes on heads and focal points. Spray cans can go speckled and grainy, especially when nearly empty, so use a fresh, well shaken can in short bursts. With neither, drybrush white over a dark prime in several light passes, keeping the brightest paint on top.

Some white inks spray smoothly but never fully harden, so they lift under washes or one-coat paints. Test first, or use a white acrylic paint thinned for the airbrush. Skip zenithal on models that will be almost all metal or lit by glows or moonlight.
